items.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
items.summary: Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems. NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety […]
items.content:
Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems.

NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research, providing $50 million in accelerated computing access through BOLD at the University of Oxford, SOFAIR at UCL and Imperial College London. 

In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize, joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges.

 

Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

 

Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK

In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households. 

Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems.

Healthcare 

In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients.

Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence. 

Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed. 

Apian, SYNLAB and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care.  

Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback. 

Smart Cities

On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K. 

Digital Jersey, Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services.

Financial Services

In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions. 

Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling.

Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM, a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure. 

NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations. 

Quantum

Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift. 

Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems.

Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. 

Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

items.title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
items.summary: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make […]
items.content:
Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently.

Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive.

Software partners including ABA Technology, Akila, Galene AI, Honeywell Technologies, K2K, Linker Vision, Milestone, Onetera, ThinkDeep and Younite are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services.

Video courtesy of Linker Vision.

NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere.

Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

 

In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region, K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management.

Video courtesy of K2K.

In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or, Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale.

Video courtesy of Akila.

In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials.

In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI, Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data. 

At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges, Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce.

In the Nordics, Younite is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival. 

These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw. 

Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations.

Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies.

Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities

For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents.

System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations.

Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow.

Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona.

items.title: Equitable Intelligence in Practice: A Fairness Audit of Open Large Language Models for Library Reference Services
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.18935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As libraries explore large language models (LLMs) as a scalable layer for reference services, a core fairness question follows: can LLM-based services support all patrons fairly, regardless of demographic identity? LLMs could broaden access to information assistance, but they may also reproduce societal biases embedded in their training data and undermine libraries' commitments to impartial service. In this chapter, we apply an evaluation protocol that combines diagnostic classification, which detects systematic differences between responses, with linguistic analysis, which helps interpret them. Across three widely used open models (Llama-3.1 8B, Gemma-2 9B, and Ministral 8B), we find no compelling evidence of systematic differentiation by race/ethnicity, and only minor evidence of sex-linked differentiation in one model and one setting. We discuss implications for equitable AI adoption in libraries and the importance of ongoing monitoring in aligning LLM-based services with social justice goals.
items.author: Haining Wang, Jason Clark, Angelica Pe\~na

items.title: The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.02753v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Python programs pay for their imports at every process start, a cost that is invisible in steady-state benchmarks but dominant for command-line tools, test workers, and serverless cold starts. Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) on largely anecdotal evidence. We measure the import cost of the 500 most-downloaded PyPI packages, every quarterly release since mid-2021, under six CPython versions (3.9-3.14) on two platforms (Apple M5/macOS and Intel Xeon/Linux): all 66,816 package-version-interpreter cells, plus the release histories of 65 distributions beneath shared namespaces, and targeted experiments that isolate individual effects. Import cost is heavily skewed (median 12.3 ms, 99th percentile 400 ms on macOS). For the median package, 68-79% of import time is spent importing the standard library, while third-party dependencies are the largest component in the slowest decile. The cold first import is almost entirely bytecode compilation on Linux, but on macOS 67% of the cold penalty remains when bytecode is precompiled: we trace it to the operating system's security assessment of each new native library, which every fresh environment pays again. A package's own import code grows by a median 4.0-5.0% per year; resolving dependencies as of each release raises the median trend of the total from 1.8% to 3.0-3.4% per year. CPython 3.14 executes package code faster than 3.9 but imports more and slower standard-library modules, a net 1.16x slowdown on macOS and 1.07x on Linux. What dependents actually import from a package costs a median 1.0x its top-level import but 10.9-13.4x at the 90th percentile. Global lazy mode makes import statements essentially free and breaks 10 packages. Harness, analysis code, and dataset are public.
items.author: Trinath Sai Subhash Reddy Pittala

items.title: FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.11308v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability.
  We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,649 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 49 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.91%. This cost-reduction trend holds across different LLM backends and repeated runs.
items.author: Yiming Zhang, Jiangrong Wu, Yuhong Nan

items.title: Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.04058v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to port scientific codes across heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) programming models, such as translating CUDA to OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos or SYCL. However, current evaluations use compilation success, token-level similarity, or developer-written tests from static benchmarks, which cannot reliably ensure behavioral correctness. We present Kaizen, a metamorphic fuzzing and differential testing framework for evaluating the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code. Kaizen uses metamorphic fuzzing via source-code mutation to generate semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing to explore behavioral diversity, and differential testing to expose semantic divergences between original and translated applications that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results. We evaluate Kaizen on CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 scientific applications from seven domains using three fine-tuned LLMs at kernel-level and full-program granularity. Our evaluation reveals that (1) compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; (2) LLM-translated programs exhibit systematic compile-time error patterns, with nine categories for kernel-level translation and 27 for full-program translation; (3) semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose; and (4) full-program translation is substantially harder than kernel-level translation. These findings highlight the need for correctness-oriented evaluation of LLM-assisted HPC code translations.
items.author: Oscar Ludwig, Ninad Anklesaria, Zheming Jin, Swaroop Pophale, Kausar Moshood, Christian J. DeVore, Brandon Gill, Cassius Villareal, Keita Teranishi, Manish Motwani

items.title: WebCQ: Cooperative Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scalable Web GUI Testing
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.22502v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL)-based techniques have shown promise for GUI testing. However, as the complexity of modern GUI software increases, existing MARL-based approaches (e.g., MARG and Fastbot) struggle to scale due to the inherent limitations of their underlying tabular reinforcement learning algorithms. This limits their applicability to large-scale commercial GUI software, especially web applications with vast state spaces and many interactive elements. To fill this gap, we propose WebCQ, a novel MARL-based approach for scalable web GUI testing. WebCQ incorporates QTRAN for multi-agent coordination and a lightweight synchronization mechanism, allowing it to work under asynchronous web testing scenarios. It extracts semantic and exploration features for each UI event to form an action vector. This vector is concatenated with the current state vector and fed into the policy network, enabling DQN-based decision making within a dynamic action space. We evaluated WebCQ on eight large-scale commercial websites. Under the same time budget and agent count, WebCQ explored 33.3% more states and executed 42.2% more unique actions than MARG, while triggering more failures on six of the eight websites under test. It also demonstrated strong scalability, maintaining higher action throughput during 20-hour experiments, and achieving greater performance improvements as the number of agents increased. These results show that WebCQ overcomes key limitations of existing MARL-based approaches, providing a scalable and effective solution to enhance modern web GUI testing.
items.author: Yujia Fan, Sinan Wang, Zebang Fei, Yao Qin, Huaxuan Li, Yepang Liu

items.title: Porting Declarative UI to HarmonyOS: A Heuristic-guided Approach for lightweight LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.07085v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As an emerging operating system, HarmonyOS has a significant demand for software migration, where the User Interface (UI) translation accounts for a critical link. However, recent UI development has shifted to declarative paradigms, e.g., Kotlin Jetpack Compose (KJC) for Android, SwiftUI for iOS, and ArkUI for HarmonyOS, making prior translation approaches inapplicable because they target either backend logic or legacy imperative UIs. Thus, related research is limited.
  To systematically evaluate KJC/SwiftUI-to-ArkUI migration, we build a parallel benchmark of 100 KJC and 100 SwiftUI files across eight scenarios, plus 52 real-world UI pages from nine open-source apps. Evaluating nine direct-translation setups (including diverse LLMs and agents), we find Compilation Success Rate (CSR) spans 0.00%-35.00%; common strategies (reference screenshots and compiler-guided repair) lift capable setups to 94.00%-99.00% CSR but fail on lightweight LLMs. By manually analyzing a 3,102-sample subset, deriving a regular-expression pattern for each failure family, and applying these patterns to generalize the resulting taxonomy to the full 29,593-sample set, we find residual errors rooted in (1) broken structure, (2) nonexistent APIs, and (3) missing resources (e.g., colors, strings, and icons).
  Accordingly, we propose ArkTrans, a declarative UI translation framework that maps these roots to deterministic structure supply, ArkUI knowledge and resource reference injection via a demonstration example, and iterative repair targeting residual errors, via four steps: Metadata Extraction, Skeleton Construction, LLM-driven Translation, and Compiler-Guided Iterative Repair. With Qwen3.6-27B, ArkTrans raises CSR from 0.00% to 70.00% on KJC and 64.00% on SwiftUI, achieving strong visual fidelity, and attains 65.63%/80.00% CSR on real-world pages, far outperforming the best common strategy at lower token cost.
items.author: Kunwu Zheng, Pengyu Xue, Zhen Yang, Tianlong Chen, Xiran Lyu, Peishi Lai, Mengying Zhao, Junjie Chen, Yutian Tang, Huizhi Zhang, Xianhang Li, Linhao Wu, Chengyi Wang

items.title: CUJBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Browser-to-Backend Failure Diagnosis
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.23455v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated failure diagnosis requires correlating browser-visible symptoms with backend observability signals, yet existing benchmarks do not evaluate this cross-modal reasoning task. Constructing one is non-trivial: multi-modal failure scenarios are costly to annotate, and live-environment capture introduces stochasticity that makes cross-run agent comparison unreliable. We present CUJBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark to combine browser-visible failure evidence with backend observability in a diagnostic framing. CUJBench addresses annotation cost through an LLM-assisted generation pipeline with a multi-agent review loop and a three-layer annotation scheme, producing 87 labeled scenarios across five fault families, and ensures reproducibility by packaging each failure as a deterministic multi-modal snapshot with a fixed tool interface. Evaluating six LLMs under retrieval, browser-only, and full-toolset baselines, the benchmark yields an overall accuracy of 21.6% with a ceiling of 52.5%, well below saturation. Contrary to expectation, browser-only agents outperform full-toolset agents in aggregate, with expanded evidence access inducing unfocused exploration rather than improved synthesis. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-modal synthesis as the primary bottleneck: agents retrieve the decisive evidence but fail to attribute it correctly, a failure that persists across all six models and that model scale and richer tool access alone cannot resolve.
items.author: Haoming Meng

items.title: SpecSyn: LLM-based Synthesis and Refinement of Formal Specifications for Real-world Program Verification
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.21570v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Program verification is a formal technique to rigorously ensure the correctness and fault-freeness of software systems. However, constructing comprehensive interprocedural specifications for full verification obligations is time-consuming and labor-intensive, giving rise to automated specification generation approaches. Despite the significant advancements in these approaches brought by Large Language Models (LLMs), existing LLM-empowered approaches still suffer from significant limitations: they lack effective strategies for handling sizable input programs, and are typically equipped with no mechanisms to evaluate and guarantee the strength of the generated specifications. The limitations impair their ability to extract precise specifications from real-world complicated programs to support the verification of target properties, thereby hindering the applicability of existing approaches in verification tasks on real-world programs. To remedy this gap, we propose SpecSyn, a novel LLM-based specification generation method. SpecSyn first decomposes the input program into individual segments, which are handled respectively by the subsequent iterative specification generation process. Innovatively, we incorporate into the process a specification refinement mechanism based on semantic-non-equivalent program mutations and variant discrimination, assessing and enhancing the semantic strength of the generated specifications. Extensive experiments show that SpecSyn maintains high precision over 90% and outstanding recall over 75%, significantly outperforming existing LLM-based approaches. In further evaluations, SpecSyn successfully handles 1022 out of 1421 target properties for open-source programs, proving its applicability on real-world program verification tasks.
items.author: Lezhi Ma, Shangqing Liu, Yi Li, Qiong Wu, Han Wang, Jiawan Wang, Lei Bu

items.title: Developer Experience with AI Coding Agents: HTTP Behavioral Signatures in Documentation Portals
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.02544v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The rapid adoption of AI coding agents and AI assistant web services is fundamentally changing how developers discover, consume, and interact with technical documentation. This paper studies that transformation across three interconnected dimensions: documentation accessibility, content analytics, and feedback systems. We present an empirical study of HTTP request fingerprints from nine AI coding agents (Aider, Antigravity, Claude Code, Cline, Cursor, Junie, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot (VS Code agent mode), and Windsurf) and six AI assistant services (ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, Google NotebookLM, MistralAI, and Perplexity) accessing a live developer documentation endpoint, revealing identifiable behavioral signatures in HTTP runtime environments, pre-fetch strategies, User-Agent strings, and header patterns. Our study shows that AI agent access compresses multi-page navigation into a single or two requests, making traditional engagement metrics - session depth, time-on-page, click path, and bounce rate - unreliable indicators of actual documentation consumption. We discuss practical adaptations for developer portal teams, including tokenomics-aware documentation design, adoption of emerging machine-readable standards (AGENTS.md, llms.txt, skill.md, agent-permissions.json), MCP server-based feedback channels, and analytics instrumentation for AI referral traffic.
items.author: Oleksii Borysenko

items.title: Debt Behind the AI Boom: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of AI-Generated Code in the Wild
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.28592v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI coding assistants are now widely used in software development. Software developers increasingly integrate AI-generated code into their codebases to improve productivity. Prior studies have shown that AI-generated code may contain code quality issues under controlled settings. However, we still know little about the real-world impact of AI-generated code on software quality and maintenance after it is introduced into production repositories. In other words, it remains unclear whether such issues are quickly fixed or persist and accumulate over time as technical debt. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale empirical study on the technical debt introduced by AI coding assistants in the wild. To achieve that, we built a dataset of 302.6k verified AI-authored commits from 6,299 GitHub repositories, covering five widely used AI coding assistants. For each commit, we run static analysis before and after the change to precisely attribute which code smells, correctness issues, and security issues the AI introduced. We then track each introduced issue from the introducing commit to the latest repository revision to study its lifecycle. Our results show that we identified 484,366 distinct issues, and that code smells are by far the most common type, accounting for 89.3% of all issues. Between 7.5% and 14.8% of each assistant's commits introduce at least one issue. More importantly, 22.7% of tracked AI-introduced issues still survive at the latest version of the repository. These findings show that AI-generated code can introduce long-term maintenance costs into real software projects and highlight the need for stronger quality assurance in AI-assisted development.
items.author: Yue Liu, Ratnadira Widyasari, Yanjie Zhao, Ivana Clairine Irsan, Junkai Chen, David Lo

items.title: yProv4DV: Filling the visualization gap in reproducible research workflows
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.20437v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While results visualization is a critical phase to the communication of new academic results, plots are frequently shared without the complete combination of code, input data, execution context and outputs required to independently reproduce the resulting figures. Existing reproducibility solutions tend to focus on computational pipelines or workflow management systems, not covering script-based visualization practices commonly used by researchers and practitioners. Additionally, the minimalist nature of current Python data visualization libraries tend to speed up the creation of images, disincentivizing users from spending time integrating additional tools into these short scripts. This paper proposes yProv4DV, a library lightweight designed to enable reproducible data visualization scripts through the use of provenance information, minimizing the necessity for code modifications. Through a single call, users can track inputs, outputs and source code files, enabling saving and full reproducibility of their data visualization software. As a result, this library fills a gap in reproducible research workflows by addressing the reproducibility of plots in scientific publications.
items.author: Gabriele Padovani, Sandro Fiore

items.title: SACS: A Code Smell Dataset using Semi-automatic Generation Approach
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.15342v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code smell is a great challenge in software refactoring, which indicates latent design or implementation flaws that may degrade the software maintainability and evolution. Over the past of decades, the research on code smell has received extensive attention. Especially the researches applied machine learning-technique have become a popular topic in recent studies. However, one of the biggest challenges to apply machine learning-technique is the lack of high-quality code smell datasets. Manually constructing such datasets is extremely labor-intensive, as identifying code smells requires substantial development expertise and considerable time investment. In contrast, automatically generated datasets, while scalable, frequently exhibit reduced label reliability and compromised data quality. To overcome this challenge, in this study, we explore a semi-automatic approach to generate a code smell dataset with high quality data samples. Specifically, we first applied a set of automatic generation rules to produce candidate smelly samples. We then employed multiple metrics to group the data samples into an automatically accepted group and a manually reviewed group, enabling reviewers to concentrate their efforts on ambiguous samples. Furthermore, we established structured review guidelines and developed a annotation tool to support the manual validation process. Based on the proposed semi-automatic generation approach, we created an open-source code smell dataset, SACS, covering three widely studied code smells: Long Method, Large Class, and Feature Envy. Each code smell category includes over 10,000 labeled samples. This dataset could provide a large-scale and publicly available benchmark to facilitate future studies on code smell detection and automated refactoring.
items.author: Hanyu Zhang, Tomoji Kishi

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Fine-Tuning in Code-Related Tasks
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.15094v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have proven highly effective in automating software engineering tasks, bridging natural language and code semantics to achieve notable results in code generation and summarization. However, their scale incurs substantial computational costs, making full fine-tuning impractical. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like QLoRA enable efficient specialization with lower resource demands. Recent studies show QLoRA-optimized Large Code Models (LCMs) perform strongly across diverse tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this effectiveness persists when a single model is QLoRA fine-tuned for multiple code-related tasks. The interaction between Multi-task fine-tuning and QLoRA optimization, and how transfer learning affects correctness and quality of generated artifacts, remains largely unexplored. We investigate Multi-task QLoRA fine-tuning --- a representative parameter-efficient method from the LoRA family --- across three representative tasks: code generation, translation, and summarization. We evaluate functional correctness through execution-based and similarity-based metrics, complemented by comprehensive code quality analysis--an aspect largely overlooked in prior work. Our findings show that Multi-task QLoRA effectively leverages transfer learning, achieving competitive or superior performance at the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B configurations relative to both Single-task QLoRA and Multi-task full fine-tuning. Larger models demonstrate more consistent balance between correctness and quality, whereas smaller models preserve functionality but exhibit a higher incidence of quality-related issues.
items.author: Md Zahidul Haque, Saima Afrin, Antonio Mastropaolo

items.title: An Empirical Study of the Realism of Mutants in Deep Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2512.16741v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The core assumption behind using mutants as substitutes for real faults is that they represent them faithfully. In traditional software testing, this representativeness has been empirically studied by examining the behavioral relationship between mutant detection and real fault detection. In deep learning (DL), mutants are generated by applying mutation operators to either pre-training or post-training artifacts. However, the realism of mutants in DL remains largely unverified.
  To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first empirical comparison of pre-training and post-training mutation approaches in DL with respect to realism. We introduce a statistical framework that quantifies realism using two complementary metrics: coupling strength and behavioral similarity to real faults. We evaluate the framework on four publicly available bug datasets: CleanML, DeepFD, DeepLocalize, and defect4ML. Mutants are generated using state-of-the-art tools representing both mutation approaches.
  Results show that pre-training mutants exhibit significantly stronger coupling and higher behavioral similarity to real faults than post-training mutants, indicating greater realism. Operator-level analysis shows that this advantage is systematic across individual mutation operators and ranks the operators by realism within each approach. However, the substantial computational cost of pre-training mutation underscores the need for more effective post-training operators that match or exceed the realism of pre-training mutants.
items.author: Zaheed Ahmed, Philip Makedonski, Jens Grabowski

items.title: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Log Smells
items.summary:
arXiv:2412.09284v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Logging is an important part of modern software projects; logs are used in several tasks such as debugging and testing. Due to the complex nature of logging, it remains a difficult task with several pitfalls that could have serious consequences. Several other domains of software engineering have mitigated such threats by identifying the early signs of more serious issues, i.e., ``smells''. However, in the context of software logging, the concept of smells has only been investigated in a limited and narrow scope. The goal of this study is to systematically organize logging issues reported in the literature into a taxonomy of log smells that can help practitioners to better understand logging quality issues. To further help the practitioners and to identify issues that need more attention from the research community, we also map the identified smells to existing tools repairing them. We conducted a survey of the scientific literature to identify logging issues and related tools. After extracting relevant data from 61 articles, we used open coding to define logging issues and applied card sorting to derive log smells from these issues. Finally, we classified the tools based on their reported output. We present a taxonomy of nine log smells, describe several facets for each of them, and report the results of a preliminary validation of the taxonomy using a dataset of logging issues extracted from open-source projects. We also review existing tools repairing/removing some of these facets, highlighting the lack of tools addressing some log smells and identifying future research opportunities to close this gap. Our findings indicate that software logging is susceptible to a wide variety of log smells affecting both the logging code and the resulting log files. Understanding these smells, along with their causes and consequences, can help reduce their occurrence and improve logging quality.
items.author: Nyyti Saarim\"aki, Zahra G. Yazdi, Donghwan Shin, Domenico Bianculli

items.title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.18585v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node.js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X.js, a live benchmark of real-world Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X.js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X.js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X.js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.
items.author: Jos\'e Afonso, Jo\~ao Madeira Pereira, Ronghao Ni, Limin Jia, Jos\'e Fragoso Santos, Pedro Ad\~ao

items.title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17445v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.
items.author: Bodong Hou, Zhixin Pan

items.title: Separating Statistical Inference from Experimental Runtime: An Architecture for Sequential Scientific Analysis
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15824v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Sequential statistical procedures are increasingly embedded in scientific systems in which observations arrive incrementally from heterogeneous sources. In such systems the statistical update is only one part of the computation: observations must also be acquired, aligned across inputs, ordered, delivered, persisted, and replayed, and results must be passed to systems that display them or act on them. Sequential methods are nevertheless missing from the general software toolkit. They run inside proprietary experimentation platforms and commercial statistical packages, or exist as offline functions over complete data, and the batch fit interface that dominates machine-learning libraries has no place for a procedure that listens, keeps state, and decides when to stop. We propose an architecture that separates statistical inference from data topology, execution runtime, run lifecycle, persistence, and external action. Its central abstraction is the Sequential Procedure: a state-transition function that maps an inferential state, a valid statistical input, and a statistical random state to a new state and a scientific output. The procedure does not define how observations are acquired, paired, scheduled, stored, or acted upon. We specify the architecture semantically rather than through an object model, derive seven conformance invariants that any implementation can be tested against (among them synchronous/asynchronous, checkpoint, replay, and batch equivalence), and describe a dependency-free reference implementation in which all seven hold bitwise. Lorden's 2-SPRT for the Kiefer-Weiss problem serves as the reference procedure; the same contract accommodates sequential estimators, Bayesian filters, change-point detectors, and stateful predictive models.
items.author: Alexander Stepanov, Andrej Novikov

items.title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15729v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive.
  Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.
items.author: Junming Liu, Marcel B\"ohme

items.title: When the Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity for Deployment and Coding-Agent Approvals
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15137v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment tool's own record of its inputs or a manifest declared in the repository.
items.author: Md Imran Hossen

items.title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14453v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.
items.author: Ruidong Han, Zhensu Sun, Chengyan Ma, Yuqing Niu, Siqi Ma, David Lo

items.title: DICE: Tilting the Odds through Interface Attackson System One Model
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14404v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: System One models offer typed judgments that applications can turn into decisions. Their answers, however, are conditional on the state and question supplied by surrounding components, and on how the application uses the response. We study this boundary in a Jev-based pipeline with bounded substitutions at three adapter outputs: state extraction, question generation, and output interpretation. Across three small synthetic studies, each adapter can change the final decision while Jev and its authentic API responses remain outside attacker control. The cases expose distinct failures of source fidelity, answer meaning, and response relevance. Checks that bind these relationships stopped the corresponding interventions we tested, although source verification also rejected some valid clean decisions. The pilot identifies where correct request-level judgments can lose their connection to the original task; it does not estimate the prevalence of these failures in deployed systems.
items.author: Ben Dong, Tianyi Lu, Zhonghao Guo, Qian Wang

items.title: Assessing the Quality of Concrete Scenarios Generated from Scenario Classes for Automated Driving
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.18169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A scenario-based development approach has become state of the art for automated driving systems. Once a set of scenario classes covering the operational design domain is available, concrete scenarios are generated from these scenario classes, e.g., to be used for hazard analysis and risk assessment or for the system's verification and validation. For such applications, a high diversity among the generated concrete scenarios is paramount. The question arises how the quality of collections of concrete scenarios can be assessed in such a setting. In this work, we aggregate scenario distance measures into so-called quality functions that quantify the diversity of concrete scenario collections in the context of automated driving. In particular, we consider the case where scenario classes are formalized as constraint systems and the associated concrete scenario space is not explicitly known. Based on a set of desired properties we construct candidates for such quality functions and give proofs for their property fulfillment. To show the practical relevance of quality functions, we perform a variety of experiments in the context of an abstract scenario-based virtual verification toolchain for automated driving systems. More specifically, we use quality functions to compare the effectiveness of variation methods for sampling, examine the choice of different scenario distance measures, and investigate the effects of temporal aspects on concrete scenario collection quality.
items.author: Lina Putze, Thies de Graaff, Jan Steffen Becker, Christian Neurohr

items.title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.18165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
  We present Soliduzz, an approach for finding miscompilations in EVM smart-contract compilers using assertion-driven equivalence oracles. Soliduzz uses product programs to encode semantic equivalence as executable assertions. The key shift is to compile these self-checking programs and let off-the-shelf fuzzers and symbolic execution engines explore the resulting bytecode for assertion violations, without requiring compiler-specific support from the analyzer.
  Soliduzz instantiates this idea with two complementary families of metamorphic transformations. The first starts from equivalent expressions and lifts them into smart-contract code that deliberately exercises EVM-specific features such as storage, data locations, control flow, contract interactions, and inline assembly. The second generalizes Equivalence Modulo Inputs (EMI) from fixed concrete inputs to symbolic input spaces. Our symbolic EMI records coverage in the original computation and uses it to guard mutations in the transformed computation. Together, these transformations produce product programs that assert that paired computations yield the same outputs.
  We evaluate Soliduzz on three EVM smart-contract compilers (solc, solx, and vyper) using several analysis tools. Overall, Soliduzz exposes 29 bugs. Of these, 24 are compiler bugs: 6 miscompilations, 17 internal compiler errors, and 1 hang. The remaining 5 are bugs in the analysis tools.
items.author: Alexander Stromberger, Christoph Hochrainer, Valentin W\"ustholz, Maria Christakis

items.title: Mobile App Analysis in the New Era: Challenges and the Road Ahead
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mobile applications (apps) have grown into complex, multi-platform systems that support diverse services and operate within varying regulatory and distribution contexts. Traditional analysis techniques have established a strong foundation for ensuring quality, security, and compliance, but face increasing challenges as mobile apps evolve. This article presents a three-layer perspective to examine these challenges. The Artifact Layer highlights how heterogeneous code bases and protection mechanisms reduce the analyzability of packaged apps. The Runtime Layer addresses growing execution complexity, from multi-modal interactions and super-app architectures to AI-driven autonomous operations. The Ecosystem Layer considers broader contexts, including emerging platforms, fragmented distribution channels, and region-specific regulatory requirements. New characteristics across these layers interact and compound, creating difficulties that existing approaches are not designed to handle. For each layer, we identify key challenges and potential research directions, including framework-aware analysis, adaptive testing, and policy-aware compliance verification. We also discuss how large language models bring new analytical capabilities to the field, while their integration into apps raises new security and privacy concerns. This article aims to clarify where established methods fall short and highlight directions for future research in this evolving field.
items.author: Jiale Wu, Tianming Liu, Yanjie Zhao, Haoyu Wang

items.title: State-Aware Generation of Deployable Websites from Visual Prototypes and Requirements
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17861v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating deployable websites from visual prototypes and textual requirements is increasingly feasible with multimodal models, yet keeping generated projects consistent with their prototypes remains challenging. Prototypes specify layouts and visual elements, while requirements describe interaction workflows and deployment constraints. Existing UI-to-code methods and coding agents often treat layout reconstruction, interaction implementation, and project editing separately, allowing visual elements, files, workflows, dependencies, and render evidence to lose their correspondence across generation, verification, and update. We call this problem prototype-to-project state drift. We propose VisStateCoder, a state-aware framework that maintains these correspondences in a Project State Graph. The graph connects four types of state nodes through typed links and supports prototype grounding, graph-guided generation, and render-evidence-guided scoped updates that map failed checks to affected files while preserving files outside the update scope. We evaluate VisStateCoder on Vision2Web using five foundation models across Static Webpage, Interactive Frontend, and Full-Stack Website tasks. Averaged across models, VisStateCoder improves overall scores over the strongest baseline for each model by 26.1 and 22.6 points on Interactive Frontend and Full-Stack Website tasks, respectively. It also reduces verified-state drift, measured by checks that pass in one update round but fail later, compared with alternative state representations. An annotation study of 50 tasks finds that the constructed graphs achieve 95.6% edge-level F1.
items.author: Ruwei Pan, Junlei Shen, Linhao Wu, Zixiong Yang, Qisheng Zhang, Yifan Li, Tianyu Ma, Yakun Zhang, Lu Zhang, Hongyu Zhang

items.title: Cross-Project Bug Localization: What Works, What Doesn't, and Why
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17578v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bug localization models require substantial within-project training data that newly active or small open-source projects rarely have. Cross-project learning (CPL) promises to close this gap by reusing labeled bugs from mature projects, but prior CPL studies evaluate a single model against ample-data within-project baselines that data-scarce projects cannot reach. We ask whether CPL's effectiveness is a property of the transfer setting or depends on model architecture. We evaluate three architecturally distinct models, embedding-based BLAZE, convolutional TRANP-CNN, and GNN-based adversarial COOBA, on 63 source to target pairs from 13 open-source Python projects under identical bug corpora, data splits, retrieval candidates, and baselines. The primary baseline is within-project limited training (WP-small, 20% of target labels, the same target-side share as CP-transfer). CPL outperforms WP-small most clearly for TRANP-CNN (Cohen's d = 0.95, win rate 81.0%, p < 0.001, robust to clustering pairs by target project), and less so for BLAZE (d = 0.49, win rate 60.3%, p = 0.002; not significant once pairs are clustered by target). COOBA, under our re-implementation, shows a small gain that does not survive multiple-comparison correction (d = 0.27, p = 0.027). Negative transfer affects 9.5% of TRANP-CNN pairs and 30.2% of BLAZE's and COOBA's. Cross-model direction agreement is only 44-54%: the same pair can help one architecture and harm another, although the models' gains are positively correlated (rho = 0.24-0.42). CPL outcomes are therefore architecture-dependent: practitioners should validate CPL for their chosen model, and CPL studies should report results per architecture.
items.author: A Eashaan Rao, Sridhar Chimalakonda

items.title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.
items.author: Gabija Pasiunaite, Ryan McMorrow, Brian Clark, Liran Tal, Luke Tu

items.title: DeepGroundRepair: From API-Grounded Generation to Shape-Aware Repair for Deep Learning Programs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16897v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning programs are fundamental to modern AI applications, and automatically generating them from natural language requirements can substantially reduce DL development effort. Large language models have demonstrated promising capabilities for this direction. However, generated DL programs often remain unreliable because they must satisfy domain specific API usage constraints and tensor shape dependencies, violations of which can cause API level syntactic issues and runtime failures. Existing retrieval augmented generation and feedback guided code repair methods do not adequately address these DL specific constraints.
  In this paper, we propose DeepGroundRepair, a three stage framework that establishes a generation localization repair workflow to improve the reliability of LLM-generated DL programs. Its key idea is to progressively narrow the generation and repair spaces using DL specific knowledge and runtime tensor information. Specifically, it grounds generation in task-relevant API knowledge, localizes the upstream causes of tensor shape mismatch failures, and uses runtime tensor shapes to guide parameter repair.
  We evaluate DeepGroundRepair on the 100 model-level DL programming tasks in DeepEval using six open-weight LLMs across TensorFlow, PyTorch, and PaddlePaddle. We compare it with four baselines: two generation-only methods and their counterparts incorporating traceback guided self debugging. The results show that, relative to these baselines, DeepGroundRepair reduces the combined number of API-level syntactic issues by an average of 5.4 per 10 program files and achieves an average relative improvement of 85.3% in code executability. Compared with the two self debugging baselines, it improves semantic consistency by an average of 18.1% and reduces token cost by an average of 28.4%.
items.author: Xiangyue Ma, Zhen Wang, Xuhui Lu, Xiaoting Du, Chenglong Li, Jun Li, Haotian Li, Zheng Zheng

items.title: Domain-Knowledge Driven Configuration Tuning of Kubernetes Workloads
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial software applications often require engineers to tune the software deployment platform. Configuration tuning identifies valuable configurations that minimize costs while ensuring the application performance. However, finding these configurations is difficult. The number of tunable configuration parameters in industrial applications is large, and engineers cannot assess different configurations in production because users may experience performance degradation. This work targets Kubernetes: A system for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. This paper proposes a domain-knowledge-driven solution for finding configurations of industrial applications in a practical time. The solution relies on a catalog of constraints encountered by domain experts in similar applications. Depending on the problem under analysis, engineers can customize the optimization problem by selecting the relevant constraints from the catalog for the application at hand. We rely on two alternative solvers to find an optimal configuration: The first is based on heuristics, while the second reuses existing optimization-based solutions. We implemented our solution within an industrial tool from a software company specializing in performance engineering and optimization. We compare our solution to a baseline, considering a set of predefined configuration values provided by engineers. Our results confirm the effectiveness of our solution: Compared to the baseline, the heuristic-based and optimization-based solutions provide significant average savings of 11591 USD/mo and 15874 USD/mo per Kubernetes, respectively, accounting for 24.03% and 32.90% of the costs, in practical time (0.71 seconds per extraction for the heuristic-based and 45.54 seconds per extraction for the optimization-based solution).
items.author: Federico Imberti, Luca Cavagnis, Stefano Cereda, Giovanni Gibilisco, Claudio Menghi

items.title: Software Testing Meets Bayesian Workflow: A Literature-Driven Artifact Study of Probabilistic Programs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated testing is an effective software quality assurance method, but it is rarely used for probabilistic models. This is despite the heavy use of probabilistic programming for data analytics in research and engineering, where the consequences of errors are dire. A key obstacle is the specification of testable correctness properties for probabilistic models, known as the oracle problem. Like machine learning, probabilistic programming is used precisely where no analytical specification exists: had we been able to write one, we would have written an algorithm instead of fitting a model. An alternative is partial, proxy correctness specifications. The statistics literature already offers many, but as quality guidelines that require human judgment: comparing plots, visually analyzing shapes of distributions, assessing whether parameter values are ''far'' or ''close enough''. These guidelines are not systematically automated. In this work, we elicit, implement, and study testable correctness properties of probabilistic models. We extract 17 broadly applicable properties for probabilistic models from one of the most widely used textbooks in Bayesian data analysis, Statistical Rethinking by McElreath. For each property, we select and implement a test oracle, and study its utility for automatic testing, using a population of 59 probabilistic models from academic and industrial sources. We find realistic use cases (models under test) for all the properties. We observe that the vast majority of tests are not flaky in practice, despite the theoretical potential for flakiness. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the effectiveness of mutation testing for probabilistic models, showing that standard mutation operators do not capture faults tracked by the probabilistic properties.
items.author: Oleg Jarma, Maja Dall, Ra\'ul Pardo, Mahsa Varshosaz, Andrzej W\k{a}sowski

items.title: BRQGen: Towards Adaptive Completeness Assessment and Follow-Up Question Generation for Bug Reports
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many bug reports lack the necessary information required to reproduce issues. In early studies, large language models have been employed to generate follow-up questions to enhance incomplete reports. However, they ask a fixed number of questions regardless of whether the report is incomplete. We propose BRQGen, an iterative framework that identifies missing or ambiguous information in bug reports and generates targeted follow-up questions, only if necessary. Reports with no identified gaps are classified as sufficient. When the author responds, BRQGen evaluates whether the answers provide the requested information and generates further questions for any exposed gaps. We curated a novel dataset of 429 incomplete bug reports from Home Assistant and Brave Browser, each containing at least one maintainer follow-up question. Each question is mapped to the author's answer and assigned a label indicating whether the requested information could have been provided directly through the issue template. Earlier maintainer requests were associated with author responses, whereas delayed requests were associated with no response. Among responding authors, requests within one hour received median replies after 0.52 hours in Home Assistant and 1.45 hours in Brave, versus 9.76 and 13.49 hours after four hours. BRQGen covered 35.4% (Qwen 3.8 Flash) to 51.8% (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) of the 1,073 ground-truth follow-up questions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash managed to ask 45.7% of all detailed questions and 63.9% of all generic questions. Gemini 3 Flash Preview reached the highest macro-F1 for completeness assessment of 49.3%, but with a post-hoc analysis by getting only the gaps with high severities, Qwen 3.8 Flash reaches 73.6% macro-F1 score. Completeness assessment improved when at least one identified gap had high severity, and nearly all ground-truth questions were captured within the first two iterations.
items.author: Tevfik Emre Sungur, Akif Emre K\"o\c{s}\"u\c{s}, U\u{g}urcan Do\u{g}ru\c{c}am, Eray T\"uz\"un

items.title: Reviewing Beyond the Change: Repository Size and Existing Code Across Agent and Human Pull Requests
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15567v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reviewers sometimes name existing repository items outside the change under review. We ask whether such references are more common in larger repositories, and whether the pattern differs between agent-authored and human-authored pull requests. An instrument resolves names in inline review comments against the base-commit repository; size-matched negative controls estimate chance matches. Among 92,042 comments on agent pull requests in 2,034 GitHub repositories, 6.5 per cent name an existing item outside the change. An internally pre-specified log-linear model finds an odds ratio of 1.35 per tenfold increase in code files (interval 1.15 to 1.59), and size-matched negative controls indicate that chance matching does not account for the rise. Exploratory analyses suggest that the association is concentrated from small to mid-sized repositories and is imprecise among large ones. Human pull requests in 1,845 of these repositories show a similar association. A pre-specified comparison finds a small agent excess just within the bound set as negligible, but the evidence does not establish a robust agent-specific difference. The instrument misses many references, so reported shares likely understate prevalence, and the validation cannot estimate how recall changes with repository size.
items.author: Sabry E. Farrag

items.title: Comparing the Pre-trained Models of Source Code by Re-pre-training under a Unified Setup
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent years have seen the successful application of large pre-trained models of source code (CodePTMs) to code representation learning, which have taken the field of software engineering (SE) from task-specific solutions to task-agnostic generic models. By the remarkable results, CodePTMs are seen as a promising direction in both academia and industry. While a number of CodePTMs have been proposed, they are often not directly comparable because they differ in experimental setups such as pre-training dataset, model size, evaluation tasks and datasets, etc. In this paper, we first review the experimental setup used in previous work and propose a standardized setup to facilitate fair comparisons among CodePTMs to explore the impacts of their pre-training tasks. Then, under the standardized setup, we re-pre-train CodePTMs using the same model architecture, input modalities, and pretraining tasks, etc., as they declared and fine-tune each model on each evaluation SE task for evaluating. Finally, we present the experimental results and make a comprehensive discussion on the relative strength and weakness of different pre-training tasks w.r.t. each SE task. We hope our view can inspire and advance the future study of more powerful CodePTMs.
items.author: Changan Niu, Chuanyi Li, Vincent Ng, Bin Luo

items.title: PassSum: Leveraging Paths of Abstract Syntax Trees and Self-Supervision for Code Summarization
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code summarization is to provide a high-level comment for a code snippet that typically describes the function and intent of the given code. Recent years have seen the successful application of data-driven code summarization. To improve the performance of the model, numerous approaches use Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) to represent the structural information of the code, which is considered by most researchers to be the main factor that distinguishes code from natural language. Then, such data-driven methods are trained on large-scale labeled datasets to obtain a model with strong generalization capabilities that can be applied to new examples. Nevertheless, we argue that state-of-the-art approaches suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) inefficient encoding of ASTs; (2) reliance on a large labeled corpus for model training. As a result, such drawbacks lead to (1) oversized model, slow training, information loss and instability; (2) inability to be applied to programming languages with only a small amount of labeled data. In light of these weaknesses, we propose PassSum, a code summarization approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses via (1) a novel input representation which contains an efficient AST encoding method; (2) introducing three pre-training objectives and pre-training our model with a large amount of (easy-to-obtain) unlabeled data under the guidance of self-supervised learning. Experimental results on code summarization for Java, Python and Ruby methods demonstrate the superiority of PassSum to state-of-the-art methods. Further experiments demonstrate that the input representation we use has both temporal and spatial advantages in addition to performance leadership. In addition, pre-training is also shown to make the model more generalizable with less labeled data, and also to speed up the convergence of the model during training.
items.author: Changan Niu, Chuanyi Li, Vincent Ng, Jidong Ge, Liguo Huang, Bin Luo

items.title: Verifying Autoware Controller Node by Combining Model Verification and Runtime Monitoring
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15418v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Formal modeling and verification of autonomous driving systems remain challenging due to the vast operational space and the complexity of the control logic. We propose a hybrid verification approach that combines formal model verification and runtime monitoring for the trajectory-following control node of Autoware, an open-source autonomous driving platform. We formalize the controller as a hybrid system in differential dynamic logic (dL), and introduce an abstract model that captures the essential control dynamics. We then prove safety and liveness properties of the model using the KeYmaera X proof assistant. Complementarily, we monitor the constraints that assure the compatibility between the model and the Autoware implementation across numerical simulation runs using the Autoware toolchain, quantifying to what extent the implementation's behavior is subsumed by the verified model. The experimental results confirmed that (i) monitoring provides a sound evaluation of target following with accuracy bounds, and (ii) the Autoware implementation reaches the target with an accuracy of approximately 0.2-0.4 (m) in position and 0.8 (m/s) in velocity.
items.author: Daisuke Ishii

items.title: Testuary: Agentic Test Generation with Zero-Shot Parallelism
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic approaches for automated test generation can reach high-quality results, but they improve a given test suite incrementally, so a weak starting point may lead to many iterations or insufficient tests. To address this, we present Testuary, which provides the agentic phases with an improved starting point. Testuary first generates multiple test suites through independent, parallel zero-shot requests, checks and repairs them deterministically, and combines them into a single suite with a novel structural merging approach. A runtime-weighted set-cover reduction removes redundant tests without losing covered lines, branches, or killed mutants. After that, two agentic phases target the remaining gaps in coverage and mutation score. We compare Testuary with established search and LLM-based test generation approaches. The non-agentic first phase alone already significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art. After the agentic phases, Testuary achieves on average more than 99.9% line and branch coverage as well as a mutation score of 98.6%, significantly outperforming all compared baseline approaches. Testuary needs fewer model requests and its test suites are on average smaller and faster than those of the compared agentic approach.
items.author: Kevin Kammler, Dominik Sobania

items.title: Do Modifications Made by Coding Agents Make Subsequent Software Maintenance Harder?
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14768v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents increasingly maintain repositories over time, where each change becomes the starting point for subsequent tasks. Yet existing benchmarks either start tasks from developer-written code or cannot separate later-task difficulty from the effects of an agent's earlier changes. We ask whether agent-written code makes subsequent maintenance harder and whether the cost stems from inherited test failures or the code itself. We introduce SWE-Maintain, comprising 100 three-event maintenance episodes from 50 real-world Python repositories, with hidden tests certified across each sequence. Each later task is evaluated twice with the same agent and tests: from the developers' preceding patches (Developer-History) and from the agent's own changes (Agent-History). Across five coding systems, two backbone models, and 1,996 paired later events, Agent-History reduces later-task resolution by 5.6 percentage points on average.
