We propose Koa-decision, a framework for low-latency atomic actions -- fast, single-step decisions such as classification, semantic endpointing, Boolean checks, and scoring -- formulated as constrained generation with single-token outputs. By introducing atomic label tokens and applying supervised fine-tuning, our method reduces classification to a deterministic one-step decoding problem. Across standard benchmarks, Koa-decision delivers competitive accuracy with consistently low and stable latency. On a production intent-routing benchmark, Koa-decision reaches 85.5% accuracy -- competitive with the strongest frontier models (Claude-4.8-Opus, Gemini-Pro-3.1) and ahead of GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro -- while answering in about half a second, several-fold faster than every frontier model (up to ~7.5x at the median) under identical serving conditions. Against the dedicated single-token system Jev/TypeSafe, Koa-decision is competitive on accuracy and faster at the median, while also handling multimodal inputs and multi-label outputs that single-label text systems do not.
items.author: Shenghong Dai, Shiva Kumar Pentyala, Yingchi Liu, Shubham Mehrotra, Suman Banerjee, James Zhu, Bin Bi, Sitaram Asur, Phil Mui

items.title: From Protocols to Evidence: Bounded Claims for AI in Service of the Common Good
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.11910v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Claims that AI systems improve decisions, broaden access, reduce harm, or empower users can exceed what their evaluation supports. This gap motivates our ongoing work on RISE AI. In this paper, we examine the proposed framework in light of Pope Leo XIVs Magnifica Humanitas, particularly its treatment of human dignity, ownership, and technological power. We develop three linked propositions. First, AI adoption can reveal unmet human needs and institutional weaknesses, while deployment can change how institutions respond to them. We propose a rupture test to examine whether deployment repairs or compounds existing failures, substitutes for human support, or conceals problems behind improved performance. The test would compare deployment with existing practice and feasible human or non AI alternatives. Second, responsible AI must examine the institutional conditions surrounding a system, including who owns the infrastructure, controls its use, and bears responsibility for its consequences. Third, favorable evaluation cannot by itself establish respect for human dignity or moral and political legitimacy. We distinguish evidence-bounded deployment, which limits claims to what the evidence supports under specified conditions, from measurement-bounded governance, which identifies constraints that favorable results cannot override. We outline a proposed RISE AI framework for applying these propositions across Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment.
items.author: Nitesh V. Chawla, Paulo Benanti

items.title: Structured Multi-Level-Set Inversion for 3-D Electromagnetic Inverse Scattering
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.08594v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many dielectric targets encountered in 3-D electromagnetic inverse scattering exhibit piecewise-homogeneous material distributions, which provide useful structural information for inversion. To exploit this property, this paper proposes a structured multi-level-set inversion (SMLSI) method within a physics-driven neural network (PDNN) framework. Instead of directly parameterizing the contrast distribution, SMLSI represents it in terms of object support and material distribution. Multiple level-sets are mapped to soft-support functions and combined through a soft-union operation to construct the object support. The normalized contributions of these soft-support functions, together with trainable complex relative permittivities, determine the material distribution within the support. The level-set residuals are parameterized by a coordinate-based neural network, and the trainable parameters are optimized from scattered field data. Structure-aware regularization terms are introduced to promote binary object support and spatially coherent material regions while reducing material mixing and redundant activation of level-set supports. Adaptive regularization weighting is further employed to reduce the dependence on manual parameter tuning. Numerical experiments demonstrate that SMLSI improves reconstruction accuracy over direct contrast parameterization and enables the recovery of irregular 3-D geometries, closely spaced objects, and multiple material regions. Compared with CSI and $L_{2/3}$-FBE-WCIE, SMLSI achieves more accurate reconstructions on representative synthetic targets. Experimental validation using 3-D Fresnel data further demonstrates its applicability to measured scattering data.
items.author: Yutong Du, Zicheng Liu, Bo Qi, Yali Zong, Peixian Han

items.title: Topological Fraud Detection in Latent Transaction Spaces
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.08445v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Working entirely on topologically anonymized embeddings, we perform fraud detection using iterative rounds of unsupervised filtering followed by supervised sniping. The result is an ultra-low latency privacy--preserving triage that allows institutions to flag suspicious activity without compromising Personally Identifiable Information.
items.author: Avraham Bourla

items.title: A First-Order Learning Algorithm for Online Resource Allocation with Constant Regret
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.05895v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study a finite-horizon online resource allocation problem with initial resource capacities proportional to the horizon. In each period, a request type is observed and one action is chosen from a finite menu. Each action earns a reward and consumes a vector of resources. We present a primal first-order learning policy that, in each period, performs one gradient ascent update of the action coordinates associated with one request type, for a fluid relaxation in which resource overuse incurs a quadratic penalty. The policy achieves $O(1)$ expected additive regret relative to the hindsight optimum, with a bound independent of the horizon $T$, under a general arrival model. This model includes independent and identically distributed arrivals with unknown probabilities, independent nonstationary arrivals with known probabilities, independent nonstationary arrivals with unknown probabilities and one historical sample path, and Markov-modulated arrivals with an unknown Markov chain. The policy does not solve any linear program, and the regret bound does not require a nondegeneracy assumption on the fluid linear program.
items.author: Menglong Li, Jiawei Zhang

items.title: Hessian-Informed Conformation Augmentation for Potential Energy Surface Curvature in Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.05233v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have successfully learned potential energy surfaces (PES) and atomic forces, many practical applications, such as vibrational analysis and transition state search, rely heavily on the PES Hessian. Yet standard MLIPs are trained on energy and forces only, and using the Hessian as an additional training objective requires backpropagation whose memory cost grows quadratically with the number of atoms. To address these limitations, we propose two Hessian-derived data augmentation schemes: isotropic Gaussian displacement (\textbf{UniAug}) and normal mode-weighted displacement (\textbf{ModeAug}). Both methods utilize simple Taylor expansions, generating physically grounded molecular structures with highly accurate energy and force labels. By preserving the underlying MLIP architecture and training procedure, this approach contributes to improving energy and force predictions in various benchmarks. Comprehensive evaluations across non-equilibrium and equilibrium datasets demonstrate that our approach enhances model accuracy where reference forces are large and training data are limited.
items.author: Bumju Kwak, Jeonghee Jo

items.title: Evaluating and Recalibrating Probabilistic Classifiers from One-Bit Threshold Queries
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.05125v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Standard calibration evaluation and recalibration methods assume access to predicted probabilities. We study one-bit threshold access, a setting in which probabilities are hidden and the evaluator observes only whether the predicted probability exceeds a single chosen threshold per sample. Under this restriction, we show that classifiers can nevertheless be evaluated and recalibrated without reconstructing their hidden scores. We derive a consistent estimator of True Calibration Error, unbiased estimators of strictly proper scoring rules, and a one-bit objective for Temperature Scaling whose expectation matches the standard log-loss objective. Across these settings, we quantify the statistical cost incurred by replacing standard probability-access procedures by our one-bit estimators. Finally, we instantiate the framework for black-box LLMs, where the logit_bias API parameter allows us to realize the required threshold queries in zero-shot binary question answering.
items.author: Roman Plaud, Antoine Saillenfest, Matthieu Labeau, Thomas Bonald, Willem Waegeman

items.title: Subliminal Learning as Trait-Direction Drift: A Mechanism and Targeted Control under SFT Distillation
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.01091v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Beyond intended capabilities, model distillation can transfer hidden traits from a teacher. A teacher biased by a system prompt can generate semantically clean training data, such as numeric sequences, that still causes a downstream student to inherit the hidden preference, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. Prior work has identified several parts of this process. How the signal builds up during training and produces behavioral transfer remains unclear, making targeted mitigation difficult. We propose and validate trait-direction drift as a mechanism for subliminal learning: biased generation creates measurable preference gaps in teacher data, and student-recognizable gaps induce trait-aligned updates during supervised fine-tuning that accumulate into behavioral transfer. Guided by this mechanism, we propose probe-space corridor regularization, a targeted defense that constrains drift along a calibrated trait direction during distillation. The method substantially reduces hidden-trait transfer, preserving task performance: for example, it lowers malicious-response transfer from 29.55% to 6.45% with low main-task accuracy cost, and consistently suppresses animal-preference transfer across the main Qwen setting. The preference-gap, training-trajectory, and intervention evidence links subliminal learning to trait-direction drift and motivates corridor regularization as a targeted control during distillation.
items.author: Zhixuan Liu, Zhichen Dong, Yuyu Fan, Xiangtian Li, Chao Yang

items.title: Sparse Koopman Autoencoders Identify Local Dynamical Regimes in Multibasin Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.29057v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Koopman autoencoders (KAEs) seek a higher-dimensional latent representation in which nonlinear dynamics evolve linearly. However, many interesting systems have multiple basins of attraction, and both theoretical and empirical work has shown these multibasin systems cannot generally admit a single finite-dimensional global Koopman embedding under standard assumptions. We posit that encoders with a sparsity-inducing objective encouraging few active latent coefficients will provide latent supports as an inspectable basin-modeling principle for Koopman autoencoders. We use these encoders producing sparse latents in training Sparse Koopman Autoencoders (SKAEs) without basin labels or other regime annotations, and treat the learned latent supports as model-produced regime variables after training. Across a range of procedurally generated multibasin systems and chaotic flows, we show that SKAEs have superior forecasting performance compared to dense-latent KAEs. We also perform a mechanistic study that shows latent supports produced by SKAEs are both essential for the quality of the representation and useful for identifying basins on basin-interior states, whereas dense-latent KAEs collapse to an uninformative single support family. These results identify sparse latents and their corresponding supports as label-free, interpretable regime variables for Koopman learning in nonlinear systems with multiple local dynamical laws.
items.author: Aidan Li, Uday Kiran Reddy Tadipatri, Mahan Fathi, Sarath Chandar, Ross Goroshin

items.title: Parser Transitions Already Reveal Structural Responsibility: KV Persistence for Structured Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.28276v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents use structured generation for JSON, SQL, and function calls. Constrained decoding ensures valid formats, but KV compression can discard history needed for correct function and argument selection. Structural responsibility can diverge from model saliency: importance scores can overlook generated tokens' structural roles. Parser transitions already computed for legality encode these roles, including required arguments and structural boundaries, providing a free retention signal. We introduce PASK (Parser-Aware Structural KV Persistence), which reuses this signal for KV persistence by layer group without online importance estimation. Task-error sensitivity sets protection floors, while attention-output distortion ranks upgrades under the remaining budget. Offline calibration produces a frozen table for structural lookup and budget accounting. PASK outperforms budget-controlled baselines on function calling and text-to-SQL, improving BFCL accuracy by up to 8.67 pp over the strongest comparator. Against Full KV, it cuts peak GPU memory by 47.5 percent and achieves up to 3.3 times TPOT speedup.
items.author: Linze Wu, Xinrui Chen

items.title: Circuit Condensation: Post-Training that Concentrates a Behavior's Causal Circuit
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.27254v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: One approach in mechanistic interpretability explains model behavior through circuits: the components and connections that carry it. Frozen discovery often returns hundreds of edges, making them hard to inspect, compare, or verify exhaustively. We introduce Circuit Condensation, which post-trains models to concentrate behaviors into smaller causal graphs. Each round prunes low-attribution edges and trains a low-rank adapter to match the original through what remains. It keeps the cut only if task accuracy and held-out perplexity remain within tolerance. Across four behaviors and eight models, condensed circuits are smaller than the strongest published frozen-weight baseline in 30 of 32 settings, by 8.1x on average and up to 316x. Repeating the search without weight updates produces larger circuits in 29 of 32 settings, showing that weight updates drive the reduction rather than search alone. For 19 small circuits, exhaustive subset tests show that 11 are exactly minimal and identify removable edges in the rest. Pair ablations reveal dependencies that single-edge tests miss. On indirect object identification, condensation isolates 24 heads, including 17 with documented roles, whereas a matched frozen circuit needs 61 heads, 36 without documented roles. The result is a sufficient subcircuit of the published mechanism rather than a reconstruction of it. The resulting circuit tracks the original model's next-token distribution and, at matched edge count, predicts its errors better than a frozen circuit in 10 of 11 evaluable settings.
items.author: Sai Adith Senthil Kumar

items.title: A Token-Level Analysis of Sampled-Token Reverse-KL On-Policy Distillation
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.25643v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student on its own trajectories with token-level signals from a frozen teacher, yet how a sampled loss allocates updates across tokens remains poorly understood. We analyze the gradient of the per-token K2 estimator of reverse KL with respect to the student logits. The $\ell_1$ norm of this gradient factorizes into the absolute teacher--student log-probability gap and a student-side softmax factor that grows as the sampled token becomes less likely under the student. In our math-distillation runs, these per-token norms are highly non-uniform: low-student-probability tokens account for a disproportionate share of their sum and are also enriched in large teacher--student gaps. As a lightweight intervention suggested by this analysis, we study Surprise-aware Reweighting (SuRe), a detached, bounded weighting rule that further amplifies this existing allocation. Across two Qwen3 student scales, SuRe improves several math metrics over vanilla OPD and shows no clear degradation on the selected out-of-domain benchmarks. Our primary contribution is therefore a gradient-level characterization of reverse-KL OPD trained with the K2 estimator, with SuRe as one empirical instantiation.
items.author: Bing Shao, Jiazheng Zhang, Long Ma, Yujiong Shen, Senjie Jin, Xin Guo, Yuming Yang, Mingxu Chai, Zhiheng Xi, Boyang Liu, Junlin Shang, Peixin Wang, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang

items.title: AQLoRA: A Zero-Search Recipe for Fast Quantized LoRA Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.23816v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Quantized fine-tuning (QLoRA) saves memory but not time. It dequantizes every 4-bit weight on the fly, so it trains more slowly than fp16 LoRA. We present AQLoRA (Adaptive-Quantization LoRA), a recipe that buys part of that time back. One CPU pass ranks layers by NF4 reconstruction error, with no search and no calibration data, and keeps a fixed fraction of them in fp16. Those layers skip dequantization, which is where the speed comes from. A quality setting adapts every layer. A speed setting adapts only the top blocks, so the backward pass stops early. The selection matches the accuracy of Unsloth's hand-curated dynamic-4bit list.
  We evaluate on Commonsense-170K across six models and four architecture families, from 1.4B to 14B. The speed setting trains 11.3 +/- 2.3% faster than well-tuned QLoRA and gives up 0.1 to 1.5 accuracy points. It was faster in all thirteen independent timing sessions, at worst by 7%. The quality setting trains 4.8 +/- 2.0% faster, matches QLoRA's accuracy on every model, and is within a point of fp16 LoRA. The memory premium depends on the architecture: 0.06 to 0.8 GiB on the 1-4B models, 0.5 GiB at 7B, 1.9 GiB at 14B. These error bars are measured between independent sessions, not within one. Timing on shared hardware needs three rules: fix the measurement duration, not the step count; measure the noise floor from a duplicated arm; and repeat whole sessions, since on one model three sessions that each passed the floor test spread over 8.2 points.
  We validate the recipe with controls and report the two that failed. Choosing adapter layers by weight density is no better than random. Choosing protected layers by quantization error is not either, on five models at three budgets with memory-matched controls and downstream on two. The number of protected layers sets the speed; which layers they are does not measurably change accuracy.
items.author: Md Romyull Islam

items.title: SIGMA: Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-faced Adaptive Traffic Control for Reliable Intelligent Transportation Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.18263v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Traffic signal control is a challenging sequential decision-making problem requiring a balance between throughput, vehicle delay fairness, signal stability, predictable switching, and emergency vehicle prioritisation. Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches often rely on predefined objectives and offer limited adaptability to changing operational priorities. They may also generalise poorly across geometrically equivalent intersections. To address these limitations, SIGMA (Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-faced Adaptive traffic control) is proposed as a multi-faced RL framework augmented with a large language model (LLM) for dynamic objective adaptation and orientation-invariant policy learning. Natural language emergency instructions are translated into priority vectors that guide a multi-faced actor-critic controller. Symmetry-aware rotational augmentation supports transfer across homogeneous four-way intersections, while an offline-to-online learning strategy enables stable initialisation and adaptation to evolving traffic conditions. Structural properties concerning emergency service levels, graceful degradation under LLM failure, and sensitivity to traffic demand perturbations are established, alongside bootstrap-based statistical validation. Experiments in SUMO across four urban intersections modelled on Kolkata traffic scenarios compare SIGMA with fixed-time, actuated, and Deep Q-Network controllers. Reductions in average waiting times, emergency waiting times, and queue lengths are observed, alongside improved traffic throughput. Empirical reliability and ablation analyses further assess robustness to component failures and geometric orientation. SIGMA integrates language-guided objective adaptation, multi-faced policy learning, and statistical reliability assessment into an adaptive framework for intelligent traffic control.
items.author: Pratham Payra,  Jagadish, Tanmay Sen, Tanujit Chakraborty

items.title: Certified but Private: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Neural Network Guarantees
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.17070v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: With the growing deployment of machine learning models, formal guarantees of the robustness and fairness of these models have become increasingly important in safety-critical and legal-compliance settings. However, model parameters are often commercial secrets that cannot be disclosed to auditors or end users. To this end, we present PANDA, a scalable system that uses zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to prove the robustness and fairness properties of a model without revealing its private parameters. PANDA is built on top of CROWN, an efficient robustness certification framework that is used in many state-of-the-art formal verification tools for neural networks. The core contribution of PANDA is a novel algorithm for proving linear relaxation bounds for non-linear activation layers, yielding simple, lightweight proofs. Remarkably, our system can generate proofs of local robustness for neural networks with more than 2.9M parameters in 5 minutes, and can verify them in 10 seconds. Prior ZKP-based robustness system rely on exponential-time algorithms that cannot scale to nontrivial networks. In contrast, PANDA scales polynomially in the number of neurons in a network, allowing us to support neural networks 4 orders of magnitude larger than previous approaches with significantly reduced prover overhead.
items.author: Youwei Zhong, Ben Merbaum, Timos Antonopoulos, Ning Luo, Charalampos Papamanthou, Katerina Sotiraki, Ruzica Piskac

items.title: Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.11256v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Institutions use commercial AI detectors for academic integrity, yet detectors cannot distinguish AI editing from full LLM drafts and may treat both as misconduct. In a controlled study of published English abstracts (four domains; 2013 to 2015 vs. 2023 to 2025), we quantify this policy failure under proxy human/AI labels at tau=0.50. Light "refine abstract only" edits, a proxy for guideline-compliant AI assistance, are flagged at 38 to 80%. Unmodified 2023 to 2025 originals are flagged at 9 to 15%, with non-STEM rates far above STEM (p<0.001); elevated scores track long-token and Academic Word List density, not authorship intent alone. After Undetectable AI humanization, evasion is near-total: fewer than 4% of AI-labeled rewrites remain flagged (post-humanization detection rate <4%; FNR >96%). Honest AI-editing results in a higher sanction risk than humanizer-assisted evasion. Therefore, detector scores should not serve as standalone misconduct evidence.
items.author: Jonathan A. Karr Jr, Grigorii Khvatskii, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla

items.title: Forecasting Without Full Identification: Reliability and Computational Cost in Clot-Growth Simulation
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.08165v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We forecast clot growth from sparse early measurements with incomplete biochemical information. Using 1,000 simulated trajectories, we compare inverse search, which weights candidate inputs by their agreement with early observations, with a direct multilayer perceptron (MLP) predicting future clot size. Inverse search is more accurate when tissue factor alone, or tissue factor and fibrinogen, are unknown. When all five inputs are unknown, direct prediction achieves 2.16% pooled relative $L_2$ forecast error, outperforming search with 8,192 candidates using a forward MLP (3.25%) or latent neural ordinary differential equation model (3.36%). A conditional error bound separates candidate disagreement, weight on poor early fits, surrogate error, and candidate coverage. Increasing randomized quasi-Monte Carlo candidate budgets from 512 to 32,768 reduces numerical variation. A covariance score ranks additional assays by expected forecast value while accounting for measurement noise. At 10% range-scaled assay noise, incorporating assay uncertainty reduces forecast error from about 5% to below 3% for both surrogates. An independent reaction cascade verifies candidate integration against tensor quadrature, with mean normalized forecast-integration error below $10^{-5}$ at 32,768 candidates. These results demonstrate accurate clot-growth forecasting without full biochemical identification and support selecting prediction strategies and additional measurements according to accuracy, reliability, and computational cost.
items.author: Lennon J. Shikhman, Lily DiPaulo, Ying Qian, He Li

items.title: Online Conformal Prediction Beyond Feedback
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.07139v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Online conformal prediction (OCP) provides theoretically principled uncertainty quantification for arbitrary black-box classifiers and non-i.i.d. data streams by constructing prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the true label at a user-specified frequency. OCP usually updates prediction sets using feedback from previously deployed predictions. We instead study an OCP setting *beyond feedback*: on each round, the learner can *either* output a prediction set *or* query the correct label, but not both. Thus, no deployed prediction is ever evaluated directly. We reduce this problem to a partial monitoring game in which prediction actions return no observation and a separate query action reveals the label. To solve this game, we develop *OCP with queries* (OCPQ), a label-efficient forecasting algorithm designed for this beyond-feedback setting. Using an adequate reward construction, for any black-box classifier and any (non-i.i.d.) oblivious data stream of length $T$, OCPQ has $O(T^{2/3})$ expected regret and expected coverage of at least $\beta-O(T^{-1/3})$ for a user-defined $\beta$, while querying only an expected $T^{-1/3}$ fraction of rounds. This provides coverage comparable to bandit-based OCP methods while requiring no feedback from deployed predictions. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
items.author: Joar Skalse, Edoardo Pona, Osvaldo Simeone, Nicola Paoletti

items.title: Every Cache Entry Earns Its Place: Global Allocation of Resolution and Coverage for KV Cache Compression
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.07001v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long contexts, KV cache storage and repeated access have become a major bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage. Therefore, we propose GraceKV, a global approach for the allocation of resolution and coverage in KV cache compression, and formulate the compression process as a global resource allocation problem under a fixed cache budget. GraceKV treats each layer-KV-head-slot combination as an atomic unit and builds a prototype tree. Leaf nodes correspond to token-level KV entries, while each internal node uses a single prototype to compress the KV space covered by its children. A set of non-overlapping nodes in the tree forms the representation of an atomic unit. Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache budget. Finally, the nodes retained across all trees form the compressed KV cache. This process adaptively determines the allocation of cache resources among atomic units globally and the balance between resolution and coverage. GraceKV requires no additional training, and the entire compression and inference process is performed on the GPU. Systematic experiments across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show that GraceKV ranks first in 25 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128-fold compression. These results validate the effectiveness of global budget allocation in coordinating information coverage and local resolution.
items.author: Haolin Tian, Yuzhe Liu, Tonghan Wang

items.title: SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.06179v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models for low-resource languages still make frequent grammatical errors. Alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO can correct them. However, they require human judgements, which are scarce for languages such as Icelandic. Automatic rewards offer an alternative, yet models can learn to exploit them without improving (reward hacking). We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), which builds preference pairs using dependency parsers. Such parsers already exist for many low-resource languages. SAGA's reward combines parse quality with lexical diversity. It keeps only pairs whose reward gap reaches a threshold and trains on them with DPO. On Danish, Icelandic and Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, SAGA raises reward-parser success by 18 to 28 points. It improves all four model families we test, although one Icelandic run is flagged for reward hacking. An independent parser confirms the gains, and native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in Danish (69%) and Icelandic (80%). Online RL methods exploit the Icelandic reward. On the same base model, SAGA scores higher on both parsers. Existing linguistic resources, combined with safeguards against reward hacking, can therefore stand in for human judgements. This makes grammatical alignment possible for the many languages that have parsers but no such data.
items.author: Hoda Fakharzadehjahromy, Emil Wiman, Andreas Bueff, Hafsteinn Einarsson, Fredrik Heintz

items.title: KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.05475v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective on mathematical reasoning and retrieval tasks. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 52.0 for the same skill as text (SkillOpt) and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, a single shared interface serves eleven diverse skills at once with no loss in average accuracy. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill
items.author: Zhaowei Han, Xiang Zhang, Bing Han, Kai Liu, Danqi Hu, Jie Liu

items.title: EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.04968v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: An LLM agent can acquire persistent improvements by evolving its harness---the executable program governing model calls, tool use, verification, and recovery---without updating model weights. When the same harness serves users with different workloads, isolated evolution limits the sharing of useful discoveries, while centralized adaptation can introduce conflicting task-specific changes. We introduce EvolveNet, a framework for collaborative harness evolution that connects local specialization with shared capability accumulation. Clients evolve the same broadcast harness on their local workloads in parallel, and a server composes their adaptations into an updated shared program. Redistribution makes accepted discoveries available to all clients, allowing subsequent local evolution to build on improvements accumulated across the collaboration. EvolveNet supports this process through evidence-guided, scope-typed program aggregation and behavioral validation. Our theoretical analysis provides sufficient conditions for retaining and combining complementary improvements despite program interactions. Experiments across five settings show improved shared-harness performance, with ablation and behavioral analyses supporting the contribution of composition beyond specialist selection alone.
items.author: Jun Nie, Yonggang Zhang, Qianshu Cai, Yiu-ming Cheung, Xinmei Tian, Bo Han

items.title: SAKI: Score-Aware Low-Rank Key Indexing with Random-Matrix Noise Correction for KV Retrieval
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.03228v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Existing low rank KV cache methods preserve either model weights or key variance, neither of which directly reflects the attention scores used during inference. We derive the expected attention score distortion caused by rank r key compression and show that it yields a covariance weighted low rank objective. Under a margin condition, controlling this distortion also improves top k recall. The optimal rank r solution has a closed form asymmetric factorization obtained from the SVD of the covariance weighted query key operator. This motivates SAKI, a training free KV cache index that directly preserves attention scores rather than key reconstruction quality.
  Across LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B v0.1, and Llama 3.2 3B, SAKI outperforms key PCA at every tested rank. At rank 32, it removes 13 to 30 percent of PCA's remaining top 64 recall error, including improvements from 0.748 to 0.799 on LLaMA 3.1 8B and from 0.786 to 0.850 on Qwen 2.5 7B. It improves 68 to 89 percent of attention heads per model, with the largest gains in deeper layers. Predicted score MSE reductions closely match empirical measurements, with a Pearson correlation of 0.997, while ablation studies confirm that the gains arise from optimizing the attention score objective rather than covariance weighting alone. Analysis of the scoring operator further explains why weight only, invariant subspace, and key reconstruction methods can be suboptimal. SAKI uses random-matrix theory to separate genuine covariance signal from autocorrelated sampling noise, matching PCA with only 512 calibration tokens and adding value exactly where PCA sees no reliable signal.
items.author: Lin Zhang

items.title: Progressive Agent Skill Generation via Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.01678v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent large language model agents often use external skills as modular procedural units that condition inference and improve complex task solving. Thus, automatically generating high-quality skills from documents or experience has become an important problem. Existing skill generation methods largely rely on heuristics or pipeline-style consolidation, which must be specially designed for different evidence sources. In contrast, learning-based approaches offer a more unified way to model skill generation across heterogeneous sources. However, learning-based skill generation remains challenging because skills lack a natural supervision signal based on relevance or correctness; their value can largely be determined only by whether they improve the behavior of the agent on downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose Skill-$\alpha$, a reinforcement learning method that learns a unified policy for progressive skill generation. Specifically, we construct each skill by repeatedly applying the learned policy to successive source evidence and introduce a novel rollback reward that evaluates each edit by comparing downstream execution under the original and edited skills on an anchored query. Extensive experiments show that Skill-$\alpha$ generates more effective skills than methods based on heuristics or pipelines in both document-to-skill and experience-to-skill settings. Under the main GPT-4o worker, Skill-$\alpha$ improves average downstream success rates over the strongest skill-generation baseline by 3.1 points on CL-Bench and 6.7 points on tau2-bench. Further ablations and analysis validate the importance of rollback reward and progressive generation.
items.author: Junhao Shen, Chengzhi Piao, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng

items.title: Flow Matching with Missing Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.28698v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Flow matching assumes fully observed training data, which many real-world applications rarely provide. We study Missing-Data Flow Matching, which treats the missing coordinates of training samples as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over the values they could take. We first prove that the oracle correction is exact: completing from the true pattern-conditioned posterior recovers the complete-data flow-matching objective under any missingness mechanism. Under missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing at random (MAR), this posterior equals the ordinary complete-data conditional, while under missing not at random (MNAR) it generally depends on the missingness mechanism and may require additional structure to identify. Our finite-sample analysis then answers design questions that the algorithm leaves open. Missingness transfers estimator variance rather than adding it, and for the fixed-parameter loss estimator one completion per example matches complete-data variance and is optimal under a fixed evaluation budget. A learned completion model contributes population completion bias, which we bound by its expected conditional Wasserstein distance to the true completion law. Experiments numerically validate the theoretical predictions, show that deterministic rather than frozen imputation reduces generated conditional variability, and place our method alongside strong classical and deep imputation baselines on real tabular data.
items.author: Fairoz Nower Khan, Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Peizhong Ju

items.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.27188v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.
items.author: Lennon J. Shikhman, Michael Galarnyk, Aadi Dash, Nicholas A. Welsh

items.title: Per-Context Reverse Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.26417v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning often fails because rollouts from the unassisted evaluation start rarely reach later task stages. Reverse curricula address this by starting some training rollouts from easier intermediate states, called scaffolds. The main choices are which intermediate starts to use (scaffold access) and how to distribute training across them (scaffold allocation). Most prior curricula pace removal on one shared schedule, which can fail when task instances, or contexts, learn at different rates. We introduce an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that gives every context its own curriculum. We use binary rollout success to decide whether to move a context's start forward or back. A stalled frontier also gets an occasional harder-start trial. A counting construction shows that synchronized global pacing can be insufficient when contexts need conflicting amounts of assisted practice. Across six navigation and manipulation settings, scaffold access improves learning and enables success in three where unassisted training fails within the reported budget. None of the global schedules we tested solved both groups in the constructed conflict. The per-context controller did. Group-level pacing works if the labels capture how contexts learn. Without those labels, per-context pacing still handles differences within a group. These results suggest pacing assistance separately for contexts that learn at different rates.
items.author: Siddharth Aphale, Ayushman Singh

items.title: RIS-Kernel: A Model-Agnostic Architecture for Long-Context LLM Inference via Sparse Attention
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.21927v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Full self-attention in large language models scales as O(N^2), limiting long-context analysis to 65k tokens and requiring costly GPU clusters. The Reduced Interaction Sampling (RIS) inference engine addresses this as a model-agnostic architecture. Without modifying weights, RIS introduces sparse stochastic attention geometries that operate under extreme pruning (up to 99% under 1% density) while preserving factual retrieval. While foundational graph-theoretic RIS formulations establish an asymptotic O(N log N) bound, this work evaluates a practical fixed-density regime on unaccelerated commodity CPU systems. We validate RIS on Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct across two regimes. At 32,768 tokens (where native dense attention serves as the upper bound), RIS-Stochastic at 1% density and 70 ensemble seeds achieves 75.00% accuracy, outperforming the native dense baseline (71.88%), while 5% density at 10 seeds matches it (71.88%), demonstrating that multi-seed sparsity filters sequence-level noise. Crucially, a controlled ablation evaluating a single static mask at matched budget (N=1, d=0.50) yields only 53.12% accuracy, proving that multi-seed topological diversity, rather than raw edge density, drives contextual recovery. Under tight budgets, RIS-Structural reaches 65.62% accuracy at 1% density with 10 seeds (recovering 50.0% of the gap over the 59.38% zero-context floor) and 68.75% (75.0% recovery) with 30 seeds. At 65,536 tokens, where dense attention triggers out-of-memory faults, RIS yields retrieval gains of up to 14.06 percentage points over the zero-context floor (51.56%), confirmed as marginally significant under McNemar's paired test (p = 0.078 < 0.10). All evaluations run on commodity CPU servers (16-128 GB RAM), demonstrating that long-context LLM inference is feasible on standard academic hardware without GPU acceleration.
items.author: Anderson R. Santos

items.title: Learning What Matters: Causal Evidence Sets for Global Context Pruning
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.21692v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pruning a long context means committing to the blocks a model will keep, and a common selector is distilled from a dense teacher's attention. That assumes attention shows which context the answer depends on. We test the assumption on retrieval tasks where the evidence is known exactly, by masking context and measuring whether the answer changes. Attention and causal dependence disagree. Teachers attend to outdated facts the answer does not use, and a selector distilled from that attention routes a multi-hop task at 36% to 98% across runs. The same selector trained on causal evidence sets reaches 99% or better on every run, and known evidence labels beat attention-imitation and accumulated-attention eviction through 32B when the context must be pruned before the question arrives. A reconstruction compressor, KVzip, is stronger on natural-text QA with native per-head KV eviction. Under our paragraph-level adaptation, its scores do no better than labels recovered by intervention.
items.author: James E. Allchin

items.title: Modeling Fly Social Behavior with Agent-Centric Pose Forecasting
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.19548v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Understanding animal behavior at an algorithmic level -- what animals attend to, how they form internal representations, and how this maps to action -- remains a central challenge in neuroethology. We explore how well large generative models capture properties of fly social behavior. We combine transformers with agent-centric representations. Models input egocentric sensory observations and output egocentric movements, mirroring biological constraints. Social behavior emerges from agents independently sensing and responding to one another. We demonstrate that this simple model captures many properties of fly behavior, outperforming the world-centric representation and achieving SOTA on MABe 2022-fly. We systematically evaluate properties of the representation important for capturing the behavior distribution through a series of lesioning experiments. These comparisons were enabled by a new, general-purpose library for animal-centric pose forecasting.
items.author: Eyrun Eyjolfsdottir, Kristin Branson

items.title: H$^2$SD: Hybrid Hindsight Self-Distillation
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.18955v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable outcome supervision for language model reasoning, but scalar trajectory rewards offer limited guidance for token-level credit assignment. Existing self-distillation methods incorporate privileged teacher information through fixed strategies: direct distribution matching may destabilize successful behavior, while magnitude modulation provides limited corrective guidance after failure. We propose Hybrid Hindsight Self-Distillation (H$^2$SD), which adapts both teacher context and update strategy to trajectory correctness. For successful trajectories, the teacher conditions on the verified student response and a rephrasing instruction to rescore the original tokens. These scores modulate reward-derived updates while preserving advantage signs. For failed trajectories, a verified reference hint guides corrective supervision through reverse KL distillation. Across Sudoku, Calcudoku, Arrow Maze, and mathematical reasoning with two Qwen3 models, H$^2$SD achieves an overall average accuracy of 43.33\%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.43 percentage points while maintaining stable optimization.
items.author: Qiye Cai, Yichuan Ma, Weitao Ma, Peiji Li, Yongkang Chen, Yicheng Zou, Linyang Li, Xiaocheng Feng, Bing Qin

items.title: DRNOISE: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents in Misleading Evidence Environments
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.17291v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep research agents increasingly operate over the open web, where relevant records coexist with redundant summaries, outdated reports, and misleading documents. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether agents preserve sound evidential standards when an ordinary-looking false document is deliberately seeded into a searchable environment and offers a direct shortcut to a conflicting answer. We introduce DRNOISE, a 100-task benchmark for answer recovery under misleading evidence. Each task has a unique gold answer supported by two corroborating indirect record chains; the paired noisy condition adds one plausible document that states a conflicting answer directly. The benchmark spans ten families of evidence operations. Among models with strong clean-task performance in the shared agent framework, this single intervention causes 66--88 percentage-point accuracy drops. Trace analyses reveal a pattern of verification inertia: agents often retrieve truthful records yet defer to the answer-like document without adequately checking its claim against the underlying evidence. Generic verification prompts reduce but do not close this gap. The setting is especially relevant to open-web deployment, where plausible falsehoods arrive through ordinary-looking pages without explicit adversarial instructions. Reliable deep research therefore requires more than retrieval and citation; it requires active reconciliation of direct claims with record-level evidence.
items.author: Jun Nie, Zhiqin Yang, Zhenheng Tang, Yonggang Zhang, Xiaowen Chu, Xinmei Tian, Bo Han

items.title: From hyperplanes to hyperellipsoids: a pedagogical bridge from linear classifiers to single-qubit mixed-state classifiers
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.15433v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Quantum machine learning ideas are typically absent from traditional machine learning curricula and are instead introduced in upper-level courses on quantum information processing and quantum computing. We propose a route for bringing quantum ideas into the standard machine learning classroom directly after the introduction of binary linear classifiers. Specifically, we develop a pedagogical bridge between linear classifiers and single-qubit mixed-state classifiers by characterizing their geometric model structure. This characterization reveals that a single-qubit mixed-state model for binary classification can be viewed as the ``ellipsoidal version'' of a standard linear classifier: rather than learning a hyperplane that separates data, the model learns a hyperellipsoid.. We present this connection as an accessible bridge from familiar classical machine learning concepts to quantum machine learning, and encourage instructors to use it as a natural entry point for introducing quantum ideas in the undergraduate machine learning classroom.
items.author: Kaitlin Gili

items.title: On Generalizing Preference-based Reinforcement Learning to Multi-Objective Problems
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.11432v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) from pairwise human-generated trajectory comparisons. We generalize preference-based RL by formalizing a novel setting in which the expert can also label trajectory pairs as incomparable when neither trajectory "dominates" the other. We introduce the learning problem and the desiderata that a model should satisfy, showing that, when multiple objectives are present, no compliant model admits a negative log-likelihood that is convex in the utility difference. Then, we propose a novel Bradley-Terry-inspired rationality model that enables incomparability and infers a multi-dimensional reward function, and discuss its compliance with the desiderata. We upper bound the divergence between the true and learned comparison distributions when a dataset is available, separating the rate of approach to the optimum from a non-vanishing term due to non-convexity. Then, we study how learned parameters affect downstream guarantees, highlighting the impact of invariance on Pareto optimality.
items.author: Simone Drago, Marco Mussi, Leonardo Bianconi, Alberto Maria Metelli

items.title: Efficient Long-Horizon Learning for Learned Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.06772v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Learned optimization aims to improve upon hand-designed optimizers (e.g., Adam and Muon) by meta-learning small neural network optimizers over a distribution of tasks. While recent work has greatly advanced the architectural design and inductive biases of learned optimizers (LOs), their meta-training remains biased toward short-unroll learning on particular tasks, resulting in redundant computation and leaving LOs often unable to compete with hand-designed optimizers. We introduce Efficient Long-hOrizon (ELO) learning, an efficient meta-training algorithm that (1) reallocates wasted meta-training compute to longer failure regimes, achieving efficient long-horizon learning, and (2) enforces decoupled progressive expert supervision, providing stable meta-learning signals that additionally improve the generalization of LOs. Our empirical study evaluates ELO for meta-training both element-wise and matrix-based LOs. Across downstream language modeling (GPT-2 and GPT-3 on FineWeb) and image classification (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1K) tasks, ELO substantially improves the long-unroll performance and out-of-distribution generalization of the base LOs. In particular, ELO-Celo2 outperforms well-tuned AdamW and Muon on GPT-2 (30M and 124M) language pretraining. \textit{Notably, all ELO baselines require less than 7 H100 GPU-hours for meta-training.}
items.author: Xiaolong Huang, Benjamin Th\'erien, James Harrison, Eugene Belilovsky

items.title: A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.05615v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. We ask: is dense intervention necessary? We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation. Across our experimental settings, we further find that the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.
items.author: Nima Eshraghi, Lovedeep Gondara, Yuqing Huang, Sagarika Suresh, Leizer Teran, Jithin Pradeep, Xiaotong Xu, Fanny Chevalier

items.title: Qantara: Bridge-Flow Training for Multi-Paradigm JEPA Inference
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.04978v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) underpin a growing family of latent world models for control from raw pixels. Published JEPA world models for pixel-based control (PLDM, DINO-WM, LeWM, V-JEPA-2-AC) each commit at training time to a single inference paradigm, trajectory optimisation in a learned dynamics model, so a checkpoint trained to plan cannot be read off as a policy without retraining. Deferring that choice to inference would let the constraints that bind at deployment, per-step latency and whether a goal observation can be supplied, pick the path. We present Qantara, an end-to-end JEPA of about 21M parameters whose joint training objective pairs a Brownian-bridge interpolant between consecutive clean latents on the state axis with noise-to-data flow matching on the action axis. One checkpoint serves three inference paradigms without retraining: latent planning, behaviour-cloning action sampling, and a video-inverse composition that predicts the next latent without action conditioning, then recovers the action bridging the two. Training samples the two noise levels along the edges of the (action-noise, state-noise) square, one edge per inference dispatch, so each path is trained where it is queried. Replacing that sampler with uniform sampling over the square at matched compute drops Push-T planning from 90.1 to 53.3 success rate (SR). On the LeWM control suite at a matched 10-epoch budget, Qantara averages 91.2 SR over the four environments and reaches 93.7 on OGBench-Cube, +7.7 over DINO-WM and +17.0 over LeWM, each measured against the stronger of that baseline's published score and our retrain of it. From the same weights the two goal-blind paths, which receive no goal image, reach 82.1-83.2 SR on Push-T and 70.8-72.8 on Cube at roughly 15-65x lower inference cost, and fall to near-noise on Reacher, whose released training corpus comes from a random policy.
items.author: Ruslan Rakhimov, George Bredis, Yuriy Maksyuta, Daniil Gavrilov

items.title: Auditing Finite-Lag Statistics of Recurrent Representations
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01746v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hidden-state trajectories are computational traces that record how recurrent representations evolve as networks process sequences. When exact state repeats are unavailable, one way to estimate conditional motion is to borrow successors from nearby states, yielding a finite-bandwidth successor smoother. However, this procedure can change the displacement being measured. At a median-distance bandwidth, write-phase displacement energy is about $1.88\times$ the exact value for GRU and LSTM. Elman instead shows near agreement in total energy despite large, opposing finite-bandwidth contributions. We therefore compute the conditional-mean energy fraction exactly on repeat-copy. Training reverses the architecture ordering of this fraction, with GRU and LSTM rising to about $94\%$ while Elman falls to about $55\%$. The centered remainder is small in energy but can still expose input information. For LSTM, linear four-bit decoding rises from $0.804$ on total displacement to $1.000$ after exact conditional centering.
items.author: Kanishka Reddy

items.title: FlexTab: A Flexible Encoder-Decoder Architecture for In-Context Learning Across Diverse Tabular Tasks
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.30336v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce FlexTab, a flexible encoder-decoder architecture for in-context learning on tabular data that pairs a single, task-agnostic encoder with a suite of task-specific decoders. Unlike existing tabular in-context learners, which entangle feature representations with a specific prediction target, our design produces target-agnostic row embeddings that can be leveraged across a wide range of downstream tasks within a table-native in-context learning setup. We demonstrate this flexibility on seven distinct problems: classification, regression, anomaly detection, clustering, entity matching, retrieval, and entity classification in relational databases. Both the encoder and the task-specific decoders are trained on tasks generated from a large corpus of real-world, unlabeled tables. FlexTab achieves state-of-the-art performance on classification, regression, anomaly detection, entity matching, and retrieval, while remaining competitive with specialized models on entity classification in a relational setting. These results demonstrate that a single shared encoder, paired with task-specific decoders, can serve as an effective general-purpose backbone for diverse tabular prediction problems. The inference code and checkpoints are publicly available at: https://github.com/SAP-samples/flextab .
items.author: Marek Polewczyk, Maximilian Schambach, Marco Spinaci, Sam Thelin, Johannes H\"ohne

items.title: Blackknife: Query-Free Black-Box Rewiring Attacks on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.29240v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) perform well on graphs with multiple node and relation types, but their robustness to attacks with restricted structural access remains insufficiently understood. We propose Blackknife, a query-free, strict black-box evasion attack that observes only the one-hop structures of the attacked nodes, their ground-truth labels, and raw features within the permitted action space. No victim-model outputs are used to train the surrogate, generate perturbations, or select attacks.Blackknife trains a shared surrogate using only observable edges and relation types, then optimizes structural perturbations through continuous relaxation and projected gradient ascent. Each rewiring operation deletes one edge and adds another of the same relation type, preserving the target node's total degree and degree for each relation type. A cosine-similarity penalty and an adaptive structural classifier further regularize the perturbations through bilevel optimization. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate competitive attack success rates across five victim architectures and three defense settings. The results expose HGNN vulnerabilities under jointly restricted graph access and query-free attack generation.
items.author: Honglin Gao, Junhao Ren, Lan Zhao, Yue Yang, Peilin Du, Jindong Chang, Gaoxi Xiao

items.title: Lifelong In-Context Learning with Transformers Requires Parametric Forms of Attention
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.25342v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Lifelong continual learning remains an obstacle on the path to human-like intelligence. Modern transformers show sparks of intelligence with in-context learning. The quadratic nature of attention, however, prohibits transformers from performing this process on arbitrarily long sequences. In this work, we argue that extending in-context learning to lifelong settings is a practical solution for continual learning in AI agents. In particular, we argue that parametric forms of attention are needed to understand a lifetime of context with transformers on a fixed hardware budget. These attention mechanisms learn the relationship between keys and their associated values at test-time with parametric regression. Our generalization of parametric approaches (linear attention, state-space models, fast weight programmers, and test-time training layers) contrasts with nonparametric counterparts like softmax attention. They replace the ever-growing key-value cache with an online-trainable neural network, maintaining a constant memory footprint. We highlight how parametric attention currently fall short of lifelong learning due to limited memory capacity or costly online updates. To address these issues, we pose a set of open questions with novel insights to guide the field toward long-horizon agents.
items.author: Luke McDermott, Robert W. Heath Jr., Rahul Parhi

items.title: Horizon Adaptive Offline Policy Learning via Value Stitching
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.21136v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Learning accurate value functions plays a decisive role for reinforcement learning (RL) agents to solve long-horizon, complex tasks. Conventional temporal-difference (TD) learning objectives suffer from value-estimation bias that accumulates over the horizon, while extended-horizon modeling methods, such as n-step TD backups and Q-chunking, adopt a rigid, fixed-horizon value-modeling recipe that is often not flexible enough to capture complex value structures in long-horizon, multi-stage tasks. In this paper, we show that enabling value updates with dynamic horizon composition can yield a strong offline policy learning scheme. Our method, Horizon Adaptive Offline Policy Learning via VAlue STitching (VAST), replaces fixed-horizon backups with recursive, horizon-adaptive value composition. Its key ingredient is to couple value optimization with a future state- and horizon-length-conditioned auxiliary value function that is learned through direct data supervision, and a stitching policy that optimally selects the reward-maximizing horizon length and future sub-goal to achieve horizon-adaptive value stitching. This design enables direct estimation and compositional "stitching" of variable-length returns grounded in actionable sub-goal states, providing an accurate and greedily exploitable value-supervision signal for offline policy optimization. Across 50 tasks on OGBench, VAST outperforms fixed-step, extended-horizon methods, and generative-value offline RL baselines, achieving strong performance particularly in high-complexity, long-horizon decision-making tasks.
items.author: Kexin Zheng, Xianyuan Zhan, Xintao Yan

items.title: Constrained Diffusion Models with Primal-Dual Inference
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.17192v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This paper develops constrained diffusion models with primal-dual inference (PDI) to sample from optimal distributions of entropy-regularized optimization problems with \emph{average} constraints. We formalize constrained sampling in the Lagrangian dual domain, where the optimal distribution takes the form of a Gibbs distribution indexed by the optimal dual variable. Rather than estimating this dual multiplier before sampling and freezing it throughout generation, PDI jointly infers the optimal primal distribution and its parametrizing dual variable. Each reverse diffusion step denoises using the score field associated with the current multiplier and then updates the multiplier through dual ascent using the estimated constraint violation of the denoised samples. To enable this conditional score field, we train a single dual-conditioned score network over the family of Gibbs distributions induced by the dual variables encountered during inference. We prove that the dual iterates converge to a neighborhood of the dual optimum, and that the generated distribution approaches that of an oracle sampler that knows the optimal multiplier, up to a bias floor. We evaluate PDI on constrained sampling from a mixture of Gaussians, wireless resource allocation, and portfolio management.
items.author: Samar Hadou, Yigit Berkay Uslu, Alejandro Ribeiro

items.title: Understanding Helpfulness and Harmless Tension in Reward Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.13209v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reward models (RMs) are a key component of reinforcement learning from human feedback, enabling the alignment of large language models with human values such as helpfulness and harmlessness. However, these alignment goals can conflict, leading to interference when optimised jointly. We refer to this conflict as alignment tension and investigate how it manifests in RMs. To this end, we train RMs optimised for helpfulness, harmlessness, and a combined helpful-harmless objective, and compare their behaviours and internal representations. We find that mixed-objective RMs frequently underperform their single-objective counterparts, suggesting substantial interference between alignment goals. Using activation-based interpretability methods, we identify neurons associated with helpfulness and harmlessness and show that they causally promote their corresponding behaviours while often suppressing the opposing one. At the same time, we find that a substantial fraction of neurons are shared across objectives. These shared neurons exert a disproportionate influence on model behaviour and encode incompatible representations. Our findings provide mechanistic evidence for how alignment objectives are represented and interact within RMs, offering new insights into the challenges of multi-objective alignment and motivating the development of more disentangled and controllable alignment methods.
items.author: Eshaan Tanwar, Pepa Atanasova

items.title: Demystifying Hidden-State Recurrence: Switchable Latent Reasoning with On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.13106v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Latent chain-of-thought compresses reasoning through continuous hidden-state recurrence, but existing approaches are difficult to optimize with standard on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) and hard to analyze mechanistically. We introduce SWITCH, a switchable latent reasoning framework that addresses both challenges with two discrete boundary tokens:  enters latent reasoning and  exits it. These discrete anchors make policy ratios well-defined for standard on-policy RL while providing natural intervention points for mechanistic analysis. We train SWITCH with a visible-to-latent curriculum and Switch-GRPO, which propagates gradients through recurrent latent computation. SWITCH consistently outperforms prior hidden-state-recurrence approaches at similar model scales. Mechanistic analysis reveals that (i)  implements a localized, learned switching policy rather than a stylistic artifact; (ii) the latent step performs problem-specific, causally important computation; and (iii) this computation is concentrated in a single hidden-state transition upon entering latent mode. Together, these results show that hidden-state-recurrence latent reasoning can be both effectively optimized with on-policy RL and directly analyzed mechanistically, enabling us to study how RL reshapes internal reasoning computation. Code is available at https://github.com/LARK-AI-Lab/SWITCH.
items.author: Jiayu Yang, Chao Chen, Shengen Wu, Yinhong Liu, Yuxuan Fan, Lujundong Li, Songning Lai, Chengwei Qin, Zhijiang Guo

items.title: Learned Structure Shows Up Earlier in the Task's Own Basis: A Controlled Look at a Synchronisation Precursor in Grokking
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.12966v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Analyses of grokking usually read hidden activations in one basis, most often the Fourier basis modulo $p$. We ask how much the answer to "has the network organised yet?" depends on that choice. The measure FSD$_{\rm gen}$ averages each unit's activation over inputs with the same answer and counts how many units share the same strongest irreducible representation. For modular multiplication we read one answer-averaged profile in three orders: discrete-logarithm order, in which the characters of the multiplicative group become Fourier modes; natural order; and random orders. Across 60 networks at $p\in\{59,97,113\}$, the discrete-log reading reached a fixed threshold before both other readings in 60 of 60 networks (59 of 60 when it had to hold 500 steps). Because untrained networks already score higher in discrete-log order, we also required an equal rise above each reading's untrained level; the discrete-log reading was still first in at least 16 of 20 networks at every prime. At $p=59$ and $p=97$ this happened during the memorisation plateau in 35 of 39 networks; at $p=113$ in 12 of 20. Memorisation preceded grokking in all 179 runs that grokked, by more than any synchronisation signal on average, so a lead over grokking is not by itself evidence of a detected circuit. Synchronisation time is only weakly related to grokking time (pooled $\rho=0.18$). On six finite groups, read with the same measure in every basis, the irreducible-representation reading came before random element orders on all six; with equal-rise thresholds this held in every case on four groups, in 7 of 10 on $\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ and in none on $D_{16}$, where about half the profile power lies in one-dimensional representations the measure leaves out. We also correct a conjugate-pair artefact that roughly halves the measure on abelian groups. This version withdraws the causal and predictive claims of v1.
items.author: Achyuthan Sivasankar

items.title: PhaseQuant: Mitigating Activation Quantization Collapse via Residual-Stream Dynamics
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.12487v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) inference, but reliably quantizing activations remains challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are all quantized to 4-bit precision. A key difficulty lies in massive activations, whose extreme values dominate the activation range and amplify quantization error. State-of-the-art methods mitigate massive activations through transformation-based smoothing, such as orthogonal rotations and affine scaling, but overlook the cross-layer dynamics of the residual stream. In this paper, we show that massive activations emerge and disappear in a phase-wise pattern across network depth, injecting abrupt updates into the residual stream. These updates cause the newly injected layer-wise signal to dominate the 4-bit quantization scale and weaken the accumulated residual information. To characterize this behavior, we introduce two metrics, the Update Dominance Ratio (UDR) and the Historical Retention Score (HRS), and show that static transformation-based smoothing cannot fully resolve the resulting dynamic quantization instability. Based on this analysis, we propose PhaseQuant, a phase-aware mixed-precision post-training quantization policy for activation quantization. PhaseQuant identifies quantization-sensitive layers from residual-stream dynamics and assigns 8-bit activation precision only to these layers, while keeping weights, KV caches, and all remaining activations at 4-bit precision. It can be directly integrated with strong PTQ baselines such as QuaRot, SpinQuant, and FlatQuant. Experiments on LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 show that PhaseQuant consistently improves perplexity and zero-shot QA performance under W4A4KV4 quantization, while achieving 1.05$\times$--1.07$\times$ throughput improvement with modest memory overhead. These results demonstrate a practical path toward robust low-bit LLM inference.
items.author: Zimo Zhao, Maolin Wang, Bowen Yu, Bowen Liu, Xiao Han, Xiangyu Zhao

items.title: Novel Aspects of IEEE SA P3109 Arithmetic Formats for Machine Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.04028v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The IEEE P3109 draft standard defines a parameterized family of binary floating-point formats and associated operations, with a focus on facilitating machine learning. These formats allow efficient and consistent representation of values in a small number of bits. The defined formats are parameterized over width and precision in bits, signedness, and the presence of infinities. Operations are defined by decoding floating-point values to the set of closed extended reals: the reals augmented with positive and negative infinity and NaN (Not a Number). Explicit treatment of NaN and infinite operands ensures that only real arithmetic is invoked in operation definitions. Extensive rounding and saturation modes are defined; stochastic rounding is included. Operations are exception-free, accelerating throughput, with exceptional situations communicated through return values, e.g., NaN. Operations on blocks of values sharing a common scale factor are defined in terms of the underlying operations in a uniform manner. System vendors may describe approximate implementations via a novel scale-invariant measure, akin to units in the last place. Standard function definitions and various other properties are mechanically verified and generated using formal specifications.
items.author: Andrew Fitzgibbon, Christoph M. Wintersteiger, Jeffrey Sarnoff

items.title: Interaction-Limited Safe Continuous-Time RL for Dynamical Medical Treatment
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.01051v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Dynamic medical treatment requires deciding treatment intensity and intervention timing, while patient states evolve continuously and adverse events may occur between clinical interactions. Most existing treatment learning methods assume fixed schedules or enforce safety only at discrete decision points. We propose Interaction-Limited Safe Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning, a framework that jointly optimizes treatment administration and clinical interaction timing under trajectory-level safety constraints. Our key idea is to reformulate the continuous time treatment problem as an option-based semi-Markov decision process, where each option specifies a continuous-time treatment policy and its duration. We develop a safety-tightening mechanism showing that suitably constructed constraints at interaction times guarantee safety over the full continuous-time trajectory with high probability. We further establish finite-sample guarantees for policy learning from logged treatment trajectories and introduce a practical data-driven conservative surrogate. Experiments show that the proposed adaptive interaction-timing mechanism improves both safety and treatment effectiveness over equidistant interaction schemes across different safe policy optimization methods.
items.author: Yuepeng Wang, Ken Kawano, Akifumi Wachi, Yongqi Zhou, Richard Weiss, Yoshihiko Fujisawa, Mehrshad Sadria, Ying Chen, Xin Liu, Sebastien Gros, Xiao Hu, Kyoung-Sook Kim, Mengmou Li, Katsuki Fujisawa, Kenji Wakabayashi, Xun Shen

items.title: Do You Even Need More Data? Rethinking LLM Deployment for Label-Scarce Tabular Classification with TabLens
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.24417v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Every tabular classification task requires sufficient labeled data. When labels are scarce, practitioners can collect more examples, encode domain expertise into features, or accept lower performance. Large language models offer an alternative by leveraging knowledge acquired during pretraining. This raises three questions: (i) can zero-shot inference reduce the need for labeled data; (ii) can a richer prompt reduce the need for more examples; and (iii) can encoded domain knowledge compensate for missing data? To answer each under explicit, testable conditions, we introduce TabLens, a benchmark of 91 real-world and synthetic datasets across eight domains, plus eight industrial datasets with free-text columns.
  First, below a complexity threshold estimable from a dataset's intrinsic dimensionality before running an LLM, zero-shot inference matches the accuracy of up to about 16 labeled examples. This holds whether the model generates an answer or, more cheaply, scores candidate labels by log-probabilities, which loses almost no accuracy except for the smallest models. Above the threshold, the advantage disappears. On datasets with free-text columns, however, zero-shot LLMs outperform 16-shot TabPFN-3 Plus without manual feature engineering.
