items.title: Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations
items.summary:
At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet. Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance. This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives [...]

Read More...

The post Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet.
  • Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance.
  • This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives significant advertiser value and capacity efficiency.

Inference fleets face a capacity paradox: They can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta, we built a system that aggregates these pockets into a shared opportunistic capacity pool and turns them into better ads recommendations. By putting otherwise idle capacity to work, the system helps people see more relevant ads and improves advertiser outcomes without requiring additional capacity orders.

Using this opportunistic capacity safely is difficult. It’s distributed across team-owned capacity allocations, regions, and accelerator types, and may be reclaimed with little notice. The ads inference system must therefore adapt workload as capacity supply changes without overloading the dedicated capacity that serves baseline workload.

We address this challenge with two complementary elasticity levers. Rank More Ads (RMA) adjusts the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages. Serve Better Models (SBM) adjusts the share of requests routed to a more powerful model.

Physical and logical isolation protects the capacity reserved for baseline serving. Separate feedback loops control RMA candidate volume and SBM model coverage, while value-aware load shedding at both servers and clients allows the system to degrade gracefully when capacity is suddenly reclaimed. Together, these mechanisms allow optional work to expand and contract with opportunistic capacity while protecting latency and reliability.

The Inference Capacity Paradox: Globally Constrained, but Locally Idle

Inference fleets must maintain enough capacity to meet demand under strict latency and reliability targets. However, demand and capacity rarely align perfectly across time, regions, resource combinations, and accelerator types. Capacity can therefore remain idle in parts of a fleet even when the fleet is constrained overall. Common causes include:

  • Peak-provisioning and demand-variation mismatch: Inference fleets must be provisioned for peak demand, while traffic varies by time of day and season. Capacity needed during peak periods can therefore remain temporarily idle when demand is lower.
  • Model-development and capacity-delivery timing mismatch: Inference capacity arrives on supply-chain timelines, whereas models are developed and launched on separate schedules. This creates a gap between when capacity becomes available and when models are ready to consume it.
  • Regional resource-ratio mismatch: Inference workloads require accelerators as well as supporting resources such as CPUs. When these resources are not available in the required proportions, one resource can remain idle while another limits serving capacity.
  • Accelerator-type mismatch: Inference fleets can span multiple accelerator vendors, generations, and architectures. Workloads are not always portable across these accelerator types, which can strand capacity on hardware that cannot immediately serve the available demand.

These mismatches create an industry-wide inference capacity paradox: A fleet can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta’s scale, these temporary pockets can collectively represent substantial capacity and create better ads recommendations when used safely.

From Fragmented Reservations to a Shared Opportunistic Capacity Pool

Across a heterogeneous fleet at Meta’s scale, instantaneous idle inference capacity is inevitable — even with proactive planning designed to minimize structural mismatches. However, because this capacity is inherently tied to fluctuating baseline demands, it comes with distinct operational constraints — it’s preemptible (can be reclaimed at any time), highly volatile in its availability, and carries no long-term guarantees.

To successfully consume this volatile resource without compromising baseline performance, workloads must exhibit certain structural properties:

  • A high degree of workload elasticity: The workload can quickly add or remove a large amount of optional work as the pool changes without affecting baseline expectations.
  • Sustained quality at scale: The workload can continue to meaningfully improve output quality across the range the opportunistic pool can supply. This type of workload often already uses a large amount of dedicated capacity due to this property.
  • Limited cross-service dependencies: A self-contained workload reduces the number of upstream and downstream systems that must respond to volatile capacity.

Two Complementary Elasticity Levers

Based on these structural properties, we identified two complementary levers that meet these criteria to consume this idle capacity and generate large value upside.

Rank More Ads (RMA)

For each user request, the ads recommendation system must select a small number of ads from millions of candidates in less than a second. The system uses a sequence of ranking stages in which increasingly powerful machine learning models evaluate progressively smaller candidate sets. The later stages only evaluate the top candidates from the previous stage.

RMA increases the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages when opportunistic capacity is available. Evaluating more candidates increases the chance of finding ads that are relevant to the user. Because the additional candidates pass through CPU-heavy upstream (e.g., retrieval, feature processing) as well as accelerator-heavy inference, RMA generally requires both CPU and accelerator surplus.

Serve Better Models (SBM)

The ads evaluation can use models with different levels of complexity. More powerful models can improve prediction quality, but it’s not efficient to use them for every request with dedicated capacity.

SBM changes the share of requests evaluated by the more powerful models as accelerator capacity changes. It keeps the number of ads entering the ranking stages constant, so upstream CPU demand remains comparatively stable. This allows SBM to use accelerator-only surplus that RMA cannot consume.

The SBM model-router component uses request-value signals to prioritize the requests expected to benefit most from a more powerful model.

Why Both Levers Are Needed

The two levers consume different combinations of resources. RMA requires both CPU and accelerator capacity, while SBM can use accelerator capacity without substantially increasing upstream CPU work. Together, they can use a broader range of opportunistic capacity than either lever alone.

The incremental impact of each lever also changes with traffic, current coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates to serve better ads or by routing more requests to a powerful model for improved prediction accuracy. We periodically adjust the allocation between RMA and SBM based on their measured performance and resource requirements.

Safely Using Opportunistic Capacity for Ads Inference

Opportunistic capacity can be reclaimed faster than the control loops that regulate work across a large serving fleet. We therefore design the system around one requirement – losing opportunistic capacity may reduce incremental ranking work, but it must not overload the capacity that serves the baseline workload. We support this requirement through isolated routing targets, two workload-specific feedback loops, and fast local load shedding.

Protecting Baseline Traffic Through Physical and Logical Isolation

Optional work must not consume the capacity reserved for baseline serving. SBM and RMA enforce this separation differently.

For SBM, the isolation is physical. The baseline and more powerful models use separate routing targets. Dedicated replicas are sized to serve requests with the baseline model, while replicas on opportunistic capacity serve requests selected for the more powerful model. When opportunistic capacity contracts, the system reduces the share of requests routed to the more powerful model. Those requests use the baseline model instead, whose capacity is already provisioned for them.

For RMA, the isolation is logical. The system calculates how much additional candidate-ranking work can be supported by the model replicas deployed on opportunistic capacity and uses total capacity to set a global budget for RMA. Each model replica may receive a mixture of baseline and additional work; individual requests do not need to be physically separated. Baseline traffic is protected by limiting the total incremental work to the amount that these replicas can support.

When opportunistic capacity contracts, RMA reduces its global candidate-volume target and SBM reduces its more-powerful-model coverage. In both cases, the system removes optional work rather than allowing it to spill onto the capacity reserved for baseline serving. This keeps baseline traffic within its latency and reliability targets.

Controlling Candidate Volume With Latency Feedback

RMA uses a closed feedback loop composed of a central proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller and client-side enforcement. Looking through a simplified lens, the controller uses observed tail latency to calculate a target for the number of ads sent to downstream ranking, and clients apply that target to new requests. When latency is below the target, the controller increases the number of ads ranked. When latency rises, it reduces the number. This allows RMA to use the latency signal, which is influenced by the capacity situation, to converge on a sustainable candidate volume as conditions change.

Routing Requests With Value-Aware Model Selection

SBM uses a corresponding feedback loop with central control and client-side routing. The central controller sets the target coverage for the more powerful model, and the client-side model router decides which eligible requests use that model and which continue through the baseline model.

The router uses a request-value signal to group requests into segments based on predicted likelihood of user engagement with the ad. An explore-and-exploit process periodically measures the incremental outcome of using the more powerful model in each segment and updates the allocation between the two models. This is necessary because the incremental benefit of the more powerful model does not always align with the absolute value of a request. The process also preserves exploratory traffic across segments so the system continues to collect the observations needed to adapt, rather than reinforcing an outdated routing decision.

A calibration loop keeps the realized traffic share close to its target as the traffic mix changes across regions and over time. When capacity contracts, the central controller reduces the target coverage and the client routes fewer requests to the more powerful model. Requests removed from the opportunistic path continue through the baseline model.

Multi-Layer Value-Aware Load Shedding

The RMA and SBM feedback loops continuously align opportunistic work with available capacity, but their central components operate on the order of minutes. A sudden preemption can therefore remove capacity before clients receive new targets. The system adds value-aware protection for both workloads that can react immediately:

Server-side shedding: If the opportunistic pool loses capacity before the clients’ view has caught up, servers immediately remove lower-value opportunistic work. For RMA, they reduce the number of candidates processed within individual requests; SBM applies an equivalent value-aware shedding policy to requests routed to the more powerful model. This absorbs rapid changes close to the serving bottleneck.

Client-side shedding: The RMA and SBM clients use the latest controller targets as the guideline but also observe the server status directly. When it’s observed that the server is overloaded, clients shed lower-value opportunistic work directly, i.e., RMA requests fewer additional ads, while SBM routes fewer requests to the more powerful model.

Both forms of load shedding react within a few milliseconds, bridging the interval before the controller-client loops converge. Both server-side shedding and client-side shedding use value signals when selecting work to remove, which minimizes the effect during the transition.

Current Work and What Comes Next

Increasing Workload Elasticity

We aim to use more opportunistic capacity productively by extending the operating range of RMA and SBM and broadening the set of elasticity levers. For RMA, this means supporting higher candidate volumes across ranking stages; for SBM, using more powerful models that turn additional accelerator capacity into better predictions. We are also developing new levers such as precomputation elasticity, which performs work ahead of request time and is therefore less constrained by the location and timing of live traffic.

Expanding the Usable Capacity Pool

Opportunistic capacity is fragmented across regions and accelerator types, and it’s useful only when compatible models and supporting resources are available in the same place. We are expanding model portability and cross-region inference capabilities so that more of the available capacity can be used efficiently.

Automating Value-Based Capacity Allocation

The incremental impact of each lever changes with traffic, coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates or by routing more requests to a powerful model. We are building an optimization-based system to automatically adjust the allocation of AI inference capacity to its possible elasticity levers based on the benefits to users and advertisers. The goal is to maximize the return of the capacity subject to the constraints that each use case has in terms of regional constraints, hardware compatibility, and durability requirements for the idle capacity, among others.

Acknowledgments

This work reflects critical contributions from a cross functional v-team across Meta:
David Amsallem, Mohit Bharti, Maddie Digne, Stephen Dimmick, Maomao Ding, Amit Dutta, Sebin George, Aashik Gowda, Atul Goyal, Mohak Goyal, Nelson Guo, Tiger Hao, Yaning Huang, Dianshi Li, Yang Li, Bai Liu, Bofeng Liu, Wei Liu, Yisi Liu, Daniel Molina Hurtado, Maciej Naruszewicz, Arka Pal, Annan Pan, Brian Park, Brian Peschka, Michael Shao, Bikash Sharma, Alexander Sun, Weiman Sun, Kaiyue Tao, Patrick Taylor, Kevin Tong, Ellie Wen, Chao Xie, Lu Yang, Sihan You, Hansen Zhang, and Anthony Zhu

items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.summary:
StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutoring tools before they are tested with learners. It models how individuals may engage with tutors, giving feedback to improve tutor performance across subjects like chess, writing, and mathematics.

The post Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers
  • AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale 
  • StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student 
  • The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance 
  • Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor 

In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration.

StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. 

Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. 

Measuring what a student simulator needs to do

A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable.

Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.

StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance.

These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. 

Training personalized simulators from sparse student records

StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.

Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.  

StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. 

The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. 

StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.

Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors

The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.  

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. 

The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. 

Looking ahead

StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. 

The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. 

The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

items.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
items.summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at […]
items.content:
As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably.

At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. 

NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure.

Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing.

NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances 

At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: 

  • NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. 
  • NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. 
  • Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations.
  • Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era.
  • NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics.
  • NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs.

Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. 

The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance.

 

Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP

NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative.

Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale.

For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs.

MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse.

The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time.

Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories.

 

NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory

NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale.

At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: 

  • NVIDIA Config Manager: Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/
  • NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine: Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins
  • NVIDIA Rack Management Service: Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management.
  • Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller: Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days.

Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. 

Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform.

 

NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories

For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on.

At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta to publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. 

The OCP Grid Resilience Specification, published by Google, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds.

With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers.

Being NVIDIA DSX reference design-compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. For operators building Vera Rubin AI factories, there’s now a straight line from open community standard to a running system.

 

Visionbay.ai Designs 800VDC AI Factory for the Vera Rubin Era

As AI factories grow larger and more powerful, one challenge looms over them all: delivering enough power to the accelerated computing systems driving the next generation of AI.

At OCP, Visionbay unveiled plans for K-1, a next-generation AI factory platform designed around an 800 VDC architecture and built with future NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments in mind. The project combines NVIDIA’s 800 VDC reference architecture with power and thermal technologies from Vertiv to create a scalable foundation for high-density AI infrastructure.

The design addresses a growing industry challenge. As AI training, inference and reasoning workloads expand, rack power densities continue to rise. Traditional low-voltage power distribution becomes increasingly difficult to scale, requiring more copper, more cabling and more power-conversion equipment.

By adopting NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture, K-1 creates a path toward higher-density AI infrastructure while preserving flexibility for existing deployments. Rather than requiring a complete transition on day one, the platform is designed to phase in 800 VDC distribution where it delivers the greatest benefit, helping operators prepare for future generations of accelerated computing without extensive facility redesign.

The architecture is designed around cluster-level power centers that centralize AC-to-DC conversion and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources. The approach simplifies downstream power delivery, supports modular expansion and creates repeatable building blocks for future AI factory growth.

K-1 also reflects the system-level design philosophy behind NVIDIA AI factories, where power, cooling and computing are engineered together. With support for liquid-cooled infrastructure, scalable power distribution and future Vera Rubin-class deployments, the project demonstrates how ecosystem partners are translating NVIDIA’s AI factory architecture into deployable infrastructure designed for the next era of accelerated computing.

 

Meta and NVIDIA Advance AI Networking With Spectrum-6 and Multiplane Technology

At the event, Meta and NVIDIA announced that Meta is adopting NVIDIA Spectrum-6 102.4Tb/s Ethernet switches to build larger, higher-performance NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories on open networking. 

Spectrum-6 delivers twice the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4, and provides a lossless Ethernet AI fabric at 200G per lane, with high effective bandwidth and performance isolation that keeps one job’s traffic from slowing another’s.

Meta’s Spectrum-6-based switch, N-IceCube, slots into IcePack, Meta’s 100T, liquid-cooled rack. N-IceCube runs the Facebook Open Switching System (FBOSS), Meta’s open source network operating system that contributed to OCP to support efficient networking at hyperscale. 

FBOSS is built on the Switch Abstraction Interface, an OCP standard NVIDIA helped develop, providing a vendor-independent way of controlling switch hardware. Together, these technologies support agentic AI factories of more than 100,000 GPUs that train and serve massive mixture-of-experts models.

The announcement marks the next step in a collaboration that combines Meta’s experience operating AI infrastructure at hyperscale with NVIDIA’s networking technology.

At the heart of this collaboration is Spectrum-X Multiplane technology, enabled by Spectrum-6 switches and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. Multiplane distributes GPU traffic in hardware across up to eight independent network planes, enabling AI factories to scale beyond 100,000 GPUs with fewer switch tiers and lower infrastructure costs. Multiple paths between GPUs improve network utilization and resilience: when a component fails, traffic shifts to the remaining planes, keeping GPUs productive and AI applications running, even at reduced bandwidth.

Meta and NVIDIA worked together to strengthen that resilience through deployment experience and rapid engineering iteration. The teams validated improvements across on-premises and cloud environments. 

“We are excited about our close partnership with NVIDIA in making multiplane fabrics operationally scalable and performant, a critical requirement both for our own infrastructure builds and for our joint cloud partners,” said Omar Baldonado, senior director of data center and AI networking at Meta. “Extending FBOSS to Spectrum ASICs means we can run that same software stack across our fabrics, and Meta’s new Spectrum-based switch, N-IceCube, brings that into Icepack – our liquid-cooled 102.4T network rack for scale-out that connects upcoming generations of accelerators in our fleet.”

Together, Meta and NVIDIA are developing an architecture and operational playbook that other AI infrastructure operators can adopt, turning lessons from demanding production workloads into more scalable, resilient and efficient AI factories.

 

With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco Reinvent Pluggable Optics for AI Factory Scale

As AI factories scale to support larger models and surging inference demand, every component of the infrastructure stack must deliver more performance, efficiency and simplicity — right down to the network connection itself. 

At OCP, NVIDIA and Cisco announced plans for USFP, a new optical pluggable transceiver module form factor designed to help AI factory builders scale next-generation AI fabrics while improving bandwidth density and power efficiency.

With approximately the same footprint as the widely adopted 200Gb/s-per-lane OSFP form factor, USFP will provide a path to 400Gb/s-per-lane networking and will extend a transceiver-based deployment model already proven across generations of data center networks. Packing 16 full-duplex lanes with plans to scale up to 32 lanes, USFP will deliver four times the bandwidth density of traditional 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optics. 

The result is the ability to connect more compute resources without adding network tiers that can increase latency, power consumption and complexity.

The new form factor is designed for the scale and efficiency demands of next generation AI factories, supporting higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the flexibility and serviceability that have made pluggable optics a mainstay of modern data centers. It also will deliver roughly 1.3x greater power efficiency, helping operators move more data with less energy.   

To help drive an open ecosystem, NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol on cages, connectors and modules, with plans to advance USFP through a community-led, multi-source effort. Together, the companies are laying the foundation for more scalable, efficient and interoperable AI factory networking.

 

Google Falcon Transport Supports NVIDIA ConnectX-10 for Interoperable AI Networking

NVIDIA and Google also announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs, helping improve network efficiency for large-scale AI infrastructure. 

Falcon is a transport protocol designed to deliver data reliably over Ethernet networks, which can otherwise drop packets under congestion. It supports AI and storage workloads through multipath load balancing, programmable congestion control, hardware loss recovery and per-connection security.

This collaboration combines NVIDIA hardware acceleration with DOCA software to implement Falcon and extend NVIDIA networking to Google’s data center transport. NVIDIA and Google NICs can communicate over a common transport while applications retain standard RDMA programming interfaces.

By distributing traffic across paths, adapting to congestion, recovering dropped packets and protecting connections, Falcon helps workloads make better use of available bandwidth and maintain predictable performance as Ethernet fabrics scale.

Learn more by joining NVIDIA at OCP.

In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human…

items.title: v2.1.296
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a code key to the Claude apps gateway's managed.policies[]: the same settings as cli, also applied in Claude Desktop's Code tab; beside desktop, it turns on Claude Desktop's gateway mode
  • Added autoCompactWindow to subagent frontmatter and --agents definitions, so a subagent can auto-compact earlier than the main conversation's window
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_SUBAGENT_MODEL to run every workflow agent on one model while other subagents keep theirs
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS environment variable to set a longer maximum delay for the backoff when retrying an overloaded (529) request
  • Added a note in /plugin on a plugin whose hooks are left out because another enabled plugin has the same name
  • Added an allow_large option to the Read tool so Claude can read a text file past the usual size limits in one call when it needs the whole file and the context has room
  • Fixed managed-settings PreToolUse hooks that deny a tool call with "continue": false, and managed prompt hooks that block one, refusing the call but not ending the turn
  • Fixed PostToolUse hooks in managed settings not applying updatedMCPToolOutput in some sessions
  • Fixed headless sessions starting a folder's .mcp.json or plugin MCP server that was switched off for that folder, after changing directory or reloading plugins
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway that serves allowedProviders with "gateway" locking out laptops that name that gateway in user settings
  • Fixed a saved Claude apps gateway sign-in being ignored on machines whose managed settings set forceLoginMethod to gateway with no forceLoginGatewayUrl (regression in 2.1.295)
  • Fixed --teleport opening an empty conversation when the session's history could not be read
  • Fixed token counts for Haiku 5.5 and other models that take only adaptive thinking, which failed behind some gateways and were counted with budget thinking elsewhere
  • Fixed resumed subagents being told that the user rejected a tool call that a session shutdown had interrupted
  • Fixed hook output being altered when it contained text resembling a plugin hint tag
  • Fixed secret redaction in shared transcripts and debug logs missing some values that follow a key with no value, including in JSON written inside a shell string
  • Fixed a stray 52;c;… escape sequence printed on screen after copying in older VTE-based terminals such as MATE Terminal
  • Fixed toasts and notifications waiting unseen for as long as the /diff panel or dialog was open
  • Fixed Esc or an interrupt during a UserPromptSubmit hook or a mod's prompt.submit hook ending headless sessions, clearing the typed prompt, or letting the unchecked prompt through
  • Fixed SessionStart hooks of a plugin loaded after a headless session starts being skipped when a different plugin with the same name, or another spelling of it, had already run
  • Fixed claude self-hosted-runner printing misleading errors when registration is refused: it now names the org admin setting, or says a restarted on-demand runner needs a fresh work order
  • Fixed a self-hosted runner session's git fetch, pull and push failing while another session of the same repository starts on a runner with --capacity above 1
  • Fixed workflow scripts silently truncating results, agent options and other values nested deeper than about 20,000 levels, and deeply nested results writing huge task output files
  • Fixed a plugin's served $ methods running in the main session's working directory instead of the calling agent's, and ignoring the turn their calling hook holds
  • Fixed $.agent.register succeeding from a mod's hook that was still running after the mod was reloaded or removed; the call is now refused
  • Fixed $.http.fetch in mods refusing a HEAD request when the response declares a Content-Length over the 4 MiB body limit
  • Fixed claude plugin marketplace add, marketplace update and plugin install failing with an internal error for a marketplace named like constructor; add now refuses such names clearly
  • Fixed a plugin secret named constructor or prototype being deleted by the next save of that plugin's options
  • Fixed cloud sessions skipping auto mode's checks on Claude in Chrome actions that a saved permission allows when their feature flags had not loaded
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a finished turn after a restart when an MCP tool result had ended that turn
  • Fixed Bash permission checks auto-approving some commands that assign the BASH_ARGV0 shell variable and then use it; these now prompt for approval
  • Fixed Edit and NotebookEdit replacing every non-ASCII character in files that are not valid UTF-8 (Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GBK); such edits are now refused
  • Fixed a prompt sent just after ← being run twice, once unseen in the foreground, when the background service was slow to answer
  • Fixed a prompt sent while SessionStart hooks were still running vanishing when ← moved the session to the background; it is still not sent, but ↑ now brings it back
  • Fixed a late-loading plugin's SessionStart hook output reaching the new conversation after /clear in headless sessions
  • Fixed PowerShell commands not seeing variables that hooks write to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE (when the file holds only plain assignments)
  • Fixed Claude calling cloud sessions non-interactive and suggesting /mcp or claude mcp when an MCP server needs authentication
  • Fixed /code-review ending on a raw JSON array in cloud sessions, the Agent SDK and IDE integrations; the findings now print as a numbered list
  • Fixed auto mode occasionally refusing one update to your own artifact, saying its sharing had changed when it had not
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai never finishing their install, and being downloaded again at every sync, when several sessions share a config directory
  • Fixed a plugin synced from claude.ai being disabled when the marketplace dependency it declares was also synced from claude.ai
  • Fixed a startup hang on macOS when plugin paths copied from a Linux machine pointed under /home
  • Fixed the Workflow tool refusing script files with CRLF line endings, such as files checked out on Windows
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry tool_result events missing git_commit_id after git commit -q or git -C <dir> commit
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping a message from the saved transcript when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029)
  • Fixed claude purge leaving a prompt in the history file when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029)
  • Windows: Fixed PowerShell commands longer than about 1 KB always asking for permission, so allow rules and read-only detection now apply up to 32 KB
  • Windows: Fixed stdio MCP servers being force-killed at shutdown; stdin now closes first and the process tree is killed only if the server is still running after 300 ms
  • Windows: Fixed claude plugin install failing for GitHub owner/repo plugin sources on machines with no GitHub SSH key; the clone is now retried over HTTPS
  • Windows: Fixed rm -rf /c/Users/<name> in Git Bash not asking in bypass permissions mode
  • Improved fullscreen mode: the link under the mouse pointer is now underlined to show it can be opened
  • Improved transcript toggle (ctrl+o) responsiveness in code-heavy conversations by caching syntax-highlighted code blocks
  • Improved Claude Desktop's Code tab behind a Claude apps gateway: when a session can't start, including on a machine not set up for the gateway's code settings, the reason shows as a reply
  • Improved the errors for a refused cloud session: they now say why your organization's policy couldn't be loaded, and name an API key or auth token that overrides your claude.ai login
  • Improved --debug output to name unrecognized frontmatter fields in custom agent files, with a hint for likely typos
  • Improved auto mode: a tool call that wasn't run because auto mode's check had no usable answer now shows as a dim "Not run" row instead of a red error
  • Improved --debug output for hooks: command hooks on tool calls, prompts, SessionStart and Stop now log their command, plugin, outcome and duration when they finish, so a slow hook is identifiable
  • Improved CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC: a large transcript file is no longer rewritten when that would free under 10% of it
  • Updated /cost, the status line, --max-budget-usd and the SDK's cost figures to price Sonnet 5.5 cache reads at $0.10 per million tokens (was $0.20)
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill: lighter violet for the seventh series in light mode, softer primary text in dark mode, and compact y-axis labels like 1K
  • Changed the default limit on MCP tool descriptions sent up front and on MCP server instructions from 2,048 to 4,096 characters
  • Changed ←: a turn or ! command started while the session moves to the background is now stopped instead of finishing out of sight
  • [VSCode] Fixed claudeCode.spinnerVerbs missing from the extension's settings, so settings.json now completes and validates it; a malformed value no longer breaks the chat panel
  • [VSCode] Changed Claude in Chrome to ask before browser actions in every session, including one connected with @browser, as the terminal does; allowing a site for the session stops repeat asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed chat links written as a full Windows path, such as C:\repo\file.ts or file:///C:/repo/file.ts, not opening the file on Windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the working indicator still animating when reduced motion is turned on in your OS, in VS Code, or with the prefersReducedMotion setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt cache clock reading warm after the panel caught up on messages late, such as after the display was off or a remote window reconnected
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a status filter to the Sessions and Runners lists on a self-hosted environment's Activity tab in admin settings; you can pick several statuses at once
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed every cloud session waiting for a self-hosted runner showing the same queue position; each now shows how many sessions are ahead of it
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a message you send while Claude is still replying in a cloud session jumping above that reply when it finishes; it now stays below it, including after a reload
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude in Slack to show the footer with the session link, model and cost only on its newest reply in a thread; the reply before it drops the footer
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed links to URLs that contain parentheses breaking in some of Claude's Slack replies and task checklists, which showed stray bracket text and opened the wrong page
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude's Slack replies drawing color swatches beside codes that only look like hex colors, such as six-digit pull request numbers
  • [Claude Tag] Added creating, editing and deleting workspace and channel memory files on the Activity page's Memory tab for members with the Claude Tag Admin permission
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the plugin confirmation card Claude posts in a Slack channel showing a plugin's ID instead of its name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack posting a card to remove a plugin the channel's own settings don't include; it now explains where the plugin comes from instead
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes losing its reply when a session in a self-hosted environment moved to a new runner partway through a task
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review check sometimes staying "in progress" on a pull request after the review finished; it now shows the review's result
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review admin settings to say why a setting couldn't be saved, such as a policy restriction, instead of a generic failure message

items.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
items.summary: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through […]
items.content:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.

Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.

Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

 

Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment

Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.

Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.

DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.

Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

 

Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow

 

Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.

Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.

 

Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins

Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.

To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.

Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.

Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.

 

Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation

Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.

Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.

Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

 

Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation

Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training.

Explore the Onshape importer guide.

 

Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser

Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.

The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.

Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.

 

Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments

A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.

The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. 

Explore USD Content Agents.

Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.
