items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added onFailure: "block" for command and HTTP hooks: a hook that can't start, times out, or exits with an unexpected code blocks the action instead of letting it through
  • Added Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) support: terminals that implement it can show whether Claude Code is working, waiting on you, or done
  • Added quoted text to the /copy picker, so a drafted message copies without its > markers
  • Added a warning to claude plugin install, enable, disable and marketplace add when the settings file they write to does not load
  • Added a line on stderr, when it is a terminal, that says what a claude -p run is waiting for when it stays open after its last turn
  • Added support for timeouts.upstream_ttfb_ms on the Claude apps gateway's Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and other cloud upstreams: a value you set now limits how long a stream may take to start there, after which it fails over or gets a 502
  • Added a "Backgrounding cancelled" message when you stop the turn while ← is waiting for the current tool to finish
  • Added an optional models list to every Claude apps gateway upstream: only the listed models are sent there, on failover too, and one * in an entry is a wildcard
  • Added support for forceLoginMethod: "gateway" and forceLoginGatewayUrl in your own user settings on machines with no managed settings, so /login opens on that Claude apps gateway
  • Added advice to claude plugin validate when a plugin's README has no install line: it prints the line to paste and never changes the exit code, even with --strict
  • Added upstream_request_id to the Claude apps gateway's inference audit event: the request ID from Amazon Bedrock, the Anthropic API or another upstream, for support cases
  • Added $.ui.notify for mods: raises a native notification through your own notification setting and says which channel sent it
  • Added children to a mod's Button: strings and Text, so a row of a list is one pressable with a chip or a dim detail inside
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS to limit how long unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG) waits out 429 and 529 errors
  • Added a request-id header to the Claude apps gateway's successful inference responses, so request_id in Claude Code telemetry matches the gateway's audit log
  • Fixed every request failing on a [1m] model when a gateway, Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry refuses the context-1m beta; Claude Code now resends without it
  • Fixed claude -p text output dropping earlier responses when background work started another turn; each turn's response now prints when the turn ends
  • Fixed remote MCP servers in headless and SDK sessions staying disconnected after an outage longer than 15 seconds, or reconnecting in a tight loop to a server that drops each connection right after it connects; repeated drops now back off, up to 30s
  • Fixed remote MCP connections being dropped when a server's error reply happened to contain a network error name
  • Fixed MCP servers that repeat a pagination cursor being asked for the same page up to 20 times at every connect
  • Fixed CSS, JavaScript and XML files returned by MCP tools being saved as .bin, which the Read tool refuses; font and icon files now get their own extension too
  • Fixed Bash tool calls failing when the model passes command_description instead of description
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome not applying a site deny rule written with port 80 (host:80) to plain http:// pages on that host
  • Fixed /plugin's Errors tab removing a marketplace that failed to load, and uninstalling its plugins, on Enter without asking first
  • Fixed claude plugin marketplace add reporting success for a marketplace whose name no plugin can be installed under; such an add is now refused
  • Fixed CLAUDE_AUTO_BACKGROUND_TASKS moving a subagent to the background while an edit or shell command waited behind it, which started that call before the subagent finished
  • Fixed PushNotification saying a push was not sent in claude remote-control sessions right after a phone message, without the /config toggle, or when started from inside Claude Code
  • Fixed files sent from remote sessions being refused as "could not be vouched for" when more than 256 were sent at once
  • Fixed a rare failure to load managed settings at startup right after a login refresh
  • Fixed /tui exiting without a message, or with a raw system error, when Claude Code could not be started again
  • Fixed a link address shown as text being hidden by a colour or conceal style a reply left on, including where it wraps in a table or a question preview
  • Fixed Fable models listed in availableModels not appearing in the /model picker for sessions signed in to a Claude apps gateway; such a model now shows its built-in row in place of a modelPicker row added for the same model
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's admin spend view showing a developer's old groups and group cap after their session stopped carrying groups
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC hiding the Claude apps gateway spend limit in /usage and the status line. The spend limit request goes to the gateway the session is signed in to
  • Fixed subagents in their own linked worktree being shown the parent session's git branch, status and recent commits
  • Fixed Claude stopping at the end of the current tool when text typed in the prompt cancelled backgrounding with ←; Claude now keeps working in the foreground
  • Fixed --tools and --restricted not applying to built-in tools that register after launch, and deprecated tool names reaching tools outside the caller's tool set
  • Fixed an interrupt not ending the turn until a timeout while Claude waited for an MCP server's resource list
  • Fixed a mod's hook being handed a deeply nested tool input cut short with no error, so a guard could pass content it never saw
  • Fixed Esc not stopping a self-paced /loop that was moved to the background with ←; cancelling a pending wakeup now shows a notice
  • Fixed commands and hooks in background sessions inheriting FORCE_COLOR=3, which put color escape codes into the output Claude reads
  • Fixed claude agents starting a new background service as it exited when both were stopped with a session open (for example at a reboot), which could delay shutdown and restart an interrupted session
  • Fixed a custom agent named worker being shown as "Agent" in auto-mode denial notices and in the activity lists of task detail views
  • Fixed Bash permission checks for for-loops over glob patterns, improving permission-check accuracy
  • Fixed forked skills invoked from Workflow subagents delivering their results to the main conversation instead of the invoking agent
  • Fixed in-process agent teammates failing their first SendMessage call until they loaded the tool through tool search
  • Fixed Claude being told on resume that an unfinished background workflow may have been stopped by TaskStop, which can never be the cause
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop a long-running MCP tool call from the tasks panel or a connected client
  • Fixed a background session's /loop stopping without notice when its next wakeup came due while the session's process was down; the session now says so and Claude is told
  • Fixed raw terminal hyperlink bytes in a reply or a teammate's message being drawn as a clickable link with a hidden address
  • Fixed plugin marketplaces whose repository has large git submodules failing to add or refresh: only the submodules that hold plugin files are now fetched
  • Fixed the /advisor dialog showing a checkmark on a saved advisor model that is no longer available; it now opens on "No advisor"
  • Fixed the notification for an MCP tool call that moved to the background showing a shortened task id
  • Fixed vim mode's ~ moving the cursor past the last character of a line, so x after it did nothing, and 3~ running on into the next line
  • Fixed the cursor landing one character too far after pasting accented text copied from macOS (such as a file name) into the middle of the prompt
  • Fixed the terminal freezing, with ctrl+c ignored, when a response ran to tens of thousands of lines
  • Fixed calls a mod makes while it reloads during a plugin hooks worker restart getting past another mod's guard hook that has a .catch; such calls are now refused
  • Fixed plugins whose hooks module nests code thousands of levels deep failing to load or validate with a bare stack-overflow message
  • Fixed claude plugin test passing a session.append hook that removes tool call, tool result or thinking blocks that a real session keeps
  • Fixed Claude not being told it can resume background subagents with SendMessage after a session was killed and resumed a second time
  • Fixed a file being treated as already read after a Bash command such as cat ran without printing it
  • Fixed plugin options named constructor or prototype always reading as their default and never reloading the plugin when edited
  • Fixed a mod's hot reload missing a save made while /reload-plugins or session start was reading the mod's files
  • Fixed the mod hot-reloading question being asked again every turn for the whole session when it is approved without picking an answer
  • Fixed /model, /fast and /output-style saving their setting without asking a plugin's config.set hook
  • Fixed bold text being drawn faint in piped output when it directly follows dim text
  • Fixed replies whose quotes nest deeper every few lines freezing the terminal for seconds and using gigabytes of memory
  • Fixed a mod's hot reload missing a save made within a few milliseconds of its last reload, which left the mod on its old version until the next save
  • Fixed claude mcp serve background Bash results not naming the output file, and its tool description promising a notification that never arrives
  • Fixed an async SessionStart hook's unchanged context being added to the conversation again on every resume
  • Fixed variables a SessionStart hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool after an in-app /resume or /branch
  • Fixed a skill's allowed-tools and effort being dropped when the Skill tool finished before the response stream ended, which denied the skill's Bash commands in -p runs
  • Fixed a tampered cache of server-managed settings making a person's own plugin count as organization-managed on machines whose managed settings list or enable plugins
  • Fixed Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.x Sonnet sessions being offered tool search, which those models reject, where feature flags are unavailable
  • Fixed generated type files being written into a --plugin-dir plugin's folder in -p and SDK sessions; they are now written only where a mod is being developed
  • Fixed text with tabs or bidirectional control characters losing its end at the edge of the screen or drawing over nearby rows
  • Fixed /model saying a Max effort pick was saved as your default for new sessions; Max applies to the current session only
  • Fixed an async hook's JSON output being ignored when it is printed over several lines
  • Fixed the Read tool rejecting calls with an empty pages parameter instead of treating it as omitted
  • Fixed project-scope plugins not loading in VS Code on Windows due to drive-letter casing (#74612)
  • Fixed plugin install and uninstall at project or local scope on Windows missing the install record, or adding a second one, when only the drive letter's case differs
  • Fixed a queued message being lost when pulled back into the prompt with ↑ or Esc just after ←: prompt history now keeps it
  • Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the whole session when an SDK host closed its enable question before anyone answered; the question is now asked up to three times
  • Fixed a prompt that a mod's prompt.submit hook rewrote or dropped still being saved as typed to prompt history and to the transcript's queued-prompt records
  • Fixed non-interactive sessions telling you about MCP servers that need authentication when your request doesn't use them
  • Fixed the claude_code.auth OpenTelemetry login event not being emitted on Claude apps gateway sign-in. The event is exported when OpenTelemetry is configured on the machine or the session is already signed in to the gateway
  • Fixed a plugin that adds very large interfaces getting another plugin unloaded when the plugin hooks worker stalls
  • Fixed Edit treating a file as fully read when its contents changed without its modification time advancing
  • Fixed short command output with Windows line endings (CRLF) being drawn on a single line
  • Fixed a stopped scheduled task coming back on resume after a rewind, and a scheduled task being lost on resume after Esc or a rewind following a compaction
  • Fixed the terminal freezing for seconds or minutes while syntax highlighting code with very long lines, long runs of blank lines, or unclosed strings and heredocs
  • Fixed temporary files left under ~/.claude/seed-admin by an interrupted /ultrareview upload never being removed by the retention cleanup
  • Fixed Desktop and SDK sessions refusing to switch back to auto mode until restart after disableAutoMode was removed from settings
  • Fixed claude.ai-synced plugin hooks failing with "Plugin directory does not exist" in long-running sessions after another session synced a plugin update
  • Fixed the prompt sent after a /rewind being lost, and the removed turns coming back, when the session was moved to the background or resumed after being killed
  • Fixed cloud sessions hanging when a mod's session.receive hook asked for permission before passing a message on
  • Fixed macOS background sessions that restart together after an update sometimes running outside the stable app wrapper, so folder-access prompts could reappear
  • Fixed an MCP sign-in or reconnect that finishes late in headless and SDK sessions relisting a server set with setMcpServers() as your own
  • Fixed changing the auto-update channel in /config saving before a plugin's config.set hook was asked
  • macOS: Fixed a file count at session start that could reach other apps' data and raise the "access data from other apps" prompt when a session starts in the home folder or above it
  • Improved token counts behind a Claude apps gateway on Amazon Bedrock, which /context and large file reads use: the gateway now gets them from AWS's CountTokens API instead of a one-token model request. Grant bedrock:CountTokens to use it
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway to log a warning every 30 seconds while its PostgreSQL database is read-only, saying what fails and how to recover
  • Improved the status shown in Remote Control, claude.ai and the desktop app for a session waiting on a permission prompt to name an MCP tool by its server and readable name instead of its mcp__server__tool identifier
  • Improved background requests behind a Claude apps gateway to use Haiku 4.5 instead of the session's model, falling back to the session's model where the gateway does not serve Haiku 4.5
  • Improved how the Claude apps gateway handles models not listed under models: in Amazon Bedrock regions outside AWS's US geography. AWS always refused those requests; the gateway now tries the model in your own region, and a refusal names the model to add
  • Improved headless rate_limit_event usage-limit warnings to say whether the account has extra usage turned on
  • Improved the built-in plugin-authoring skill: it no longer tells a session with no terminal to run terminal commands, and explains sharing a mod only when asked
  • Improved Grep input handling: a search sent with grep's -l, -c or -r flag now runs instead of failing the call
  • Improved claude plugin validate and plugin loading: when a hooks module is refused over a rebound top-level var, the error now names the line that rebinds it, the cause, and a fix
  • Improved the Workflow tool's scriptPath refusal: it now says to pass the script inline via script, the route that works in sessions without a Read tool
  • Improved what Claude is told when a large file it sends fails to upload with no reason given, so it reports the failure instead of shrinking the file
  • Changed MCP tool descriptions the model loads through tool search to be cut at 16,384 characters instead of 2,048
  • Changed subagents to preload at most 32 skills from the skills field, each once; a subagent with the Skill tool can still invoke the rest
  • Changed Ctrl+C at the idle prompt of an attached background session to leave a pending /loop wakeup alone, so pressing it twice detaches and the loop keeps running; press Esc to stop it
  • Changed claude agents stopped with its background service (macOS, or Linux without the service installed): running sessions now stop in about a minute unless it is run again, and a notice says so
  • Changed claude.ai connectors to negotiate MCP protocol version 2026-07-28 by default on installs that fetch no flags; MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION=legacy opts out
  • Changed Artifact pages with no background of their own to show on white instead of off-white
  • Changed what Claude and you read when a mod denies a tool call after the tool ran: it now says the tool ran and a plugin withheld its result
  • Changed tab stops to count from where a text starts instead of from the screen's left edge: an answer indented by 2 has its first stop 8 cells in, where it was 6
  • Changed the Artifact tool's permission prompts with telemetry disabled to the same five questions other installs get, instead of asking before each read of someone else's artifact and each data edit
  • Changed scheduled and Run now routine runs in installs with telemetry disabled to publish new private artifacts, and update your own, without asking, as in other installs
  • Changed toasts from your organization's mods to show ahead of other mods' toasts instead of waiting behind them
  • Changed the Claude apps gateway to start with a warning and serve a desktop policy key its bundled Claude Desktop schema doesn't know, so new Desktop settings need no gateway upgrade
  • Changed WebSocket (ws) MCP servers: a message over 16 MiB is no longer parsed and closes the connection, the limit the other transports already have
  • [VSCode] Added a chat row for files Claude sends you: click a file's name to open it in the editor; Claude's caption shows underneath, and the row stays visible in Focus view
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Fork conversation from here" and Rewind's conversation restore failing with "Message not found in session" after a background agent's activity or one of the panel's own status lines
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+Shift+Tab, Cmd+Shift+Tab and Alt+Shift+Tab in the chat input also switching the permission mode, and Ctrl+Tab accepting the suggested prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed keyboard focus bouncing between two Claude views visible at once, which could send typed text to the wrong conversation
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the runner to stop passing CCR_AUTO_MODE_ALLOW, CCR_AUTO_MODE_ENVIRONMENT and CCR_AUTO_MODE_SOFT_DENY into a session's environment
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed git fetches being cut off while the git server was still reporting progress on a large repository; CLAUDE_RUNNER_FETCH_SERVER_PROGRESS_CAP_MS tunes or turns off the wait
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a message sent right after unarchiving a cloud session sometimes getting no reply because no container could start for it
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed some older routines starting their runs without ever giving Claude their saved prompt; those routines now run their prompt again
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved how quickly a cloud session catches up after its connection drops: activity you missed now appears all at once instead of row by row
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the setup script box in the cloud environment form: it starts taller, grows with your script, and can be resized by dragging
  • [Claude Tag] Changed the settings confirmation cards Claude posts in a Slack channel to stay open for 30 minutes instead of 10
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude's notice that a channel shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces uses organization defaults to post only when someone mentions Claude, at most once a month
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed channel links and @-mentions in a forked thread's "Continued from" card showing as raw Slack codes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Slack's Working status spinning on under a thread after @Claude !restart had already confirmed the restart
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed another app's or bot's @claude going unanswered in a busy channel where Claude had stopped reading untagged messages
  • [Claude Tag] Added a confirmation in Claude Tag admin settings before adding a channel manager moves that member to Custom roles, which can remove their other access
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review re-reviews saying no issues were found while earlier findings were still open; the comment now says how many remain open
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review still skipping a large CLAUDE.md's rules when the pull request edits that file
  • Fixed web searches and agent hook evaluations taking much longer at xhigh and max effort

  • Fixed an async hook's JSON output being ignored when it is printed over several lines
  • Fixed the Read tool rejecting calls with an empty pages parameter instead of treating it as omitted
  • Fixed project-scope plugins not loading in VS Code on Windows due to drive-letter casing (#74612)
  • Fixed plugin install and uninstall at project or local scope on Windows missing the install record, or adding a second one, when only the drive letter's case differs
  • Fixed a queued message being lost when pulled back into the prompt with ↑ or Esc just after ←: prompt history now keeps it
  • Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the whole session when an SDK host closed its enable question before anyone answered; the question is now asked up to three times
  • Fixed a prompt that a mod's prompt.submit hook rewrote or dropped still being saved as typed to prompt history and to the transcript's queued-prompt records
  • Fixed non-interactive sessions telling you about MCP servers that need authentication when your request doesn't use them
  • Fixed the claude_code.auth OpenTelemetry login event not being emitted on Claude apps gateway sign-in. The event is exported when OpenTelemetry is configured on the machine or the session is already signed in to the gateway
  • Fixed a plugin that adds very large interfaces getting another plugin unloaded when the plugin hooks worker stalls
  • Fixed Edit treating a file as fully read when its contents changed without its modification time advancing
  • Fixed short command output with Windows line endings (CRLF) being drawn on a single line
  • Fixed a stopped scheduled task coming back on resume after a rewind, and a scheduled task being lost on resume after Esc or a rewind following a compaction
  • Fixed the terminal freezing for seconds or minutes while syntax highlighting code with very long lines, long runs of blank lines, or unclosed strings and heredocs
  • Fixed temporary files left under ~/.claude/seed-admin by an interrupted /ultrareview upload never being removed by the retention cleanup
  • Fixed Desktop and SDK sessions refusing to switch back to auto mode until restart after disableAutoMode was removed from settings
  • Fixed claude.ai-synced plugin hooks failing with "Plugin directory does not exist" in long-running sessions after another session synced a plugin update
  • Fixed the prompt sent after a /rewind being lost, and the removed turns coming back, when the session was moved to the background or resumed after being killed
  • Fixed cloud sessions hanging when a mod's session.receive hook asked for permission before passing a message on
  • Fixed macOS background sessions that restart together after an update sometimes running outside the stable app wrapper, so folder-access prompts could reappear
  • Fixed an MCP sign-in or reconnect that finishes late in headless and SDK sessions relisting a server set with setMcpServers() as your own
  • Fixed changing the auto-update channel in /config saving before a plugin's config.set hook was asked
  • macOS: Fixed a file count at session start that could reach other apps' data and raise the "access data from other apps" prompt when a session starts in the home folder or above it
  • Improved token counts behind a Claude apps gateway on Amazon Bedrock, which /context and large file reads use: the gateway now gets them from AWS's CountTokens API instead of a one-token model request. Grant bedrock:CountTokens to use it
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway to log a warning every 30 seconds while its PostgreSQL database is read-only, saying what fails and how to recover
  • Improved the status shown in Remote Control, claude.ai and the desktop app for a session waiting on a permission prompt to name an MCP tool by its server and readable name instead of its mcp__server__tool identifier
  • Improved background requests behind a Claude apps gateway to use Haiku 4.5 instead of the session's model, falling back to the session's model where the gateway does not serve Haiku 4.5
  • Improved how the Claude apps gateway handles models not listed under models: in Amazon Bedrock regions outside AWS's US geography. AWS always refused those requests; the gateway now tries the model in your own region, and a refusal names the model to add
  • Improved headless rate_limit_event usage-limit warnings to say whether the account has extra usage turned on
  • Improved the built-in plugin-authoring skill: it no longer tells a session with no terminal to run terminal commands, and explains sharing a mod only when asked
  • Improved Grep input handling: a search sent with grep's -l, -c or -r flag now runs instead of failing the call
  • Improved claude plugin validate and plugin loading: when a hooks module is refused over a rebound top-level var, the error now names the line that rebinds it, the cause, and a fix
  • Improved the Workflow tool's scriptPath refusal: it now says to pass the script inline via script, the route that works in sessions without a Read tool
  • Improved what Claude is told when a large file it sends fails to upload with no reason given, so it reports the failure instead of shrinking the file
  • Changed MCP tool descriptions the model loads through tool search to be cut at 16,384 characters instead of 2,048
  • Changed subagents to preload at most 32 skills from the skills field, each once; a subagent with the Skill tool can still invoke the rest
  • Changed Ctrl+C at the idle prompt of an attached background session to leave a pending /loop wakeup alone, so pressing it twice detaches and the loop keeps running; press Esc to stop it
  • Changed claude agents stopped with its background service (macOS, or Linux without the service installed): running sessions now stop in about a minute unless it is run again, and a notice says so
  • Changed claude.ai connectors to negotiate MCP protocol version 2026-07-28 by default on installs that fetch no flags; MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION=legacy opts out
  • Changed Artifact pages with no background of their own to show on white instead of off-white
  • Changed what Claude and you read when a mod denies a tool call after the tool ran: it now says the tool ran and a plugin withheld its result
  • Changed tab stops to count from where a text starts instead of from the screen's left edge: an answer indented by 2 has its first stop 8 cells in, where it was 6
  • Changed the Artifact tool's permission prompts with telemetry disabled to the same five questions other installs get, instead of asking before each read of someone else's artifact and each data edit
  • Changed scheduled and Run now routine runs in installs with telemetry disabled to publish new private artifacts, and update your own, without asking, as in other installs
  • Changed toasts from your organization's mods to show ahead of other mods' toasts instead of waiting behind them
  • Changed the Claude apps gateway to start with a warning and serve a desktop policy key its bundled Claude Desktop schema doesn't know, so new Desktop settings need no gateway upgrade
  • Changed WebSocket (ws) MCP servers: a message over 16 MiB is no longer parsed and closes the connection, the limit the other transports already have
  • [VSCode] Added a chat row for files Claude sends you: click a file's name to open it in the editor; Claude's caption shows underneath, and the row stays visible in Focus view
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Fork conversation from here" and Rewind's conversation restore failing with "Message not found in session" after a background agent's activity or one of the panel's own status lines
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+Shift+Tab, Cmd+Shift+Tab and Alt+Shift+Tab in the chat input also switching the permission mode, and Ctrl+Tab accepting the suggested prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed keyboard focus bouncing between two Claude views visible at once, which could send typed text to the wrong conversation
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the runner to stop passing CCR_AUTO_MODE_ALLOW, CCR_AUTO_MODE_ENVIRONMENT and CCR_AUTO_MODE_SOFT_DENY into a session's environment
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed git fetches being cut off while the git server was still reporting progress on a large repository; CLAUDE_RUNNER_FETCH_SERVER_PROGRESS_CAP_MS tunes or turns off the wait
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a message sent right after unarchiving a cloud session sometimes getting no reply because no container could start for it
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed some older routines starting their runs without ever giving Claude their saved prompt; those routines now run their prompt again
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved how quickly a cloud session catches up after its connection drops: activity you missed now appears all at once instead of row by row
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the setup script box in the cloud environment form: it starts taller, grows with your script, and can be resized by dragging
  • [Claude Tag] Changed the settings confirmation cards Claude posts in a Slack channel to stay open for 30 minutes instead of 10
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude's notice that a channel shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces uses organization defaults to post only when someone mentions Claude, at most once a month
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed channel links and @-mentions in a forked thread's "Continued from" card showing as raw Slack codes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Slack's Working status spinning on under a thread after @Claude !restart had already confirmed the restart
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed another app's or bot's @claude going unanswered in a busy channel where Claude had stopped reading untagged messages
  • [Claude Tag] Added a confirmation in Claude Tag admin settings before adding a channel manager moves that member to Custom roles, which can remove their other access
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review re-reviews saying no issues were found while earlier findings were still open; the comment now says how many remain open
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review still skipping a large CLAUDE.md's rules when the pull request edits that file
  • Fixed web searches and agent hook evaluations taking much longer at xhigh and max effort

items.title: Rally Up: ‘Gears of War: E-Day’ Launches on GeForce NOW
items.summary: Gears of War: E-Day leads the charge on GeForce NOW this week, bringing Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago’s first fight against the Locust Horde to the cloud with GeForce RTX-powered performance. A new way to join the action is also coming: Fire TV users will soon be able to purchase GeForce NOW memberships directly through […]
items.content:
Gears of War: E-Day leads the charge on GeForce NOW this week, bringing Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago’s first fight against the Locust Horde to the cloud with GeForce RTX-powered performance.

A new way to join the action is also coming: Fire TV users will soon be able to purchase GeForce NOW memberships directly through Amazon, creating a more seamless path from device setup to gameplay. Keep an eye out for availability in the coming weeks.

There’s more in store this GFN Thursday, with the cloud serving up 10 games, including seven new releases.

Emergence Day Is Here

Gears of War: E-Day is now streaming on GeForce NOW following its global release on Tuesday, Oct. 6. Set 14 years before the original Gears of War, the prequel follows Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago as they confront the terrifying arrival of the Locust Horde on Emergence Day.

The series’ brutal combat, desperate survival and larger-than-life action return with a new origin story for the legendary partnership. Ultimate members can take on the Horde with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud, plus technologies including NVIDIA DLSS and NVIDIA Reflex.

From campaign missions to cooperative and competitive modes, GeForce NOW keeps the fight ready across low-power laptops, Macs, mobile devices, handhelds, Firefox and other browsers, and more — no massive downloads or expensive gaming rig required.

New on the Cloud Menu

Members can look forward to the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:

  • Gears of War: E-Day (New release on Steam and Xbox, Oct. 6), available on Game Pass
  • STAR WARS: Galactic Racer (New release on Steam, Oct. 6)
  • Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival (New release on Steam, Oct. 8)
  • Forever Ago (New release on Steam, Oct. 8)
  • Order of the Sinking Star (New release on Steam, Oct. 8)
  • Silver Pines (New release on Steam, Oct. 8)
  • Permafrost (New release on Steam, Oct. 9)
  • Graveyard Keeper 2 (Steam)
  • Solasta II (Steam)
  • Tyr (Steam)

The Xbox version of Dune: Awakening didn’t join GeForce NOW in September as previously shared. Stay tuned to GFN Thursday for updates on game availability.

Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they are released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.

Gamers who want to test out high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a day pass to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more.

What’s on the play list this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

items.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
items.summary:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.


Speaker info:
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/soukaina-abelhad/

items.title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
items.summary:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.


Speaker info:
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevetjamison/

items.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
items.summary:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.


Speaker info:
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/michelegrantleadership/

items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.summary:
A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate.

When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval.

items.title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
items.summary:
Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation.

Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations, compare visits and make spatial evidence available to the people and systems that need it.

- https://www.linkedin.com/in/jordispranger/
- https://spranic.com/

items.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
items.summary:
A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings.

The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark.

items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.summary:
A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs.

Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error.

items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.summary:
More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers.

Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review.

items.title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual
items.summary:
“Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries.

The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming.

- https://www.linkedin.com/in/hackintoshrao/

items.title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
items.summary:
A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse.

An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers.

items.title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
items.summary:
A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work.

Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings.

items.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
items.summary:
Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU.

The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself.

items.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
items.summary:
An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve.

Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct.

- https://github.com/kmaida

items.title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
items.summary:
While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop.

Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment.

items.title: The Convention Gap: Beyond Literal Content in Human-AI Cooperation
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.11489v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Cooperative AI agents are often evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation is thought to rely on implicit conventions: shared rules for reading meaning beyond the literal message. We propose the convention gap as a diagnostic of such implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, where hints are the only messages about one's own hand, the convention gap is the failure probability predicted exactly from the literal content of the hints and the visible cards, minus the observed failure rate of the cards played. We prove that the population gap (the value the gap approaches over many games) is zero when the partner's choices convey nothing beyond their literal content, given a fair shuffle and a player who uses only what was said and seen. A nonzero population gap thus indicates that partner choices conveyed more; it does not measure how much. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in public human-human games (+46 pp on plays of cards that no hint had pointed to), +16.4 pp for human plays with AI partners, and -0.6 pp in AI-AI games we simulated among rule-based agents. With three AI agents of a published human-AI study, the literal failure probability of the cards humans played was similar across partners (38-41%), yet human failure ranged from 14.4% to 34.4% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2 pp, and the contrast between partners persisted within participants. Across five levels of Off-Belief Learning agents, trained so that the first level reads past actions only for their literal content and each higher level interprets more, the gap rose monotonically from +1.6 to +21.7 pp. These results argue for reporting the convention gap on human-partnered play, not only AI-AI performance, when evaluating agents intended for human partners.
items.author: Makoto Fukushima, Hua-Dong Xiong, Ehsan Moradi Pari

items.title: Two Birds One Stone: Effective Static Detection of Resource and Communication Deadlocks in Rust Programs
items.summary:
arXiv:2401.01114v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Although Rust claims to enable fearless concurrency, concurrency errors remain prevalent in practical applications, with deadlocks particularly prominent and harmful. Current static deadlock detection techniques either do not cater to Rust programs without incorporating Rust semantics or solely concentrate on resource deadlocks, disregarding communication deadlocks. In this paper, we present RcChecker, the first static detection method that simultaneously targets resource and communication deadlocks for Rust. At its core, RcChecker introduces the signal-lock graph to characterize the interactions between threads through lock variables and condition variables. The construction of the signal-lock graph involves utilizing flow-sensitive and context-sensitive analyses to track variable lifetime details and abstracting actions associated with condition variables into signal resource holdings and requests. By examining cycles within the signal-lock graph, we can effectively identify resource and communication deadlocks in a unified way. Compared to the existing Rust deadlock detection tool, RcChecker effectively eliminates eight resource deadlock false positives and detects seventeen errors that the existing tool fails to identify. Furthermore, RcChecker reports seven previously undiscovered issues in real-world Rust applications, including two resource deadlocks and five communication deadlocks.
items.author: Yu Zhang, Kaiwen Zhang, Guanjun Liu, Yuandao Cai, Shengchao Qin

items.title: Beyond Fault Localization: A Trajectory-Level Study of LLM Agents for Microservice Root Cause Analysis
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.21310v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated microservice root cause analysis (RCA) is usually evaluated by whether the final answer localizes the fault source. This is insufficient for on-call site reliability engineers (SREs), who need the evidence and reasoning behind the fault. Evaluating the process is hard because agent trajectories interleave free-form reasoning with heterogeneous tool calls and telemetry results, making it difficult to assess agents' behavior. To assess how well RCA agents ground diagnoses in evidence, we propose a trajectory-analysis methodology that characterizes evidence navigation and utilization, SRE-oriented diagnostic intent, and recurring failure modes. Our key insight is that fault-propagation paths give a causal reference for where agents investigate and how they use evidence. With it, we analyze 5,000 trajectories from ten framework-backbone configurations (nine agent frameworks, two backbone models) on RCABench. Correct localization can hide deficiencies in causal reconstruction. Successful investigations use retrieved evidence to guide later queries, consider broader diagnostic intents, and investigate more deeply. Failed investigations drift toward unrelated services or repeat shallow queries; recurring failures arise from omitted evidence, misinterpreted evidence, and unsupported reasoning. To test whether these patterns can guide improvement, we build a lightweight defense prototype targeting the three failure families. Across two held-out benchmarks, two backbone models, and six diagnostic frameworks, the failure patterns recur; the prototype reduces their prevalence and raises Acc@1 by 3.5-35.1 percentage points in every configuration, suggesting that the mined failures generalize and are actionable. Our findings motivate a process-level view of automated RCA, in which trajectories reveal whether a diagnosis is correct, well-grounded, and open to improvement.
items.author: Qisheng Lu, Aoyang Fang, Junjielong Xu, Jin'ao Shang, Songhan Zhang, Yifan Yang, Xiaochuan Yan, Pinjia He

items.title: Escaping the Self-Repair Trap: Improving Test Oracle Generation via Dual-Context Awareness
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.05917v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for regression-oracle completion, where a test prefix is given and the current program version is treated as expected behavior. Recent approaches increasingly rely on iterative self-repair and execution feedback, but optimizing execution success does not necessarily yield strong fault-revealing oracles. This objective, widely adopted in repair-based methods, serves only as a proxy and may be misaligned with the true goal of oracle generation. Such misalignment biases the repair process, giving rise to a feedback-driven degeneration that we term the Self-Repair Trap, where iterative repair progressively drives models toward assertions that are easier to satisfy but less effective at detecting faults. To address this issue, we propose DCAware, a computationally efficient, non-iterative framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding over multi-round repair. DCAware integrates structured static context with selectively retrieved dynamic states, enabling precise and robust oracle generation without iterative feedback loops. Extensive experiments based on execution and mutation testing show that DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success, outperforming prior methods with substantially lower computational cost. Our results suggest that improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity in the studied regression-oracle setting.
items.author: Kefan Li, Hongyue Yu, Yuan Yuan

items.title: Identity-Based Signing Shifts, Not Solves, Usability: Evidence from Five Identity-Based Signing Ecosystems
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.17133v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Identity-based software signing tools aim to make software artifact provenance verifiable while reducing the burden of long-lived key management. These tools are becoming critical infrastructure for secure software supply chains and are increasingly embedded in build, deployment, and release workflows. However, there is limited cross-tool, longitudinal evidence about which usability problems arise in practice and how reported concerns change over time. This gap matters because unusable signing and verification workflows can reduce adoption or lead to misconfiguration, undermining intended integrity guarantees.
  We conducted the first mining-software-repositories study of five identity-based signing ecosystems with public development repositories: Sigstore, OpenPubKey, HashiCorp Vault, Keyfactor, and Notary v2. We analyzed approximately 3,900 GitHub issue discussions from November 2021 to November 2025. We coded each issue for reported usability concerns and affected surfaces, comparing patterns across tools and over time. Across ecosystems, reported concerns are especially prominent around CLI tooling, policy/configuration, and verification workflows. Longitudinal Poisson trend analysis shows that reported issue counts decline substantially for several repositories, increase for OpenPubKey, and show no statistically detectable overall trend for the Keyfactor repositories, while trajectories vary across concern types. These results indicate that identity-based signing reduces direct key-management burdens while relocating complexity to policy configuration, verification, cross-component coordination, and workflow integration. Our findings motivate treating verification semantics, policy validation, cross-component observability, and deployment integration as first-class usability targets.
items.author: Kelechi G. Kalu, Hieu Tran, Santiago Torres-Arias, Sooyeon Jeong, James C. Davis

items.title: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13227v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. However, the security risks arising from such cross-session skill interactions remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. Successful attack chains cover all five target security consequence categories, highlighting the broad impact of these attacks. To mitigate these risks, we propose SkillRelayGuard, which restores artifact provenance context and provides pre-execution advisory review while leaving the final execution decision to the agent. Evaluation across three agent settings shows that SkillRelayGuard reduces overall ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0%, while increasing legitimate task completion from 79.6% to 87.5%.
items.author: Dianshu Liao, Shidong Pan, Guangdong Bai, Zhenchang Xing, Xiaoyu Sun

items.title: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13170v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, while only two of four evaluated LLMs outperform an all-pattern constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1; the best reaches 51.2%. Together, the limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM gains motivate detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.
items.author: Yuying Wang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Yi Guo (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Jiachi Chen (The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain,Data Security, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou High-Tech Zone), Hanwen Zhang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Yi Sun (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China)

items.title: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.
items.author: Rakesh Podder, Viktoria Koscinski, Indrajit Ray

items.title: Vulnerable Models in the AI Supply Chain: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Propagation, and Usage Patterns
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.12893v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has established a complex supply chain, but many of these shared artifacts harbor severe vulnerabilities such as insecure serialization and architectural backdoors. While prior efforts have extensively scanned model registries to flag malicious artifacts, a critical gap remains in understanding how developers actually adopt and integrate these unsafe models into downstream software systems. We bridge this gap by conducting a large-scale empirical study on the usage and propagation of 16,977 known vulnerable models on HuggingFace flagged by InsightDB. We track their prevalence across GitHub repositories, software packages, fine-tuning chains, and deployed applications. Our analysis reveals that, despite being publicly flagged, these vulnerable models appear in over 21,000 code locations across more than 5,000 open-source repositories, with 3,757 distinct flagged models (22.1\%) actively referenced in at least one project. To understand how these models are integrated in code and identify recurring usage patterns, we categorize and analyze the recurring patterns surrounding them via a customized pipeline that combines Code Property Graphs extraction with a tailored Frequent Subgraph Mining approach. Across all patterns, we find no evidence of provenance verification or model sanitization logic, with developers frequently bypassing security parameters or delegating trust to permissive framework defaults. These findings underscore that scanning model files alone is insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for context-aware security analysis and stricter integration guardrails at the application layer of the AI supply chain.
items.author: The Anh Nguyen, Triet Huynh Minh Le, M. Ali Babar

items.title: SoftwareGym: Scaling Computer-Use Agent Training with Diverse Synthesized Software Environments
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.12611v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet synthesizing diverse and reliable software environments at scale remains challenging. Native application environments require substantial construction and integration effort, which limits application coverage and increases the risk of application-specific overfitting. Browser-hosted environments provide limited interaction depth and workflow complexity. These limitations motivate SoftwareGym, an automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI software environments with diverse interfaces, executable functionality, and runtime-verified behavior. It generates structurally diverse designs, realizes them as runnable applications, and uses GUI evaluation with iterative repair to ensure functional reliability. Using SoftwareGym, we synthesize 182 applications across twelve categories and achieve a mean GUI task pass rate of 91.5%. We construct SoftwareGym-Bench, a 120-task evaluation suite spanning the same twelve categories, and use trajectories collected from these environments for CUA training. The resulting model improves Pass@3 from 41.39% to 56.97% on the strictly out-of-domain OSWorld benchmark and achieves 40.0% on SoftwareGym-Bench. These results demonstrate the potential of synthesized software environments as scalable and transferable supervision for CUA training.
items.author: Tian Jin, Wenhao Wang, Jing Kang, Haoting Shi, Rui Ye, Yijun Lu, Siheng Chen

items.title: MARGoS: A Configuration-Driven Platform for Reproducible MARL Experiments in ARGoS
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13772v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has become a prominent research direction, particularly within collective robotics, where the ARGoS simulator is widely used to study emergent swarm behavior. Yet despite this growth, systematic support for reuse and reproducibility in MARL-based swarm robotics remains limited and insufficiently standardized: a single experiment is assembled from manually aligned simulator files, training scripts, configuration values, paths, seeds, and environment details, so reuse and reproduction stay fragile even within one research group. To address this gap, we introduce MARGoS, a lightweight, configuration-driven platform developed in this project that elevates these experiment-defining inputs to first-class, platform-managed artifacts. MARGoS enables reproducible experimentation through configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, frozen (immutable) configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles that facilitate sharing, replay, and verification of results across machines and over time. A five-dimension evaluation (architecture, efficiency, reproducibility, usability, and collaboration) supports our claim that managing experiment variation as a platform responsibility makes ARGoS+MARL experiments easier to reuse, reproduce, and hand off. Our code is available at https://github.com/tombackert/margos.
items.author: Tom Philipp Backert, Mohammad D. Soorati, Javad Ghofrani

items.title: (When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off? Benchmarking Code Review Agents on Bug Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the advances of coding agents, software developers are spending more time reviewing code than writing code. As human review velocity falls behind agentic code generation, it is tempting to build automated review agents towards a future of "lights-off" software factory with little to no human supervision. To assess the practicality of such a fully autonomous software factory, we construct CRBugBench, a new benchmark that evaluates whether review agents detect human-verified bugs.
