Introducing the Anthropic Cyber Mission
items.summary:
Today we’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on. The Cyber Mission is a new effort to support defenders with tools, research, and resources to secure their software and systems. We’re starting with two areas:

  • Critical infrastructure: Starting with securing the operational technology behind power grids, water systems, and transportation networks, and protecting government systems. Today, we’re introducing the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program (CIDP), which brings frontier models, on-site engineers, and threat research to the defenders that protect operational technology.
  • Open-source software: Finding vulnerabilities and proposing patches in the free, shared code that most software depends on, and hardening the underlying code. Today, we’re launching OSS Scanner, which offers open-source projects regular security scans from our strongest models, for free.

Frontier models can be misused to exploit vulnerabilities and conduct cyber operations. Despite best efforts, many areas of technology remain dangerously exposed. State-sponsored adversaries have spent years gaining footholds in these systems, across many sectors, so that they can disrupt them. Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment. We are recognizing their expertise in these domains and offering our support. We will also expand the Cyber Mission to release tools, research, and resources in new areas to help secure the world.

As part of Project Glasswing, partners uncovered many vulnerabilities, but we haven’t yet achieved a sufficient reduction in cyber risk. It’s easier than ever to find vulnerabilities, but verifying, prioritizing, and fixing these findings remains challenging. Based on lessons from Project Glasswing, we’re starting these new efforts to support defenders. Earlier this week, we merged Project Glasswing into our expanded Cyber Verification Program, which gives many more defenders access to our most capable models. And through the Anthropic Cyber Mission, we’ll deploy Anthropic engineering talent and provide tools and funding for those who secure critical infrastructure and open-source software.

Defending critical infrastructure

Power grids, water utilities, factories, and transportation networks run on controllers, control software, and industrial networks built to last for decades. These systems are known as “operational technology,” and they often cannot be taken offline to patch, so known vulnerabilities can stay unresolved for years. Securing them is specialized work: the equipment is proprietary, changes are risky, and a mistake can take down a plant. Operators of every size rely on a small set of trusted providers to support that work, telling them what’s exposed and which fixes to make on a running system.

Today, we’re introducing the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, which brings frontier Claude models, on-site engineers, and our threat research to those trusted providers. Its founding partners are Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation.

These organizations represent the providers that operators rely on to secure these systems: the consulting and advanced technology companies that run security programs, the security companies that guard the business and industrial networks, and the manufacturers that build and patch the equipment itself.

This work is underway. Several partners are currently working with Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Critical infrastructure is hard to defend in many ways that AI cannot fix, but we believe that frontier models can help find and repair weaknesses before those weaknesses are used to cut off power or make water unsafe. Our first step is to work with a small cohort of providers to learn which strategies are most effective and practical.

If your company builds security products or services for critical infrastructure, you can register your interest here.

As AI continues to advance, it presents an important opportunity to strengthen cybersecurity across critical infrastructure, provided it is applied responsibly, validated rigorously, and deployed with safety and reliability at the forefront. We are pleased to contribute our operational technology and industrial cybersecurity expertise to help develop practical approaches for applying AI in ways that strengthen the resilience of the infrastructure society depends on every day.
Tony Baker
VP, Digital Trust & Chief Product Security Officer, Rockwell Automation
Through our work with critical infrastructure organizations, PwC’s cyber OT practice has seen firsthand the gravity of consequences cyber breaches can have in these environments. I firmly believe that a coordinated, industry-wide effort is necessary to identify vulnerabilities, mitigate risks, and strengthen the resilience of our critical systems.
Harshul Joshi
Partner, US OT/ICS Security Lead, Cyber Data and Tech Risk, PwC
Threat actors are using AI to find and exploit exposures at machine speed. By combining Unit 42 threat intelligence and operational expertise with Anthropic’s frontier models, we’re helping operators defend against adversaries looking to attack and disrupt essential services. Together, we are giving defenders the speed and precision needed to close attack paths before exposure becomes impact.
Sam Rubin
Senior Vice President, Unit 42, Palo Alto Networks
Frontier AI is evolving faster than any single organization can track alone. That’s why the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program matters. It brings together the people who understand these environments with the frontier capabilities now available to defend them. We’re proud to contribute our experience and to learn alongside the other partners working to protect the systems the world depends on.
Moreno Carullo
Co-Founder and CTO, Nozomi Networks
The sites that need protection most, like remote substations, offshore platforms, and air-gapped plants, are exactly where traditional tools can’t reach and specialists can’t be. What no one had solved was the hours: more data than any team can work through, at more sites than any team can staff. Claude closes that gap, so our analysts and our customers’ operators spend their time on the judgment calls that keep critical systems running safely.
Dan Gunter
CEO and Founder, Insane Cyber
Critical infrastructure and the people who depend on it benefit when the vendor community shares what they learn about the opportunities and challenges that AI presents to operational environments, rather than keeping that knowledge in silos. Joining Anthropic's Critical Infrastructure Defense Program is one of the ways we help align frontier AI to a collective defense strategy built around the realities of the operational technology (OT) that keeps the lights on, water safe, and transportation running.
Jon Lavender
Chief Technology Officer, Dragos
Critical infrastructure is where cyber risk becomes real-world risk. As adversaries use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale, critical infrastructure facing machine-speed threats requires machine-speed defense. By bringing CrowdStrike’s deep security context and expertise together with Anthropic’s frontier AI expertise, we can put a greater advantage in the hands of critical infrastructure defenders.
Daniel Bernard
Chief Business Officer, CrowdStrike
Amid the rapid evolution of AI and the increasing sophistication and speed of cyber threats, ensuring cybersecurity in OT environments that support social infrastructure has become one of the highest priorities facing society today. Through participation in this program, we look forward to collaborating with Anthropic and fellow partners to further enhance cyber resilience for critical infrastructure.
Hiroaki Koiwa
Head of Cyber CoE, AI & Software Services Business Unit, Hitachi, Ltd.
As AI accelerates, critical infrastructure operators need solutions that address security vulnerabilities at machine speed. Together with Anthropic, Deloitte is helping provide these enterprises with the enablement needed to close security gaps and strengthen resilience, moving at pace with the realities of frontier AI.
Adnan Amjad
US Cyber Leader, Deloitte & Touche LLP
Operational technology is the next frontier for autonomous AI-enabled attacks. The question is no longer whether AI can affect an industrial process, but how much control it can gain, and how quickly. The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program is convening the best of private-sector innovation and investment to strengthen OT and ICS resilience across federal and commercial missions.
Andrew Turner
President of Commercial Cyber, Booz Allen
Organizations that keep our power on, medicine safe, food supply secure, and communications running face some of the most consequential cyber risks in the world. Accenture is committed to bringing our deep OT security expertise to the organizations that protect the critical infrastructure communities depend on every day. This partnership will help put AI-powered defense in the hands of those who need it most.
Harpreet Sidhu
Global Cybersecurity Lead, Accenture

In June, we launched a cyber defense program for state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. Since then, we’ve offered frontier Claude models and technical support to more than half of all US states and some of the country’s largest public critical infrastructure operators, speeding up code scanning and patching, incident response, red teaming, and other security workflows.

We are listening to and learning from the people who know this landscape best. Our approach is to work with the companies, coalitions, governments, and nonprofits that know this landscape and that operators trust, and provide support where it’s most needed.

Securing open-source software

Almost all software relies on open-source code, much of it maintained by small teams of volunteers. Under Project Glasswing, we scanned hundreds of widely used open-source projects, had humans triage and review many of the potential vulnerabilities uncovered, and privately reported what we found to their maintainers through our coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Some maintainers with the capacity to triage at scale asked us for everything our models had found in their project, reviewed or not. In response, we’re launching OSS Scanner, an opt-in service inspired by Google’s OSS-Fuzz. Enrolled projects receive periodic scans from our most capable models, free of charge. Each report includes a proof of concept of how the bug could be exploited, an explanation, and a suggested fix where one is available. The reports are model-generated and sent without human review. That means maintainers receive them faster, but it also means that some will contain inaccuracies, such as a wrong severity rating. We expect a true-positive rate above 90%, and will work to improve the true positive rate and fix quality over time. The team’s post explains how it works and how to enroll.

The service is meant for projects with the capacity to keep up with surfaced findings. For others, we will continue to share human-verified disclosures under our CVD policy.

OSS Scanner is a first step. From here, our open-source work aims to:

  • Get findings to maintainers faster. Bring OSS Scanner to more projects while keeping human-verified disclosure for those that need it.
  • Accelerate fixes. Automate triage and patching, which are still mostly manual, for projects that want it.
  • Explore new secure architectures and coding practices. Research and share methods for hardening or rewriting code with projects that want to go further than patching.

We’ll do this based on guidance from open-source maintainers and foundations, and share what works so other projects can replicate it. We funded the organizations behind widely used open-source code, including the Python Software Foundation, Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation, and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as supporting Akrites and Gold Eagle, which collect and coordinate vulnerability reports from many sources to avoid overwhelming maintainers. The Defender Advantage Fund (0xDAF), which we launched in August, supports pilot programs in these areas and keeps OSS Scanner free.

Maintainers can also apply to Claude for Open Source for free Claude Max subscriptions, and to the Cyber Verification Program for expanded access to Claude’s cyber capabilities for defensive work.

Why we're doing this

Highly cyber-capable AI models are widely available to attackers now. But defensive tools—including our own—have not yet reached enough of the defenders who need them. OSS Scanner, our Cyber Verification Program, defensive products our partners build on our platform, and Claude Security are some of our efforts here, and we’ll be adding others as soon as possible.

Our forecast is that in two years, AI will favor defense: it will be easier to catch bugs before they ship, write fundamentally secure software from scratch, and actively defend systems with models. But in the near term, that may not be true. The cost of exploiting vulnerabilities has dropped, while verifying, disclosing, and fixing them is slow and still depends on people. In Glasswing, we often saw months pass between a vulnerability being found and being fixed. With operational technology, a fix may have to wait until it can be applied safely to running machinery—in some rare cases, this might take decades.

Success means critical infrastructure such as water, power, transport, and communications keep running in the face of attacks by capable adversaries, with fewer exploitable paths in and faster recovery when something gets through. This will take years and we expect the Anthropic Cyber Mission to change as we, together with the public and private sector, learn what works.

The path ahead

Over the coming months, we’ll bring the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program to more partners and more sectors, and we’ll share what we learn along the way, including what didn’t work. We also expect other AI developers, security companies, and governments to run efforts of their own, and we’d like to collaborate with them wherever that helps defenders.

We will also expand our work to help secure open source and the broader supply chain. This includes researching new ways of writing software and new ways of defending systems. We intend to share frontier research, tools, and resources to help others secure their software and supply chain.

If you’d like to work with us:

  • Companies that build security products or services for critical infrastructure, including security vendors, system integrators, and equipment manufacturers, can register their interest in the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program as we expand it.
  • Core maintainers of critical open-source projects can enroll in OSS Scanner.
  • Security teams of any size, including operators of critical infrastructure and open-source maintainers, can apply to our expanded Cyber Verification Program for access to our models.

items.title: Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
items.summary:
Anthropic is deepening its support for American scientific research by committing $150 million over three years to the Genesis Mission, a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI. The funding will go toward making Claude available to more than 15 agencies that are part of the mission, including NASA, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.

We first announced our partnership with the US Department of Energy (DOE) and the Genesis Mission last December. Since then, we have worked with DOE to bring Claude to scientists across the national laboratories. Today, we announced this new commitment as part of the Science: A New Golden Age Summit hosted by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in Washington, DC.

Supporting American scientists

We share the administration’s view, laid out in “Science: A New Golden Age,” that AI can have a profound and positive impact on scientific discovery, and we are glad to back its efforts to support American scientists.

Researchers at federal agencies and national laboratories work on some of the world’s most difficult scientific problems. Through our commitment, we aim to help them use Claude to meaningfully advance their work. Over the next three years, we will:

  • Provide Claude, Claude Code, and API credits to several hundred Genesis Mission research projects;
  • Partner closely with agencies and national laboratories on the administration’s top science priorities, including fusion energy and quantum computing; and
  • Provide training, onboarding, and technical support to scientists on Genesis Mission projects, and help agencies new to the Genesis Mission get their first projects running.

Accelerating scientific research

This commitment is part of our broader effort to support scientific research. Earlier this year we launched Claude Science, an AI workbench that integrates the tools and packages researchers most commonly use, and opened 10,000 free and discounted Claude seats for academic scientists. We also expanded our AI for Science program, which gives credits to researchers on high-impact projects, and kicked off a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard, a shared specification for AI agents to safely operate lab instruments. Our commitment to the Genesis Mission is our next step toward helping researchers everywhere.

items.title: 2026 Usage Policy update
items.summary:
Each year, Anthropic updates its Usage Policy in response to the evolving capabilities of our models, and the feedback we’ve received from our customers. We're publishing a new version of the policy today. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.

Most of the updates in the latest version are intended to clarify existing rules. In the year since our last refresh, Claude has taken on longer, more independent work. This update provides new examples that show how our rules apply to Claude’s new capabilities. It draws on new patterns of misuse in influence operations, weapons development, and surveillance that we’ve observed in the past year (as we’ve documented in our latest threat intelligence report). We’ve also made updates to clarify our requirements for high-risk use cases in areas like health and finance, to add controls for when Claude is used to autonomously take physical actions, and to address abusive behavior toward our models.

The updated policy takes effect on November 12. The full Usage Policy and Supported Regions Policy can be found on their respective pages.

A new section on deceptive activity

As we wrote about last month, we’ve seen examples of state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms using Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites. Our policy already prohibited this activity, but the restrictions were scattered across our elections, fraud, privacy, and disinformation sections.

We've consolidated those rules into a new section titled Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity, which applies to deceptive activity of any kind (whether political or commercial). It covers efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts, along with building the tools and infrastructure for running influence operation campaigns.

Refocusing our elections section

We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope.

For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections.

Clarifying our weapons prohibitions

Our Usage Policy has always prohibited using Claude to develop weapons. Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons. The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles. These changes reflect how we’ve enforced our previous policy.

More precise language on surveillance and law enforcement

Our September threat intelligence report documented the growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents. We’ve rewritten our surveillance and criminal justice section to state more precisely what we prohibit. For instance, tracking people without their consent is prohibited, whether it happens in real time or through analysis of previously collected data. Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance.

As with the previous update to our weapons prohibitions, this update does not reflect a change in what we enforce in practice: it is just intended to make our policy more explicit. The new section also spells out which uses remain permitted, including tracking that people have agreed to (such as fraud monitoring), content moderation, journalism, and legal research.

Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases

When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop” (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.

These requirements haven’t changed with the updated version of our Usage Policy. However, users have often asked us whether a given use case has these requirements, so we've rewritten our High-risk Use Case Requirements section to answer that more directly. It now lists which kinds of recommendations are covered and which are not.

Following the launch of our Model Hardware Standard, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected.

Addressing abusive behavior toward our models

We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.

This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism.

Clarifying our Supported Regions Policy

Last year, we updated our Supported Regions Policy to restrict access to Claude for companies who are majority-owned by entities headquartered in our unsupported regions. We've updated our Supported Regions page to clarify how we enforce this policy. Our policy prohibits the use of Claude by people who are physically located in an unsupported region, by entities who are incorporated or headquartered in one, and by entities who are majority-owned or controlled by persons or entities in those regions.

Looking ahead

We'll keep updating our Usage Policy as Claude’s capabilities and risks change. As with this and our prior updates, we’ll seek input from across Anthropic, and from policymakers, subject matter experts, civil society, and the people who use our products.

items.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: A 3,500-Line Lightweight Agentic RL Framework for Training Agents with Real Harnesses
items.summary:
Training AI agents with reinforcement learning can be challenging because their tools, context, and decision-making are managed by complex frameworks. Agent Lightning connects existing agents to RL training, making it easier to improve them without rebuilding them.

The post Agent Lightning v1.0: A 3,500-Line Lightweight Agentic RL Framework for Training Agents with Real Harnesses appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework.
  • Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code.
  • Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services.
  • Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset.

AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed.

To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab). Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline.

Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements:

  • Lightweight: the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend.
  • Training on a real agent harness: agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged.
  • Native Kubernetes support: agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale.
  • A complete coding agent training example: an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples.

The limits of traditional agentic RL

Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework.

Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent.

Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1).

Four challenges in training with real harnesses

A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges:

  • Retokenization and sample merging: Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample.
  • Advantage calculation: Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level.
  • Loss normalization: Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it.
  • Training backend scheduling: Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources.

PODCAST SERIES

The Shape of Things to Come

Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future.

Listen now
Opens in a new tab

Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code

In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2).

The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training.

Collocated async RL

Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs.

Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3).

Running agents on Kubernetes

Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible.

6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain

To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points.

The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5).

items.title: SeoulMMOD: A Large-Scale Multimodal Origin-Destination Flow Benchmark
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13730v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Origin-destination (OD) flow forecasting supports urban mobility decisions by predicting the volume and patterns of human movement across a city. Most existing public OD benchmarks provide only a partial view of citywide mobility, covering a single transport service or at most two modes. With partial mode coverage, observed demand changes are difficult to separate into shifts across transport modes and changes in total travel. We introduce SeoulMMOD, a large-scale public benchmark for citywide multimodal mobility in Seoul. SeoulMMOD provides three years of hourly OD flows estimating total mobility for 6 urban travel modes across 25 districts and 426 sub-districts, together with travel-time, travel-distance, calendar, rainfall, and point-of-interest (POI) signals. Using SeoulMMOD, we benchmark 14 forecasting baselines under a common protocol and analyse the effects of spatial scaling, joint versus mode-separate training, and cross-year generalization. Results show that several spatio-temporal models that work at district level do not scale to sub-district OD forecasting, and that naive joint multi-mode training does not consistently improve accuracy. Together, the dataset and benchmark establish a reproducible testbed for multi-mode, multi-year OD forecasting at the city scale.
items.author: Taeyoung Yu, Seonbin Jo, Jiwon Kim, Junyoung Byun

items.title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.
items.author: Aravind Reddy, Deeraj S K, Mohd Wasif Raza, Saurav Prakash

items.title: Towards Understanding the Training of GFlowNets: A Theoretical Perspective
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13711v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn policies that sample discrete objects in proportion to a positive reward. They are trained by minimizing balance objectives, whose exact satisfaction guarantees correct sampling. However, a comprehensive theory linking nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially under evolving sampling distributions and backward policies, is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we develop a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. We first bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss. Then, we show that approximate stationarity controls this distribution error up to a tangent-space residual measuring parameterization incompleteness. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling and fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions, with fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected loss is $O(\bar\epsilon^2+T^{-1})$ and expected terminal symmetric KL is $O(\bar\epsilon+T^{-1/2})$ under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize the sufficient update decay to approach the residual neighborhood and preserve these rates. These results connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy and clarify how parameterization, coverage, and moving components govern GFlowNet training.
items.author: Rui Hu, Yu Chen, Zhuoran Li, Longbo Huang

items.title: Transformer-based In-Context Score Operator Learning for Diffusion Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models typically learn the generative dynamics of a single target distribution or a family of distributions indexed by conditioning variables fixed during training. This limits their ability to adapt to a previously unseen distribution from only a small set of examples. We introduce an in-context solution operator learning framework for diffusion models, in which each target distribution is treated as a task drawn from a meta-distribution and is specified at inference time by an empirical context set. Our method learns an in-context score operator that maps the context samples, a noisy query point, and the diffusion time to the task-dependent score, enabling reverse-diffusion sampling on unseen tasks without retraining or parameter updates. A key observation is that the task-dependent score admits a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean representation. Its empirical Nadaraya--Watson approximation can be represented exactly by a model in our constructed transformer class, providing a principled foundation for the proposed query-dependent attention architecture. The operator is trained through amortized denoising score matching across task distributions. We establish generalization-error bounds that quantify the effects of the context size, the numbers of training tasks and within-task samples, model complexity, and intrinsic and ambient dimensions. Numerically, we evaluate the method on a range of scientific and visual datasets, including Navier-Stokes, ERA5 climate data, QuickDraw sketches, and Food-101. The results show that the proposed method performs well on relatively simple task families, while its performance degrades as task complexity increases, thereby illustrating both the promise and the limitations of in-context learning for diffusion models.
items.author: Wuzhe Xu, Zhaiming Shen, Yulong Lu, Wenjing Liao, Rongjie Lai

items.title: VQIL: Visible Quantum Interference Learning for Perturbation Response Ranking on Graphs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13689v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning how local perturbations affect a network is important for identifying which components drive or absorb a system's response. We formulate this as seed-conditioned response ranking: given a perturbation at one seed node, ranking all other nodes by response strength. This is challenging when the model is given only the interaction topology, while the mechanism governing how perturbations propagate must be learned from data. We present VQIL (Visible Quantum Interference Learning), a trainable Szegedy quantum walk for seed-conditioned ranking. Edge weights, link phases, and per-node phase rotations are optimized end-to-end by backpropagation while the walk operator remains unitary throughout training. Node scores are obtained from a geometrically discounted coherent sum of quantum-walk amplitudes, enabling quantum interference before the final squared-norm readout. Because each learned parameter is attached to a named edge or node, the trained model provides directly inspectable hypotheses about the roles of individual graph components in the propagation mechanism. On AC power-flow perturbations over six transmission grids, with electrical parameters withheld from the model, VQIL improves Spearman rank correlation from 0.147 for the untrained walk to 0.831 and outperforms an identically trained random-walk model. On gene perturbation over five protein-protein interaction networks with Perturb-seq supervision, VQIL improves rank correlation from 0.171 to 0.620, outperforming the strongest learned classical and neural baselines. These results show that trainable quantum-walk interference provides a scalable and interpretable inductive bias for learning seed-conditioned response rankings on graphs.
items.author: Seokjun Lee, Sergio A. Ortega, Daniel K. Park, Namshik Han

items.title: On the Encoding of Calendar Features in Covariate-Informed Time Series Foundation Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13676v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) increasingly offer covariate support, with calendar information being the most common type of categorical covariate in practice, as it is available for every point in time. However, how these features are encoded is largely treated as an implementation detail rather than as an object of study, despite encoding being one of the few design choices left for pretrained models at inference time. With the present study, we demonstrate that the way information is propagated into the model substantially affects forecast accuracy of TSFMs. Therefore, we systematically compare seven calendar encodings, including three conventional target-agnostic representations (ordinal, one-hot, and cyclic) and four target encodings, across four state-of-the-art TSFMs on nine datasets from multiple domains in a zero-shot rolling evaluation. The nine datasets are influenced by social activities, such as weekends and holidays, making calendar information particularly relevant for forecasting. We find that encoding choice affects forecast accuracy across all models, with MASE differences of up to 9.9 % on non-holidays and 83 % on holidays within a single model. Effectiveness and utilization vary substantially across models. Improvements are concentrated around holidays, where calendar information provides signals unavailable from target history, while some model encoding combinations also improve non-holiday forecasts. A SHAP-based attribution analysis locates the contribution of the covariates relative to the autoregressive component and explains why some model-encoding combinations degrade performance. Our findings suggest that current benchmarks for covariate-informed TSFMs can distort model comparisons by imposing fixed encoding strategies.
items.author: Alexander Kreusel, Maximilian Beichter, Alexandra Nikoltchovska, Benjamin Sch\"afer, Ralf Mikut, Frederik Zahn, Veit Hagenmeyer

items.title: TabReliBench: Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models Beyond Predictive Accuracy
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly popular for their strong predictive performance. Many also provide posterior predictive distributions (PPDs), whose reliability remains less studied. We assess reliability through point prediction, distributional quality, marginal and subgroup calibration, and interval efficiency. We then introduce TabReliBench, a large classification and regression benchmark for these comparisons and dataset-level analyses. We find that TFMs' rankings change between TabArena and our benchmark and across reliability metrics. Regression TFMs usually achieve near-nominal marginal coverage and retain narrow intervals, but this favorable marginal behavior does not imply valid conditional coverage. Dataset-level analyses show that classification difficulty often accompanies poor calibration, whereas regression predictive performance is not a reliable indicator of calibration. Ensembling improves predictive performance but does not consistently improve calibration of PPDs; TFMs also benefit little from conformal post-processing, which does not reliably resolve subgroup gaps. Reliable TFM selection therefore requires multidimensional evaluation beyond aggregate rankings. Code is available at https://github.com/Tianqi-Zhao/TabReliBench.
items.author: Tianqi Zhao, Jia Guo, Yan Shuo Tan, Qiong Zhang

items.title: PANDA: Prior-guided Attentional Dual-path Architecture
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13635v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hypergraph Neural Networks (HNNs), designed to model higher-order relations beyond pairwise interactions, typically rely either on fixed structural weights or on normalised attention. Fixed weights can propagate misleading information in heterophilic settings, while normalisation makes attention coefficients competitive, in the sense that, in a message-passing framework, increasing the weight of one sender must reduce the weight of others in the same aggregation set. Our main contribution is the introduction of PANDA (Prior-guided AttentioNal Dual-path Architecture), a plug-in for two-stage message passing HNNs applicable to both undirected and directed settings. The main path interpolates between learned receiver-normalised attention and structural incidence priors, while a non-competitive (not normalised) auxiliary path lets each sender contribute its own transformed information. We also show that, with fixed structural coefficients, PANDA recovers a certain complex-valued convolution operator adopted in previous works. Across four HNNs spanning spatial and spectral methods in both directed and undirected settings, plugging PANDA in yields an average improvement of 5.18 percentage points across eight real-world benchmark datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/jainris/panda.
items.author: Rishabh Jain, Federico Belotti, Stefano Coniglio, Pietro Lio, Stefano Fiorini

items.title: Private and Distributionally Robust Federated Multiclass Classification
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13631v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries requires multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data collected across geographically distributed client sites. Federated learning enables collaborative training without centralizing data, but most approaches do not provide formal privacy guarantees for individual records stored at client sites and can degrade under label noise. To address these limitations, we develop a differentially private, distributionally robust framework for federated multiclass classification that provides sample-level privacy for records stored at each client. We build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved using an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm. To protect the released client updates, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local distributionally robust variable before aggregation at the central server, and we quantify the cumulative privacy loss using the moments accountant. We provide per-round sample-level $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy guarantees and an overall composed privacy guarantee across all training rounds, together with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. Experiments on simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent baselines in most tested settings, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.
items.author: Andrea P. Hernandez, Michael Ibrahim, Nagi Gebraeel

items.title: A small cognitive core explains human behavior at scale
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Psychology has proposed many principles of cognition. Each, however, was developed in isolation, leaving their combined explanatory power unknown. We assembled a small set of established principles into one model, which we call COntextual Retrieval and Encoding (CORE). CORE consists of a hierarchy of episodic memories into which prediction errors are written and whose encoding, retrieval, and forgetting depend on context. Fitted jointly to 7,036,442 choices from 137 experiments, the model predicts human choices better than black-box models and reproduces 75% of reported behavioral effects when simulated. Moreover, its latent variables show classic signatures of Bayesian learning and event segmentation. Taken together, these findings suggest that a small cognitive core accounts for much of human behavior. They also open a path toward making psychology more than the sum of its parts, by building computational models on the entire experimental record.
items.author: Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz

items.title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13599v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diagnostic information in multi-view medical imaging studies, like echocardiography, is distributed across views, each capturing different aspects of cardiac structure and function. In clinical practice, these views are first interpreted through quantitative measurements, which then support specific diagnoses. However, existing echo representation learning methods do not explicitly model measurements as an intermediate representation between views and diagnosis. As a result, individual measurements are not explicitly represented in a form that downstream diagnostic tasks can selectively use, hindering accurate diagnosis.
  Inspired by this hierarchical clinical workflow, we introduce EchoTab, a measurement-grounded representation learning framework that represents multi-view echocardiography studies using measurement-specific tokens as an intermediate representation between echo views and diagnosis. Each measurement token selectively attends to the views relevant to its estimation and is trained through tabular reconstruction to predict the corresponding measurement value. The resulting tokens form a factorized echo representation, which encode clinically meaningful structural and functional properties and can be selectively used for downstream diagnosis. Unlike the commonly used contrastive approaches, EchoTab does not require negative samples or large batch sizes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that EchoTab learns effective measurement-grounded representations that improve diagnosis classification in multi-view echocardiography and its learned attention aligns with established measurement-view relationships used by cardiologists. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/michelleespranita/EchoTab.

items.title: RAG Needs a Map: Using GraphRAG to Retrieve Connected Context — Nyah Macklin, Neo4j
items.summary:
An agent answering questions about a course needs more than the five chunks closest to a query. It also needs the connections between lessons, concepts, and the sources behind its answer. Nyah Macklin builds that retrieval path with Neo4j, combining vector search with a knowledge graph that people can inspect and query. The workshop starts with the difference between semantic similarity and relationships, then walks through GraphAcademy, an Aura database, and a Python environment. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from course material, embeddings support similarity search, and Cypher exposes the resulting structure. Vectors remain part of the system; the graph adds connected context and a way to answer questions that require traversal or aggregation.

The hands on build moves from a knowledge graph pipeline to an agent in Aura. Macklin creates a vector index, configures a lesson search tool, adds a retrieval query that returns related graph data, and enables natural language questions through text to Cypher. The agent answers a question about temperature using course content and displays its sources. A lesson count prompts a closer check of the underlying database query, showing why visible evidence matters even after the pipeline works. The final code walkthrough covers chunking, entity types, relationship types, and a schema that guides extraction rather than leaving the model to invent the graph's structure.

items.title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
items.summary:
Ask a vector store for the PRs you merged last week and it can hand back one that is semantically perfect and three years old. Peter Werry builds context engines at Unblocked, and his thesis is that RAG, meaning similarity search, is only half of retrieval. Engineering context lives in pull requests, review comments, tickets, wikis, and chat, and all of it has structure: authors, dates, states, labels, relationships. Dumping it all in a vector store and reranking fails any question with a temporal or structural half. So the other half is turning natural language into a real database query, where the model does not answer the question, it writes the query. The workshop walks six stacked pull requests that turn a stubbed query playground into a working engine over a GitHub repository.

Four pieces make the query reliable. Schema discovery samples three hundred documents and merges them into one tree, with procedural code rather than a model inferring types and enums. Identity resolution maps Peter to his GitHub login with simple fuzzy matching. Query planning passes the schema, forces a name extraction tool call, and includes the current date. Validation is deny by default: an allow list of operators keeps a function clause from running JavaScript on the server, and hidden metadata fields are wiped and reinjected for tenant isolation. A retry loop feeds validation and execution errors back to the model, which exposes the need for full text search when exact match fails. The same engine then powers a chat agent, and the Q&A covers scaling schemas with summaries, continuous ingestion, why Slack holds the why questions, MCP, and hybrid search.

items.title: Introducing Falcon ASR
One Model Family, Two Gold-Level Results: Fine-Tuning Nemotron for IOI and IMO
$L_0$ Feature Selection via Monte Carlo Tree Search in High-Dimensional Financial Regression
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feature selection is a central problem in high-dimensional financial regression, where large numbers of engineered variables and strong correlations among predictors reduce model stability and interpretability. $L_1$ regularization (Lasso) is widely used for sparse regression, but its shrinkage can be restrictive when informative signals are spread across correlated variables. Exact sparse regression avoids this shrinkage but requires solving a combinatorial optimization problem that is computationally difficult and is typically fit to minimize in-sample rather than out-of-sample error. This paper presents a feature selection framework based on Monte Carlo Tree Search with Generalized Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation (GNRPA). Feature selection is formulated as a sequential decision process, and candidate subsets are scored by their out-of-sample validation performance rather than training error. The method also supports a lexicographic objective accounting for subset size and multicollinearity. We study this approach on a contemporaneous explanatory regression task: explaining the weekly return of the NASDAQ-100 index from 1,072 engineered features spanning market, macroeconomic, and factor data. This isolates the value of subset selection under multicollinearity from the separate problem of predictive forecasting. On this task, the proposed method identifies sparse feature subsets with higher out-of-sample explanatory power than an optimized Lasso baseline, reaching an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.6961 versus 0.6313 for Lasso. These results suggest that Monte Carlo Tree Search is a practical alternative to convex regularization for sparse explanatory feature selection in financial regression, with potential value for factor attribution and risk decomposition where transparency matters as much as out-of-sample fit.
items.author: Cameron Mouangue, Tristan Cazenave

items.title: Simultaneous Competitive and Regret Guarantees for TCP Acknowledgment
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study simultaneous competitive and regret guarantees for TCP acknowledgment. Each acknowledgment serves all pending packets, and the objective is to minimize the total acknowledgment and waiting costs. It is well known that no deterministic online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio better than $2$. Given $k$ randomized online experts and $0<\varepsilon<1$, we construct a randomized online algorithm whose realized total cost is always at most $(2+\varepsilon)$ times the offline optimal cost $\mathrm{OPT}$ and whose expected regret against the expert with the smallest realized cost is $O(\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}\log(k+1)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The algorithm requires no advance knowledge of the number of packets or $\mathrm{OPT}$. Our algorithm controls switching costs between experts and uses the gap between the permitted competitive bound and its current cost to determine when to learn. We also prove lower bounds showing that, for $k\ge 2$, this regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $\mathrm{OPT}$, $k$, and $\varepsilon$, and that $\varepsilon>0$ is necessary for sublinear regret.
items.author: Tsubasa Harada, Yasushi Kawase, Hanna Sumita

items.title: Rationally Linearized MLPs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Rationally Linearized Multilayer Perceptrons(RaLiMPs), a new approach to efficiently linearizing MLPs using low-degree rational approximations of standard activation functions. Inspired by polynomial-based MLP linearization, we show that rational approximations can provide accurate representations at substantially lower degree. RaLiMPs exploit these approximations to construct kernel representations with narrow bottlenecks, enabling efficient composition across MLP layers. We provide theoretical guarantees for the resulting approximation and evaluate RaLiMPs across applications ranging from implicit 3D models to large language models. Our experiments demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency tradeoffs, with RaLiMPs achieving competitive or improved accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost.
items.author: Arijit Sehanobish, Byeongchan Kim, Avinava Dubey, Min-hwan Oh, Krzysztof Choromanski

items.title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.
items.author: Frederik E. T. Sch\"oller

items.title: Simulating Training Spikes of Deep Neural Networks by Layer-wise Random Feature Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Intermittent ``spikes'' in loss, during the pre-training of Large Language Models (LLMs), remains a mysterious phenomenon both theoretically and empirically. In this paper, we show that simple quadratic models with heavy-tailed, power-law distributed inputs can replicate these spikes. We introduce a theoretical framework and simulation algorithm to model per-layer training dynamics of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), using such quadratic models. In a case study on an Adam hyperparameter configuration (where $\beta_2$ is set close to $1$) known to induce spikes in Transformer LMs, our simulation successfully predicts bumps indicating spiky behavior from a given checkpoint. Furthermore, we derive an appropriate $\beta_2$ schedule from observed metrics, which empirically improves performance.
items.author: Ran Tian, Courtney Paquette

items.title: FedPCD: Priority-Constrained Federated Aggregation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated learning (FL) seeks to optimize a shared global model from decentralized client data. While effective for average performance, this process can produce unfair performance across clients, particularly under statistically heterogeneous data distributions. Existing fairness-aware and multi-objective FL methods address this through client re-weighting, gradient correction, or common-descent formulations, but often change the global optimization direction or treat client objectives symmetrically. We propose FedPCD, a priority-constrained federated optimization framework that separates the global optimization objective from client protection. FedPCD preserves the conventional federated aggregate as the primary objective, while allowing only the minimum correction necessary to meet client performance constraints. Across heterogeneous FL benchmarks, FedPCD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest global accuracy across all configurations and leading worst-10% client accuracy in nearly all. FedPCD further preserves competitive trade-offs between global accuracy and client performance variability. Beyond this trade-off, FedPCD demonstrates faster empirical convergence, reaching matching or superior performance in substantially fewer communication rounds.
items.author: Yousef Irshaid, Dara Varam, Mohamed I. AlHajri

items.title: PPG-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for PPG Foundation Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is increasingly recorded by wearable and clinical devices at enormous scale, and a growing number of PPG foundation models (FMs) have been developed to compute reusable representations for various downstream tasks. These models are difficult to compare: different evaluations use different datasets, task definitions, preprocessing, downstream heads, hyperparameter tuning, and baselines. We present PPG-Bench, a unifying open-source benchmark evaluating five public PPG FMs across nine open-access datasets and 26 tasks spanning cardiovascular state estimation, activity, sleep, screening, and identification. We evaluate models under four downstream regimes of increasing adaptability (linear probing, random forests, frozen MLP probes, and end-to-end finetuning), with model-specific hyperparameter optimization and subject-disjoint cross-validation. We also evaluate against three controls: random/constant baseline, a deterministic pulse-rate-variability (PRV) feature set, and a generic time-series FM (MOMENT). Across all 68 task-regime combinations, 35.3% show no meaningful FM advantage over the random/constant baseline, and in 83.8% no PPG-specific FM outperforms both PRV and MOMENT. We also find that added downstream head capacity generally improves performance, but can cause significant degradation if the model is performing at chance/constant level. Current PPG FMs therefore cannot yet claim to provide generalised and transferrable representations of PPG signals, and future evaluation in this field should include checks against simple, non-learned controls. Code for the benchmark and instructions to evaluate more models can be found here - https://github.com/mannas-ai/ppg-bench.
items.author: Arvasu Kulkarni, Mahir Jain, Aditya Ray Mishra, Sandeep Singh, Siddharth Panwar

items.title: Accelerating Linear Bandits with Persistent Candidate Sets
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Exhaustive optimistic scoring can make action selection costly in linear bandits with a large fixed set of $K$ actions, requiring $\mathcal{O}(K)$ score evaluations per round. We introduce Persistent Candidate LinUCB (\textsc{PC-LinUCB}), which maintains $k$ active actions and samples $q$ challengers uniformly from the remaining $K-k$ actions at each round. By scoring only these $k+q$ candidates, \textsc{PC-LinUCB} reduces the number of score evaluations per round to $\mathcal{O}(k+q)$. We establish problem-independent and problem-dependent high-probability regret bounds consisting of a standard linear-bandit learning term and an additive discovery cost of order $\mathcal{O}\left((K-k)\log(K-k)/q\right)$ at fixed confidence. Notably, this additional cost does not grow with the horizon. For fixed gaps and sufficiently long horizons, we establish an $\Omega\left((K-k)/q\right)$ regret lower bound under uniform challenger sampling, showing that partial candidate access itself imposes an unavoidable regret cost. Experiments show that \textsc{PC-LinUCB} substantially accelerates LinUCB while maintaining comparable regret, and that the persistent candidate mechanism can extend beyond LinUCB.
items.author: Bingkui Tong, Daria Korovaitceva, Marina Sheshukova, Sergey Samsonov, Junpei Komiyama

items.title: Why Linear Models Can Still Work in a Complex and Changing World
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13404v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear models can predict well in complex domains even when underlying mechanisms are nonlinear. We argue that this can occur because the complexity of the world exceeds the complexity that can be learned reliably from finite, partially observed data. Flexible models can exploit curvature, thresholds, and interactions that fit one hospital, period, population, policy setting, or measurement process but fail elsewhere. When this instability lies mainly in the nonlinear component, omitting it can give linear models lower prediction error in a new environment. We connect this claim to work on simple linear rules, bias and variance, regularization, best linear prediction, measurement error, distribution shift, invariance, Rashomon sets, and underspecification. Proposition 1 gives a simple squared-error case in which a nonlinear rule learned in the training environment raises target error because it transfers too weakly; finite-sample estimation error can strengthen this result. Partial observation alone is not enough: the link between observed variables and unobserved factors must vary across environments. Stable nonlinear structure favors flexible models, and linear models remain vulnerable to linear spurious relationships. Model complexity should therefore be chosen by cross-environment stability as well as training-data accuracy.
items.author: Fangzhou Lin, Dengzhe Hou, Yinxing Li, Kazunori D Yamada

items.title: PlacePulse: Learning Transferable Place Representations from Structural Geographic Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13390v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geospatial machine learning often depends on task-specific feature engineering over large collections of sociodemographic, business, and environmental variables. Geospatial foundation models offer reusable representations of place, but leading approaches typically encode dynamic signals, such as mobility and search activity, or visual signals from satellite imagery. Few models represent the static structural composition of places (who lives and works there, which businesses operate there, and which risks they face) as transferable embeddings at fine spatial resolution. We introduce PlacePulse, a structural geospatial foundation model that compresses 572 attributes, expanded to 2,288 inputs through H3 neighborhood aggregates, into 256-dimensional unit-norm embeddings for 1,055,537 H3 resolution-7 cells in the United States. We also introduce a reusable two-axis benchmark that separates intrinsic representation quality from downstream predictive utility across multiple targets and spatial supports. Intrinsically, the embeddings reconstruct standardized inputs with mean $R^2 = 0.853$, use 251 of 256 approximately decorrelated dimensions, and show strong spatial organization, with Moran's $I = 0.93$ on the leading principal component and autocorrelation persisting beyond the input radius. Extrinsically, across 74 held-out targets from 12 external sources and four spatial supports, PlacePulse outperforms a dimensionality-matched feature-selection baseline on targets unrelated to the training inputs and is competitive with Google's Population Dynamics Foundation Model, leading on health, economic, election, economic-mobility and social-vulnerability outcomes, with relative strengths that vary by domain. These findings position structural composition as a distinct and complementary modality for geospatial foundation models, not simply a fallback where behavioral or imagery data are unavailable.
items.author: Luc\'ia Garc\'ia-Duarte, Miguel \'Alvarez, Diego Vicente, Javier P\'erez Trufero, Javier de la Torre

items.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nystr\"om-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.
items.author: Giordano Vitale, Giacomo Meanti, Marco Rando, Blanca Ayuso de Dios, Lorenzo Rosasco

items.title: Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13369v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.
items.author: Jiayang Gao, Tianyi Zheng, Jiayang Zou, Fengxiang Yang, Luyao Fan, Lv Tang, Bo Li, Jia Wang

items.title: Hidden Data Challenges in Clinical Machine Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13350v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Widely reused preprocessing pipelines for electronic health records can encode assumptions about when information became available, what clinical episode a label represents, and what missingness means. These assumptions are rarely audited systematically and may propagate across subsequent studies when preprocessing pipelines are reused or adapted. Using MIMIC-IV as a case study, we identify and quantify violations of three complementary forms of preprocessing alignment, i.e., temporal, semantic, and population alignment, which manifest as temporal leakage, feature-task misalignment, and biased imputation. We show how ambiguities in timestamp semantics, episode definitions, endpoint construction, modality selection, and missingness handling can alter the information available to a model and affect the interpretation of its predictions. Through analyses of MIMIC-IV data and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that such choices may remain largely invisible in aggregate predictive performance while changing the signals on which models rely. We derive practical recommendations for temporally valid, clinically aligned, and reproducible preprocessing of MIMIC-IV and related electronic health record datasets. The code for our experiments, including our proposed preprocessing, is available at: https://github.com/m2l-lab/mimic-iv-preprocess.
items.author: Carolin Ciss\'ee, Dennis Fast, Raneen Younis, Alexander L\"oser, Wolfgang Nejdl, Zahra Ahmadi

items.title: Understanding Mamba-3 Through Oscillatory Dynamics
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mamba-3 introduces input-dependent rotations into recurrent state updates, but their contribution beyond state retention remains unclear. We interpret these ro- tations as underdamped second-order dynamics, providing a framework for in- vestigating the role of oscillation in sequence modeling. Controlled comparisons show that underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping regimes on state-tracking tasks, while language-model pretraining demonstrates benefits for long-context prediction and length generalization. Interventions in pretrained models further establish the importance of learned phase, and state analysis sug- gests that rotation regulates how retained information combines with incoming up- dates. Taken together, these findings identify underdamped dynamics as a useful mechanism for recurrent computation and suggest that oscillation supports long- context processing by regulating how information accumulates.
items.author: Shutian Liang, Yue Song

items.title: AgentTune: A Unified Training Lifecycle for Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.13335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source-available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool-using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two-tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing.
